uni-llb-criminal-procedure-bnss.title: Criminal Procedure under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
uni-llb-criminal-procedure-bnss.description: Criminal procedure under the BNSS 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024): criminal courts, FIR and investigation, arrest and its safeguards, bail, charge and trials, judgments, appeals, revision, inherent powers, maintenance and plea bargaining. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB / BA LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Foundations: scheme, definitions and criminal courts
courses.summary: Why procedure matters, the scheme of the BNSS, key definitions (cognizable, bailable, summons-case, warrant-case, complaint), the hierarchy of criminal courts and the functionaries of criminal justice.
outcomes: Explain the purpose and structure of the BNSS
Classify offences as cognizable/non-cognizable and bailable/non-bailable
Describe the hierarchy and sentencing powers of criminal courts
Identify roles of police, prosecutor, defence and court

lessons.title: Purpose and scheme of the BNSS

scenes.text: A burglary is reported at midnight. By morning police have visited, recorded statements and seized footage.
Every step – from report to final judgment – is governed by procedural law.

steps.title: Substantive vs procedural
steps.body: The BNS says what is an offence and its punishment; the BNSS says how offences are investigated, tried and punished. Procedure implements fair trial under Article 21 – Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) held that procedure depriving liberty must be just, fair and reasonable.

steps.title: The new code
steps.body: The BNSS replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 from 1 July 2024. It has 531 sections. Notable features: timelines for investigation and judgment, use of audio-video electronic means for recording, summons and trial, zero FIR and e-FIR, mandatory forensic team visits for serious offences, trial in absentia of proclaimed offenders in specified cases.

steps.title: Stages of a criminal case
steps.body:
1. Information/FIR
2. Investigation (arrest, search, seizure, statements)
3. Police report (charge-sheet) or closure
4. Cognizance by Magistrate
5. Commitment (sessions cases)
6. Charge framing
7. Trial – prosecution evidence, accused's examination, defence evidence, arguments
8. Judgment and sentence
9. Appeal/revision

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing investigation (police) with inquiry and trial (court)
- Forgetting that procedural law can apply to pending proceedings subject to saving clauses

activity.prompt: Arrange the stages of a sessions case

quiz.q: The BNSS replaced
quiz.why: The BNSS replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

quiz.q: Maneka Gandhi held that procedure must be
quiz.why: The Court read Article 21 to require fair, just and reasonable procedure.

quiz.q: Number of sections in the BNSS
quiz.why: The BNSS contains 531 sections.

lessons.title: Key definitions and classification of offences

scenes.text: A neighbour hurls insults at Meena; another neighbour steals her bicycle.
The police register one matter immediately but send her to the Magistrate for the other. Why?

steps.title: Cognizable and non-cognizable
steps.body: A **cognizable offence** is one in which a police officer may arrest without warrant under the First Schedule or any other law. In a **non-cognizable** offence the police cannot arrest without warrant and cannot investigate without a Magistrate's order. Serious offences (murder, theft, rape) are cognizable; minor ones (simple defamation, many insults) are non-cognizable.

steps.title: Bailable and non-bailable
steps.body: A **bailable** offence is shown as bailable in the First Schedule or made bailable by law; bail is a matter of right. Other offences are **non-bailable**; bail is at the court's discretion.

steps.title: Cases and complaint
steps.body:
- **Warrant-case**: relating to an offence punishable with death, life or imprisonment exceeding two years.
- **Summons-case**: any case that is not a warrant-case.
- **Complaint**: allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate with a view to action, not including a police report.
- **Inquiry**: every inquiry other than a trial by a Magistrate or Court.
- **Investigation**: proceedings for collection of evidence by police or a person authorised by a Magistrate.

steps.title: Classify
steps.body:
1. Offence with 3 years maximum → warrant-case.
2. Offence with 1 year maximum → summons-case.
3. Theft → cognizable, and depending on schedule non-bailable.
4. Defamation → non-cognizable, bailable, complaint case.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a police report is a complaint
- Using 'two years or more' – a warrant-case needs imprisonment exceeding two years

activity.prompt: Tick the statements that are correct
items: Police may arrest without warrant in cognizable offences
A warrant-case involves an offence punishable with imprisonment exceeding two years
A police report is not a complaint
Bail is a right in bailable offences

quiz.q: An offence punishable with 2 years exactly is a
quiz.why: Warrant-cases need imprisonment exceeding two years, so exactly two years is a summons-case.

quiz.q: In a non-cognizable case police can investigate
quiz.why: Police need the Magistrate's order to investigate non-cognizable offences.

quiz.q: Bail in a bailable offence is
quiz.why: An accused in a bailable offence is entitled to bail.

lessons.title: Hierarchy and powers of criminal courts

scenes.text: A murder case and a small theft case are both filed in the same district.
They end up before different courts. How is that decided?

steps.title: Classes of courts
steps.body: Besides High Courts and courts under other laws, the BNSS provides: (1) Courts of Session, (2) Judicial Magistrates of the first class, (3) Judicial Magistrates of the second class, and (4) Executive Magistrates. The BNSS dropped the separate category of Metropolitan Magistrates found in the CrPC, and abolished the Assistant Sessions Judge post as a distinct class (check your syllabus notes).

steps.title: Sentencing powers
steps.body:
- High Court: any sentence authorised by law.
- Sessions Judge / Additional Sessions Judge: any sentence authorised by law; a death sentence is subject to confirmation by the High Court.
- Chief Judicial Magistrate: any sentence except death, life or imprisonment exceeding seven years.
- Magistrate first class: imprisonment up to three years, fine up to fifty thousand rupees, or community service.
- Magistrate second class: imprisonment up to one year, fine up to ten thousand rupees, or community service.

steps.title: Which court tries?
steps.body: The First Schedule, column for 'triable by', decides: murder – Court of Session; most theft – any Magistrate. The Magistrate commits sessions-triable cases to the Court of Session.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the old CrPC fine limits (₹10,000 / ₹5,000) – the BNSS raised them
- Forgetting that death sentences need High Court confirmation

activity.prompt: Order courts from highest to lowest sentencing power

quiz.q: Max imprisonment a CJM may impose
quiz.why: A CJM may pass any sentence except death, life or imprisonment exceeding seven years.

quiz.q: A death sentence by a Sessions Court requires
quiz.why: The BNSS requires the High Court to confirm a death sentence before execution.

quiz.q: Fine limit for a Magistrate first class under BNSS
quiz.why: The BNSS raised the first class Magistrate's fine limit to fifty thousand rupees.

lessons.title: Functionaries: police, prosecutors, defence and victims

scenes.text: In court, a Public Prosecutor conducts the case against the accused, while a legal-aid lawyer defends him.
The victim's family asks whether they can appoint their own lawyer.

steps.title: Prosecutors
steps.body: Public Prosecutors and Additional Public Prosecutors conduct cases in High Courts and Sessions Courts; Assistant Public Prosecutors in Magistrates' courts. The BNSS provides a Directorate of Prosecution in each State. A prosecutor is an officer of the court who must be fair, not merely seek conviction.

steps.title: Victim's rights
steps.body: A 'victim' includes the guardian or legal heir. The victim may engage an advocate to assist the prosecution, has rights to information on investigation progress in specified cases, and can appeal against acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence or inadequate compensation (proviso to the appeal provisions).

steps.title: Accused's rights
steps.body:
- Right to consult a legal practitioner of choice (Article 22(1))
- Free legal aid when unable to afford (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979; Legal Services Authorities Act 1987)
- Right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3))
- Right to a speedy trial as part of Article 21

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a victim's lawyer can independently conduct the prosecution in sessions cases – he assists under the prosecutor's direction
- Forgetting legal aid is a constitutional right

activity.prompt: Tick constitutional rights of an accused
items: Consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice
Not to be compelled to be a witness against himself

quiz.why: The case recognised speedy trial and free legal aid as part of Article 21.

quiz.q: In Magistrates' courts the State is usually represented by
quiz.why: Assistant Public Prosecutors conduct prosecutions in Magistrates' courts.

quiz.q: Can a victim appeal against acquittal?
options: Yes, under the proviso to the appeal provision
quiz.why: The law gives the victim a right to appeal against acquittal, lesser conviction or inadequate compensation.

questions.why: Article 20(3) protects an accused from being compelled to be a witness against himself.

courses.title: Unit 2 · FIR, investigation and arrest
courses.summary: Information in cognizable cases (section 173) including zero FIR, e-FIR and preliminary enquiry; investigation powers, statements and confessions to Magistrates; search and seizure with videography; arrest and the rights of arrested persons; remand and the police report.
outcomes: Explain the FIR procedure under section 173 and remedies when police refuse
Apply the Lalita Kumari principles
State the safeguards on arrest under sections 35 onward and D.K. Basu
Explain remand under section 187 and default bail timelines
Describe the contents and timing of the police report under section 193

lessons.title: Lab: Drafting and registering an FIR (section 173)

scenes.text: Ritu is robbed on a train passing through another district. She goes to the nearest police station at the next stop.
The duty officer says 'not our jurisdiction'. What does the BNSS require?

steps.title: Section 173 – information in cognizable cases
steps.body: Every information relating to a cognizable offence, **irrespective of the area where the offence is committed**, may be given orally or by electronic communication to the officer in charge of a police station. Oral information is reduced to writing and read over; electronic information must be signed by the informant within three days to be taken on record. A copy is given free to the informant or victim. This codifies the **zero FIR** and **e-FIR**.

steps.title: Preliminary enquiry
steps.body: For cognizable offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, the officer may, with permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, conduct a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists, or proceed with investigation directly.

steps.title: Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP (2014)
steps.body: Registration of FIR is mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence; no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a case except in categories like matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption and cases with abnormal delay. The BNSS now gives a statutory preliminary enquiry for the 3–7 year band.

steps.title: If police refuse
steps.body:
1. Send the substance in writing to the Superintendent of Police, who may investigate or direct investigation.
2. Then apply to the Magistrate under section 175(3) to order investigation – the BNSS requires an affidavit and that the Magistrate may make an inquiry and consider the officer's submissions.
3. Or file a private complaint.

steps.title: Sample FIR content
steps.body: Informant details; date, time and place; description of offence; accused (known/unknown); property stolen; witnesses; reasons for delay if any; signature. Police enter it in the book and assign the FIR number and sections.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Refusing to register for want of territorial jurisdiction – a zero FIR must be registered and transferred
- Treating the FIR as substantive evidence – it is used to corroborate or contradict the informant

activity.prompt: Order Ritu's remedies if the police refuse to register
items: Give information to the officer in charge (zero FIR)
On refusal, send written substance to the Superintendent of Police
Apply to the Magistrate under section 175(3) with an affidavit
Alternatively file a private complaint before the Magistrate

quiz.q: Zero FIR means
options: FIR registered regardless of where the offence occurred
quiz.why: Section 173 allows information to be registered irrespective of the area of offence.

quiz.q: An e-FIR must be signed by the informant within
quiz.why: Electronic information is taken on record once signed within three days.

quiz.q: Preliminary enquiry under section 173(3) applies to offences punishable with
options: 3 years or more but less than 7
quiz.why: The BNSS allows a 14-day preliminary enquiry for the 3–7 year band with DSP permission.

quiz.q: Lalita Kumari held FIR registration is
options: Mandatory if a cognizable offence is disclosed
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench made registration mandatory where information discloses a cognizable offence.

lessons.title: Investigation: statements, search, seizure and forensics

scenes.text: Police search a godown for stolen phones and record the whole search on a mobile phone.
For a separate stabbing case, a forensic team visits the scene.

steps.title: Examination of witnesses (section 180)
steps.body: The investigating officer may examine orally any person acquainted with the facts; statements may be recorded by audio-video electronic means. Such statements are not signed (section 181 bars signature) and can only be used to contradict the witness at trial, not as substantive evidence.

steps.title: Confessions and statements before a Magistrate (section 183)
steps.body: A Magistrate may record a confession or statement during investigation, after warning the accused that he is not bound to confess and that it may be used against him, and being satisfied it is voluntary. The statement may also be recorded by audio-video electronic means in the presence of the advocate of the accused. In cases of certain sexual offences, the victim's statement is recorded by a Magistrate, by a woman Magistrate as far as practicable.

steps.title: Search and seizure (section 185 and 105)
steps.body: Search must be in the presence of independent witnesses where required. Section 105 mandates that search and seizure, including preparation of the list of seized items, be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably a mobile phone, and forwarded without delay to the Magistrate.

steps.title: Forensics (section 176(3))
steps.body: For every offence punishable with seven years or more, the officer in charge shall cause a forensics expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence and video-record the process.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a police statement under section 180 as substantive evidence
- Forgetting the 7-year threshold for mandatory forensic visits

activity.prompt: Tick the safeguards before a Magistrate records a confession
items: Explain the accused is not bound to confess
Warn it may be used as evidence against him
Question him to be satisfied it is voluntary
Record and sign the memorandum of voluntariness

quiz.q: Statements recorded by police under section 180 can be used
quiz.why: Police statements are used only for contradiction under the evidence law.

quiz.q: Videography of search and seizure is mandated by section
quiz.why: Section 105 requires audio-video recording of search and seizure.

quiz.q: Forensic team visit is mandatory for offences punishable with
quiz.why: Section 176(3) applies to offences punishable with seven years or more.

lessons.title: Arrest and rights of arrested persons

scenes.text: Police arrive at night to arrest a man named in a cheating FIR where the offence carries up to seven years.
His lawyer asks: was arrest necessary, or should a notice have been issued?

steps.title: Section 35 – arrest without warrant
steps.body: A police officer may arrest without warrant, among others, a person who commits a cognizable offence in his presence; or against whom a reasonable complaint/credible information exists for an offence punishable with up to seven years, if the officer has reason to believe the person committed it and arrest is necessary – to prevent further offences, for proper investigation, to prevent tampering with evidence, to prevent inducement of witnesses, or to secure presence in court – recording reasons in writing. Otherwise, a **notice of appearance** is issued.

steps.title: Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar (2014)
steps.body: Police must not arrest automatically in offences punishable up to seven years; they must satisfy themselves of the necessity under the checklist, and Magistrates must scrutinise it before authorising detention. The BNSS further requires permission of an officer not below DSP to arrest a person accused of an offence punishable with less than three years if he is infirm or above sixty years.

steps.title: Rights of arrested persons
steps.body:
- Be informed of grounds of arrest and right to bail (Article 22(1); section 47)
- Arrest memo attested by a witness; information to a relative or friend (section 48)
- Meet an advocate during interrogation, though not throughout
- Be produced before a Magistrate within **24 hours**, excluding journey time (Article 22(2); section 58)
- Medical examination
- Designated police officer in every district and police station to display arrest information
- Women arrested only by or in the presence of women officers, and ordinarily not after sunset and before sunrise except with prior permission of a Magistrate

steps.title: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1997)
steps.body: Laid down guidelines: police to wear clear identification; arrest memo; informing a relative; medical exams every 48 hours; copies to Magistrate; police control room display. Many are now statutory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting travel time within the 24 hours
- Treating arrest as mandatory in every cognizable offence

activity.prompt: Tick what the officer must do on arresting the man
items: Inform him of the grounds and right to bail
Prepare an arrest memo attested by a witness
Inform a nominated relative or friend
Produce him before a Magistrate within 24 hours
Record reasons for necessity of arrest

quiz.q: Arnesh Kumar concerns arrests in offences punishable up to
quiz.why: The Court restricted automatic arrests for offences punishable up to seven years.

quiz.q: Production before a Magistrate must occur within
quiz.why: Article 22(2) and the BNSS require production within twenty-four hours, excluding journey time.

quiz.q: Instead of arrest where it is unnecessary, police issue a
quiz.why: The BNSS provides for a notice of appearance when arrest is not required.

lessons.title: Remand, default bail and the police report

scenes.text: An accused of cheating (max 7 years) has been in custody for 61 days and no charge-sheet has been filed.
His lawyer files for 'default bail'.

steps.title: Section 187 – procedure when investigation cannot be completed in 24 hours
steps.body: The Magistrate may authorise detention, in police custody up to **fifteen days in total**, which may be taken in whole or in parts at any time during the initial 40 days (offences up to 10 years) or 60 days (offences punishable with death, life or 10 years and more) of the detention period. Total detention cannot exceed **90 days** (death, life or imprisonment not less than 10 years) or **60 days** (other offences).

steps.title: Default bail computation
steps.body: Cheating under section 318(4) BNS carries up to 7 years → 60-day limit. If arrested and first remanded on 1 March, the 60th day falls on 29 April (March 31 days: days 1–31 = 1–31 March; days 32–60 = 1–29 April). If no police report is filed by then and the accused applies and is prepared to furnish bail, he has an indefeasible right to bail (Uday Mohanlal Acharya, 2001; Bikramjit Singh, 2020).

steps.title: Section 193 – police report
steps.body: On completion of investigation, the officer forwards the police report (charge-sheet or final report) to the Magistrate. Investigation of certain sexual offences against children and women must be completed within two months of recording information. The report states the sequence of custody of electronic devices and informs the victim of progress within 90 days. Further investigation after the report requires the court's permission and is to be completed within 90 days unless extended.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating 15 days police custody as only the first 15 days – the BNSS allows it in parts within the initial window
- Forgetting that default bail must be applied for before the charge-sheet is filed

activity.prompt: Order events leading to default bail
items: Accused arrested and produced before Magistrate
Statutory 60/90-day period expires without police report
Accused applies and offers to furnish bail

quiz.q: Max total detention during investigation for an offence punishable with 7 years
quiz.why: For offences other than those punishable with death, life or 10+ years, the limit is 60 days.

quiz.q: Maximum police custody overall under section 187
quiz.why: Police custody cannot exceed fifteen days in total.

quiz.q: Default bail right is lost if
options: Charge-sheet is filed before the accused applies
quiz.why: The indefeasible right must be availed before the police report is filed.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Bail and bonds
courses.summary: Concept of bail; bail in bailable and non-bailable offences; anticipatory bail; special powers of the High Court and Court of Session; maximum detention of undertrials; cancellation of bail and the guiding case law.
outcomes: Explain 'bail is the rule, jail the exception'
Apply the factors for bail in non-bailable offences
State the conditions and limits of anticipatory bail
Compute eligibility for release of undertrials under section 479

lessons.title: Concept of bail; bail in bailable offences

scenes.text: A student arrested for a minor bailable offence cannot afford the surety amount demanded.
Is the police officer right to keep him in custody?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Bail is release of an accused from custody on a bond, with or without sureties, to appear when required. The BNSS defines bail, bail bond (undertaking with sureties) and bond (personal undertaking without sureties). State of Rajasthan v Balchand (1977): 'basic rule is bail, not jail'.

steps.title: Bailable offences (section 478)
steps.body: A person accused of a bailable offence shall be released on bail when he is prepared to give bail; the officer or court may, if he is indigent and cannot furnish surety, discharge him on executing a bond without sureties. A person unable to give bail within a week of arrest is presumed indigent.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: The student must be released; if he cannot furnish surety within a week, he is presumed indigent and released on a personal bond. Excessive bail is prohibited.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating bail in bailable offences as discretionary
- Fixing bail amounts beyond the accused's means

activity.prompt: Tick the correct statements on bail in bailable offences
items: Indigent persons may be released on a bond without sureties
Inability to furnish bail within a week raises a presumption of indigence
Excessive bail must not be required

quiz.q: In a bailable offence, bail is
quiz.why: The law mandates release when the accused is prepared to give bail.

quiz.q: 'Bail, not jail' is associated with
quiz.why: Krishna Iyer J's dictum in State of Rajasthan v Balchand.

quiz.q: Presumption of indigence arises after
quiz.why: The BNSS presumes indigence if bail cannot be given within a week of arrest.

scenes.text: An accused in a robbery case seeks bail. The prosecutor fears he will threaten witnesses.
How does the court weigh liberty against investigation?

steps.title: Section 480 – Magistrate
steps.body: A Magistrate may release an accused of a non-bailable offence, but shall not if there are reasonable grounds to believe he is guilty of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, or if he has previous convictions for serious offences – with exceptions for a child, a woman, a sick or infirm person. Identification by witnesses alone is not a ground to refuse bail.

steps.title: Section 483 – High Court and Court of Session
steps.body: They have wider powers to grant bail in any case, impose conditions, and set aside or modify conditions imposed by a Magistrate; notice to the Public Prosecutor is required for offences triable exclusively by the Court of Session or punishable with life, and the informant or victim has a right of hearing in specified sexual offences.

steps.title: Factors (Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v Ashis Chatterjee, 2010)
steps.body:
1. Prima facie case
2. Nature and gravity of accusation
3. Severity of punishment
4. Danger of absconding
5. Character and standing of the accused
6. Likelihood of repetition
7. Reasonable apprehension of witnesses being influenced
8. Danger of justice being thwarted

steps.title: Satender Kumar Antil v CBI (2022)
steps.body: The Supreme Court categorised offences, gave guidelines for bail, urged a separate Bail Act, and stressed compliance with Arnesh Kumar and timely disposal of bail applications.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating gravity of the offence as the only factor
- Imposing conditions unrelated to securing presence or protecting investigation

activity.prompt: Tick factors the court weighs for bail in non-bailable cases

quiz.q: Bail in non-bailable offences by a Magistrate is under
quiz.why: Section 480 BNSS replaces CrPC 437.

quiz.q: Wider bail powers of High Court and Sessions Court are in
quiz.why: Section 483 BNSS replaces CrPC 439.

quiz.q: A Magistrate may grant bail despite the bar to
options: A child, woman, sick or infirm person
quiz.why: The proviso relaxes the bar for these categories.

scenes.text: A businessman learns a rival has filed a complaint alleging criminal breach of trust and fears arrest.
Can he seek protection before any arrest?

steps.title: Section 482
steps.body: When a person has reason to believe he may be arrested on accusation of a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or Court of Session for a direction that in the event of arrest he shall be released on bail. Conditions may include availability for interrogation, not inducing witnesses, not leaving India without permission.

steps.title: Key cases
steps.body:
- Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v State of Punjab (1980): wide discretion; no inflexible rules; 'reason to believe' must be based on reasonable grounds.
- Sushila Aggarwal v State (NCT of Delhi) (2020): anticipatory bail need not be limited in time and may continue till the end of trial, though courts can impose time limits in appropriate cases.

steps.title: Exclusions
steps.body: Anticipatory bail is not available for offences such as rape of a woman under 16 or 12 and gang rape of women under 18, per the provision. Special laws (e.g. SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act) may also exclude it.

steps.title: Practice tip
steps.body: An application should state the FIR/complaint details, apprehension of arrest with reasons, antecedents, and undertaking to cooperate.

activity.prompt: Order the anticipatory bail process
items: Accused forms reasonable apprehension of arrest
Applies to Sessions Court or High Court
Court hears prosecution and considers factors
If arrested, police release him on bail as directed

quiz.q: Anticipatory bail is granted by
options: High Court or Court of Session
quiz.why: Only the High Court or Court of Session can grant anticipatory bail.

quiz.q: Sushila Aggarwal held anticipatory bail
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench held it can last till trial ends unless limited.

quiz.q: Anticipatory bail is under BNSS section
quiz.why: Section 482 BNSS replaces CrPC 438.

lessons.title: Lab: Undertrial detention limits and cancellation of bail

scenes.text: A first-time accused charged with an offence carrying maximum 10 years has been in jail as an undertrial for over 3 years 4 months.
Is he entitled to release?

steps.title: Section 479 – maximum period of detention
steps.body: An undertrial who has undergone detention for up to **one-half** of the maximum imprisonment for the offence (not punishable with death or life) shall be released on bail. A **first-time offender** shall be released on bond after undergoing **one-third** of the maximum. Not applicable to offences punishable with death or life, or where the person has more than one pending case in multiple offences. The jail superintendent must apply to the court.

steps.title: Worked computation
steps.body: Maximum 10 years. First-time offender: one-third = 10 × 12 / 3 = 40 months = **3 years 4 months**. So he becomes entitled once he completes 3 years 4 months. A repeat offender would need one-half = 5 years.

steps.title: Cancellation of bail
steps.body: Bail may be cancelled for supervening circumstances such as tampering with evidence, threatening witnesses, absconding or violating conditions (Dolat Ram v State of Haryana, 1995: cancellation needs cogent and overwhelming circumstances, differing from rejection).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

courses.title: Unit 4 · Cognizance, charge and trials
courses.summary: Complaints to Magistrates and cognizance; the charge and joinder; sessions, warrant, summons and summary trials; examination of the accused; trial in absentia; judgment timelines and the bar on double jeopardy.
outcomes: Explain cognizance on complaint and police report
Draft and test a charge for defects

scenes.text: After police refuse to act on a non-cognizable defamation, Rahul files a complaint before the Magistrate.
The Magistrate examines him on oath before deciding whether to summon the accused.

steps.title: Cognizance
steps.body: Cognizance means the Magistrate applying his mind to the offence for taking further action. A Magistrate may take cognizance (a) upon a complaint, (b) upon a police report, or (c) upon information from any other person or his own knowledge. Cognizance is of the offence, not the offender.

steps.title: Examination of complainant
steps.body: On a complaint, the Magistrate examines the complainant and witnesses on oath. The BNSS adds that no cognizance shall be taken without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard – a pre-cognizance hearing in complaint cases.

steps.title: Dismissal or process
steps.body: The Magistrate may postpone issue of process and inquire or direct investigation (mandatory if accused resides beyond his jurisdiction). He dismisses the complaint if there is no sufficient ground, or issues summons (summons-case) or warrant/summons (warrant-case).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating cognizance with issuing summons – they are distinct stages
- Forgetting that certain offences (e.g. defamation, offences against marriage) need a complaint by the aggrieved person

activity.prompt: Order the steps in a complaint case
items: Complainant and witnesses examined on oath
Accused given opportunity of being heard

quiz.why: Cognizance concerns the offence; the offender is identified later.

scenes.text: A charge reads: 'You committed cheating sometime in 2024'.
Defence argues the accused cannot know what case to meet.

steps.title: Contents of a charge
steps.body: Every charge states the offence, its specific name if any, the law and section, the particulars of time, place and person (and the thing) as are reasonably sufficient to give notice. It must be in the language of the court. In criminal breach of trust or misappropriation of money, the gross sum over a period up to one year may be specified.

steps.title: Joinder
steps.body: Basic rule: for every distinct offence, a separate charge and separate trial. Exceptions: up to **three** offences of the same kind within twelve months; offences in the same transaction; offences falling within more than one definition; joint trial of persons accused of the same offence or in the same transaction.

steps.title: Effect of errors
steps.body: No finding or sentence is invalid merely for error, omission or irregularity in the charge unless a failure of justice has been occasioned (Willie Slaney v State of MP, 1955). The court may alter or add to a charge before judgment.

steps.title: Correct draft
steps.body: 'That you, on or about 12 March 2025, at Shop No. 4, MG Road, Pune, dishonestly induced Ms. A to deliver ₹2,00,000 by falsely representing that you held stock of 50 laptops, and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, within the cognizance of this Court.'

steps.title: Timelines
steps.body: In sessions cases the accused may apply for discharge within sixty days of commitment; the judge shall frame the charge within sixty days from the first hearing on charge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Omitting the section
- Joining four similar offences in one trial – only three within twelve months are allowed

scenes.text: In one building: a murder trial, a cheating trial, a petty assault case and a small theft dealt with summarily.
Each follows a different procedure.

steps.title: Sessions trial
steps.body: Prosecutor opens case → discharge or charge → plea → prosecution evidence → examination of accused → defence evidence → arguments → judgment. Conducted by the Public Prosecutor.

steps.title: Warrant trial
steps.body: (a) On police report: documents supplied, discharge if groundless, else charge, evidence. (b) Otherwise than on police report: pre-charge evidence, then charge, and the accused may recall witnesses for cross-examination.

steps.title: Summons trial
steps.body: No formal charge; particulars of the offence are stated to the accused and plea recorded. Simpler procedure. Can be converted to warrant trial in offences over six months if the Magistrate thinks fit.

steps.title: Summary trial
steps.body: For offences like theft where property value is up to ₹20,000 (raised under BNSS), receiving stolen property, house-trespass, insult to provoke breach of peace, and offences not punishable with death, life or imprisonment exceeding two years. Sentence of imprisonment cannot exceed three months. Under the BNSS, summary trial is mandatory for some of these offences, and for others (up to three years) the Magistrate may try summarily after hearing.

steps.title: Examination of the accused and trial in absentia
steps.body: The court personally questions the accused to explain incriminating circumstances in evidence (section 351, formerly 313); answers are not on oath. Trial in absentia of a proclaimed offender who absconds to evade trial is allowed with safeguards after 90 days of framing of charge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Framing a formal charge in summons trials
- Imposing more than three months in a summary trial

scenes.text: Arguments concluded in January; months later no judgment had been delivered.
The BNSS now sets a timeline.

steps.title: Judgment timeline
steps.body: In a trial before a Court of Session, the judgment shall be pronounced as soon as possible and within **thirty days** from completion of arguments, extendable to **forty-five days** for specific reasons recorded. The judgment states points for determination, the decision and reasons, the offence and section, and the punishment.

steps.title: Sentencing and probation
steps.body: After conviction, the judge hears the accused on sentence. Courts may release on probation of good conduct or after admonition in suitable cases (also under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958). The court may order compensation to victims, and victim compensation schemes operate in every State.

steps.title: Double jeopardy
steps.body: Article 20(2): no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. The BNSS bars retrial of a person once convicted or acquitted for the same offence, or on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge might have been made (autrefois acquit / autrefois convict). Maqbool Hussain v State of Bombay (1953): departmental proceedings are not prosecution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying double jeopardy to departmental inquiries
- Skipping the hearing on sentence

courses.title: Unit 5 · Appeals, revision, inherent powers, maintenance and plea bargaining
courses.summary: Post-trial remedies – appeals and revision; the High Court's inherent powers and quashing; maintenance of wives, children and parents; plea bargaining; and preventive measures for public order.
outcomes: Identify the appellate forum and limits on appeal
Distinguish appeal from revision
Apply Bhajan Lal categories for quashing under section 528
Determine eligibility for maintenance under section 144
Explain the plea bargaining procedure

scenes.text: An accused pleads guilty before a Sessions Court and is sentenced. Later he wants to appeal.
Can he appeal a conviction on his own plea?

steps.title: No appeal except as provided
steps.body: No appeal lies from any judgment or order of a criminal court except as provided by the BNSS or another law. Key routes: from Magistrate → Court of Session; from Sessions Court → High Court; from High Court → Supreme Court (Article 134, and by special leave under Article 136).

steps.title: No appeal in certain cases
steps.body:
- No appeal where the accused pleaded guilty and was convicted on that plea, except as to extent or legality of sentence
- No appeal in petty cases, e.g. High Court sentence of imprisonment up to three months or fine up to the specified amount, Sessions Court up to three months, and summary trial sentences of fine only within limits

steps.title: Appeal against acquittal and by victim
steps.body: The State may appeal against acquittal with leave of the High Court. The victim may appeal against acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence or inadequate compensation, to the court which hears appeals against conviction.

steps.title: Revision
steps.body: The High Court and Sessions Judge may call for records of inferior courts to satisfy themselves about correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order and regularity of proceedings. Revision is discretionary; no revision against interlocutory orders. A revisional court cannot convert an acquittal into conviction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating revision as a second appeal
- Forgetting the bar on appeal after a guilty plea

activity.prompt: Tick correct statements about appeals and revision
items: Appeal is a statutory right, not inherent

quiz.why: Appeals from Magistrates ordinarily go to the Court of Session.

quiz.q: Revision lies against interlocutory orders
quiz.why: The revision power does not extend to interlocutory orders.

quiz.q: A conviction on a guilty plea can be appealed
options: Only as to extent or legality of sentence
quiz.why: The law limits appeal after a guilty plea to the sentence.

lessons.title: Inherent powers of the High Court (section 528)

scenes.text: After a property dispute, a relative files an FIR alleging cheating with no facts showing deception.
The accused approaches the High Court to quash it.

steps.title: Section 528
steps.body: Nothing in the Sanhita limits or affects the inherent powers of the High Court to make orders necessary to give effect to any order under the Sanhita, to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. (Formerly CrPC section 482.)

steps.title: State of Haryana v Bhajan Lal (1992) – categories for quashing
steps.body:
1. Allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offence
2. FIR does not disclose a cognizable offence justifying investigation
3. Uncontroverted allegations and evidence do not disclose an offence
4. Allegations constitute only a non-cognizable offence and no Magistrate's order
5. Allegations so absurd and inherently improbable
6. Express legal bar on proceedings
7. Proceedings manifestly mala fide or for ulterior motive

steps.title: Quashing on settlement
steps.body: Gian Singh v State of Punjab (2012): High Court may quash non-compoundable offences on settlement in predominantly civil or private disputes (commercial, matrimonial), but not heinous offences like murder, rape or offences against society. Narinder Singh v State of Punjab (2014) gave further guidelines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using inherent powers where a specific remedy exists
- Conducting a mini-trial on disputed facts at the quashing stage

items: Read the FIR and charge-sheet at face value

quiz.why: It lists categories where the High Court may quash proceedings.

quiz.q: Settlement-based quashing is generally not allowed for
quiz.why: Heinous offences affecting society cannot be quashed on private compromise.

scenes.text: Sunita and her 4-year-old daughter are thrown out by her husband who earns ₹60,000 a month.
She files for maintenance before the Magistrate.

steps.title: Who can claim
steps.body: A person having sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain: (a) his wife unable to maintain herself, (b) his legitimate or illegitimate minor child, (c) his legitimate or illegitimate adult child (not a married daughter) with physical or mental abnormality, (d) his father or mother unable to maintain themselves. 'Wife' includes a divorced wife not remarried. The order may be for monthly allowance, interim maintenance and expenses of proceedings.

steps.title: Key cases
steps.body:
- Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985): the provision is secular and applies to Muslim women.
- Danial Latifi v Union of India (2001): the 1986 Act requires a reasonable and fair provision within iddat for the future.
- Mohd. Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (2024): a divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under the secular provision.
- Rajnesh v Neha (2020): guidelines on affidavits of assets and liabilities; maintenance from date of application.

steps.title: Wife not entitled
steps.body: If living in adultery, if refusing without sufficient reason to live with her husband, or if living separately by mutual consent.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Husband's net income ₹60,000/month; dependants: wife and daughter, no other income. Courts often use about 25% of the husband's net income as a benchmark for the wife (Kalyan Dey Chowdhury v Rita Dey Chowdhury, 2017). 25% × 60,000 = ₹15,000 for the wife, plus a separate amount for the child based on needs – not a fixed rule.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the 25% figure as a statutory rule
- Forgetting parents and adult disabled children can claim

lessons.title: Plea bargaining and public order measures

scenes.text: An accused in a cheating case with a 7-year maximum wishes to compensate the victim and accept a lighter sentence.
Plea bargaining offers a structured route.

steps.title: Scope
steps.body: Plea bargaining applies to offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years, except offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country or committed against a woman or a child below fourteen. The accused must not have been previously convicted of the same offence. Under the BNSS the application must be filed within thirty days of framing of charge.

steps.title: Sentencing
steps.body: If a minimum punishment is prescribed, the court may sentence to half of the minimum. Otherwise, one-fourth of the punishment provided or extendable. For a first-time offender, the BNSS allows one-fourth of the minimum or one-sixth of the maximum as the case may be. Compensation to the victim is part of the disposition. The judgment is final, subject only to Article 32/136/226/227 remedies.

steps.title: Computation
steps.body: Offence max 7 years, no minimum, not first-time: one-fourth = 7 × 12 / 4 = 21 months. If a first-time offender: one-sixth of 7 years = 14 months.

steps.title: Public order
steps.body: Section 163 (formerly CrPC 144): an Executive Magistrate may issue an order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger, effective up to two months, extendable by the State Government up to six months. Security for keeping the peace and for good behaviour may also be ordered.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing plea bargaining for offences against women
- Thinking the order under section 163 is permanent

scenes.text: Your senior asks you to draft a bail application for a client in judicial custody for 40 days in a theft case.
Use the standard structure.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
1. Cause title: court, case number, FIR number, police station, sections
2. Parties: applicant/accused v State
3. Brief facts and date of arrest
4. Grounds: no prima facie case, nature of evidence, recovery already made, investigation complete or nearly so, no criminal antecedents, roots in society, period of custody, parity with co-accused, health/family
5. Undertakings: will cooperate, not tamper with evidence, appear on every date
6. Prayer
7. Verification and affidavit

steps.title: Sample ground
steps.body: 'That the applicant has been in judicial custody since 15.01.2026; the alleged stolen property has already been recovered; no further custodial interrogation is required; the applicant is a permanent resident with no antecedents and is ready to abide by any conditions imposed by this Hon'ble Court.'

uni-llb-drafting-pleading-conveyancing.title: Drafting, Pleading & Conveyancing
uni-llb-drafting-pleading-conveyancing.description: General principles of legal drafting, civil pleadings under the CPC, criminal pleadings under the BNSS 2023, writ petitions, appeals, affidavits, legal notices and conveyancing deeds, with hands-on drafting labs. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes. Drafts are teaching models, not legal advice.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Principles of Drafting and Pleadings
courses.summary: Plain-language drafting, structure and interpretation rules, the fundamental rules of pleading under Order VI CPC, particulars, verification, amendment of pleadings and legal notices including section 80 CPC and section 138 NI Act notices.
outcomes: Apply plain-language and precision rules to legal drafts
State the four fundamental rules of pleading
Draft verification and affidavit clauses correctly
Draft a section 80 CPC notice and a cheque-dishonour demand notice within time limits

scenes.text: A lease said the tenant would pay 'rent and maintenance of ₹10,000 per month'. Was ₹10,000 the total or only maintenance?
The dispute took three years. Clear drafting would have avoided it.

steps.title: Rules of good drafting
steps.body:
1. Know the facts and the law before writing.
2. **Plain language**: short sentences, active voice, everyday words ('before' not 'prior to').
3. **Precision**: one term = one meaning; define terms and use them consistently.
4. **Structure**: logical order, numbered paragraphs, headings.
5. Avoid ambiguity: 'and/or', vague pronouns, undefined time ('within a reasonable time' when a date is possible).
6. Use 'shall' for obligations, 'may' for discretion, 'must' for conditions.
7. Numbers in words and figures for amounts (₹10,000 (Rupees ten thousand only)).
8. Check against the statute's formal requirements (stamp, signatures, witnesses, registration).

steps.title: Redraft
steps.body:
Bad: 'The tenant shall pay rent and maintenance of ₹10,000 per month.'
Good: 'The Tenant shall pay (a) monthly rent of ₹8,000 (Rupees eight thousand only) and (b) monthly maintenance charges of ₹2,000 (Rupees two thousand only), totalling ₹10,000 (Rupees ten thousand only), on or before the 5th day of each calendar month.'

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body: Who must do what, by when, where, how much, and what happens if not done?

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using 'shall' and 'will' interchangeably. Use 'shall' consistently for duties.

quiz.why: Plain language prefers simple everyday words that carry the same meaning.

options: Avoid disputes and alteration about amounts
quiz.why: Words and figures together reduce ambiguity and tampering.

quiz.why: Consistent drafting uses 'shall' for mandatory duties and 'may' for permissions.

lessons.title: Fundamental rules of pleading (Order VI CPC)

scenes.text: A junior's draft plaint quotes ten witnesses' statements and argues case law at length.
The senior cuts it to two pages. Why?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: 'Pleading' means plaint or written statement (O. VI R. 1). Rule 2(1): every pleading shall contain, and contain only, a statement in a concise form of the **material facts** on which the party relies, but **not the evidence** by which they are to be proved. Rule 2(2)–(3): divided into numbered paragraphs, each containing as nearly as may be a separate allegation; dates, sums and numbers in figures and words.

steps.title: Four fundamental rules
steps.body:
1. Plead **facts**, not law (conclusions of law are not to be pleaded – but legal pleas like limitation may be raised).
2. Plead **material facts** only (facts necessary to constitute the cause of action or defence – Udhav Singh v Madhav Rao Scindia, 1977).
3. Plead facts, **not evidence**.
4. State facts **concisely** but with precision.
Other rules: particulars of misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, wilful default or undue influence must be stated (R. 4); conditions precedent implied unless contested (R. 6); no departure from earlier pleading without amendment (R. 7); presumptions of law need not be pleaded (R. 13); signed by party and pleader (R. 14); **verification** (R. 15) – stating which paragraphs are true to knowledge and which on information believed true, with an **affidavit** in support (2002).

steps.title: Amendment (O. VI R. 17)
steps.body: Court may allow amendment at any stage to determine the real questions; after trial commences, only if despite due diligence the party could not have raised the matter earlier (proviso, 2002). Revajeetu Builders v Narayanaswamy (2009): factors – necessity for real controversy, no injustice to other side, bona fides, limitation, nature of amendment.

steps.title: Verification model
steps.body: 'Verification: I, A.B., the plaintiff above named, do hereby verify that the contents of paragraphs 1 to 8 are true to my personal knowledge and those of paragraphs 9 to 11 are based on information received and believed to be true, and paragraph 12 is based on legal advice. Verified at Pune on this 10th day of March, 2026.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Pleading 'the defendant committed fraud' without particulars. Order VI Rule 4 requires dates, items and the specific acts constituting fraud.

activity.prompt: Belongs in a pleading?

items.text: Defendant agreed on 1 June 2025 to deliver 100 tonnes of steel
Defendant failed to deliver by 30 June 2025
Three pages discussing Supreme Court judgments

quiz.q: Order VI Rule 2 requires a pleading to contain
options: Only material facts, concisely, not evidence
quiz.why: Rule 2(1) limits pleadings to concise material facts without the evidence.

quiz.q: Particulars of fraud must be given under
quiz.why: Rule 4 requires full particulars where fraud, misrepresentation or undue influence is alleged.

quiz.q: After trial commences, amendment is allowed only if
options: Despite due diligence the matter could not be raised earlier
quiz.why: The 2002 proviso to Order VI Rule 17 restricts post-trial amendments to that situation.

lessons.title: Lab: Draft a section 80 CPC notice

scenes.text: A contractor's bills of ₹12 lakh for building a school have been unpaid by the State PWD for a year.
Before suing the State, the law requires a notice.

steps.title: Section 80 CPC
steps.body: No suit against the Government or a public officer (for acts in official capacity) shall be instituted until **two months** after notice in writing has been delivered stating the cause of action, name, description and place of residence of the plaintiff, and the relief claimed. Addressed: Union – Secretary to the Government; State – Secretary to the State Government or Collector of the district. Section 80(2): suit for urgent or immediate relief may be filed without notice with leave of court, but no relief granted without giving the Government a reasonable opportunity to respond.

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
'NOTICE UNDER SECTION 80 OF THE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE, 1908
To: The Secretary, Public Works Department, Government of Maharashtra, Mantralaya, Mumbai.
From: M/s ABC Builders, through its proprietor, 12 Station Road, Nashik.
1. Under Work Order No. PWD/NSK/221 dated 1 April 2024, our client constructed the Government School building at Sinnar, completed on 31 December 2024 and taken over on 15 January 2025.
2. Running and final bills totalling ₹12,00,000 (Rupees twelve lakh only) were submitted on 20 January 2025 and certified by the Executive Engineer on 10 February 2025.
3. Despite reminders dated 10 April and 10 July 2025, no payment has been made.
4. Our client calls upon you to pay ₹12,00,000 with interest at 9% per annum from 10 February 2025 within two months of receipt of this notice, failing which our client will file a suit for recovery with interest and costs, at your risk as to costs.
Place: Nashik. Date: 1 March 2026. Advocate for the claimant.'

steps.title: Proof
steps.body: Send by registered post AD/speed post and keep tracking proof; file a copy with the plaint showing compliance.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Filing the suit before two months expire. Without leave under s. 80(2), the plaint may be returned/rejected.

quiz.why: Section 80(1)(c) specifies a Secretary to that Government or the Collector of the district.

quiz.why: Section 80(2) allows filing with leave for urgent or immediate relief.

lessons.title: Lab: Cheque dishonour demand notice (s. 138 NI Act)

scenes.text: Ravi's cheque for ₹3,50,000 from a buyer bounced on 5 March 2026 with the memo 'Funds insufficient'; he received the memo on 7 March.
What are his deadlines?

steps.title: Section 138 ingredients
steps.body:
1. Cheque drawn for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability.
2. Presented within its validity (3 months as per RBI rules).
3. Returned unpaid for insufficiency of funds or exceeding arrangement.
4. Payee sends a written **demand notice within 30 days** of receipt of information of dishonour.
5. Drawer fails to pay within **15 days** of receipt of notice.
6. Complaint filed within **one month** after the cause of action arises (s. 142(1)(b)), before a Magistrate where the payee's bank branch is (s. 142(2)).
Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. Interim compensation up to 20% (s. 143A).

steps.title: Worked dates
steps.body: Memo received 7 March 2026 → notice by 6 April 2026 (30 days). Notice delivered 12 March 2026 → 15 days end 27 March 2026. Cause of action arises 28 March 2026 → complaint by 27 April 2026.

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
'LEGAL NOTICE UNDER SECTION 138 OF THE NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT, 1881
To: Mr S.K., 45 MG Road, Indore.
Under instructions from my client Mr Ravi Sharma: 1. You issued cheque No. 004512 dated 1 March 2026 for ₹3,50,000 (Rupees three lakh fifty thousand only) drawn on XYZ Bank, Indore, towards price of goods supplied under invoice No. 77 dated 10 February 2026. 2. The cheque, presented on 4 March 2026, was returned unpaid on 5 March 2026 with the remark "Funds insufficient", intimated to my client on 7 March 2026. 3. I call upon you to pay ₹3,50,000 within 15 days of receipt of this notice, failing which my client shall initiate proceedings under sections 138 and 142, at your risk as to costs.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Demanding amounts other than the cheque amount (like interest) without separating them; the demand must clearly be for the cheque amount (Suman Sethi v Ajay K. Churiwal, 2000).

quiz.why: The notice must be sent within 30 days of receiving the information, i.e. by about 1 July 2026.

quiz.q: Maximum fine under section 138
quiz.why: The court may impose fine up to twice the cheque amount, or imprisonment up to two years, or both.

quiz.q: Interim compensation under section 143A can be up to
quiz.why: Section 143A, added in 2018, allows interim compensation not exceeding 20% of the cheque amount.

lessons.title: Lab: Draft a plaint for recovery of money

scenes.text: Sunrise Traders supplied electrical goods worth ₹6,40,000 to Bright Electricals in Jaipur. Only ₹1,40,000 was paid.
Draft the plaint.

steps.title: Order VII Rule 1 particulars
steps.body: (a) name of the court; (b) name, description and residence of the plaintiff; (c) same for the defendant; (d) where a party is a minor or of unsound mind, a statement to that effect; (e) facts constituting the **cause of action** and when it arose; (f) facts showing the court has **jurisdiction**; (g) the **relief** claimed; (h) set-off or relinquishment allowed; (i) statement of **value** of the subject matter for jurisdiction and court fees. Rule 2: money suits state the precise amount. Documents relied on to be listed and filed (R. 14). For commercial suits (value ≥ ₹3 lakh specified value), comply with the Commercial Courts Act, including s. 12A mediation and statement of truth.

steps.title: Model plaint (key parts)
steps.body:
'IN THE COURT OF THE DISTRICT JUDGE (COMMERCIAL COURT), JAIPUR
Commercial Suit No. ___ of 2026
Sunrise Traders, a partnership firm, through partner Mr A, 10 Tonk Road, Jaipur … Plaintiff
VERSUS
Bright Electricals, proprietorship of Mr B, 22 MI Road, Jaipur … Defendant
SUIT FOR RECOVERY OF ₹5,00,000 WITH INTEREST
1. The plaintiff is a registered partnership firm dealing in electrical goods.
2. Between 1 July and 30 September 2025 the plaintiff supplied goods under invoices Nos. 101–118 totalling ₹6,40,000 (Rupees six lakh forty thousand only), received by the defendant.
3. The defendant paid ₹1,40,000 on 15 October 2025 and acknowledged the balance in an email dated 20 November 2025.
4. Balance due: ₹5,00,000 (Rupees five lakh only).
5. Pre-institution mediation under s. 12A Commercial Courts Act failed – non-starter report dated 10 February 2026.
6. Cause of action arose on the dates of supply, on 20 November 2025 and continues.
7. Jurisdiction: defendant resides and goods were supplied at Jaipur (s. 20 CPC); value exceeds specified value.
8. Valuation: ₹5,00,000 for jurisdiction and court fee; court fee paid as per the Rajasthan Court Fees Act.
PRAYER: (a) decree for ₹5,00,000; (b) interest at 12% p.a. from 1 October 2025 till realisation; (c) costs.
Verification and statement of truth; list of documents.'

steps.title: Interest
steps.body: Pendente lite and future interest under s. 34 CPC; in commercial transactions, future interest may exceed 6% but not the contractual rate.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Omitting the date on which the cause of action arose; limitation (3 years for price of goods, Art. 14 Limitation Act) is judged from it.

activity.prompt: Order the parts of the plaint
items: Name of court and suit number
Cause of action and jurisdiction paragraphs
Verification, statement of truth and list of documents

quiz.q: Facts showing the court has jurisdiction are required by
quiz.why: Order VII Rule 1(f) requires a statement of facts showing jurisdiction.

quiz.q: Limitation for a suit for price of goods sold and delivered (no fixed credit period) is
quiz.why: Article 14 of the Limitation Act gives 3 years from the date of delivery.

quiz.q: Pendente lite interest is governed by section
quiz.why: Section 34 CPC empowers courts to award interest from suit to decree and after.

scenes.text: A plaintiff dresses up a time-barred claim with vague words like 'continuing cause of action'.
The defendant applies to reject the plaint at the threshold.

steps.title: Order VII Rule 11 – rejection
steps.body: Plaint shall be rejected: (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action; (b) relief undervalued and not corrected within time fixed; (c) insufficiently stamped and not made good; (d) suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law; (e) not filed in duplicate; (f) non-compliance with Rule 9 (copies). Court looks only at the plaint and its documents (Saleem Bhai v State of Maharashtra, 2003). Clever drafting creating illusion of cause of action must be nipped in the bud (T. Arivandandam v T.V. Satyapal, 1977; Dahiben v Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali, 2020).

steps.title: Return (O. VII R. 10)
steps.body: Plaint returned to be presented to the proper court where the court lacks jurisdiction (territorial or pecuniary); the court endorses the date of presentation and return.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Claim for refund of advance paid in 2018, with no acknowledgment since: barred by limitation on the face of the plaint → O. VII R. 11(d). A suit filed in Delhi when the property and defendant are in Mumbai → return under O. VII R. 10.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Relying on the written statement to seek rejection. Only plaint averments are considered.

Suit barred by limitation on the face of it

quiz.why: Saleem Bhai held the written statement is irrelevant at this stage.

quiz.q: Arivandandam (1977) warned against
options: Clever drafting creating an illusion of a cause of action
quiz.why: Krishna Iyer J urged courts to nip vexatious, clever drafting in the bud.

quiz.q: Lack of territorial jurisdiction leads to
quiz.why: The plaint is returned for presentation to the proper court.

scenes.text: Bright Electricals is served summons on 1 April 2026. It says half the goods were defective and returned.
How long does it have, and how should it plead?

steps.title: Order VIII
steps.body:
- R. 1: WS within **30 days** of service, extendable up to **90 days** for reasons recorded (ordinary suits – directory, Kailash v Nanhku, 2005); in **commercial suits** the 120-day limit is mandatory (SCG Contracts v K.S. Chamankar, 2019).
- R. 2: new facts must be specially pleaded (e.g. limitation, fraud, payment, release).
- R. 3–5: **specific denial**; a general denial is not enough; allegations not denied are deemed admitted (R. 5). Commercial suits: denial must be specific with reasons (Order VIII R. 3A as amended).
- R. 6: **set-off** for ascertained sums legally recoverable; R. 6A: **counter-claim** treated as a plaint.

steps.title: Model WS (extracts)
steps.body:
'PRELIMINARY OBJECTIONS
1. The suit is not maintainable as the plaintiff firm's registration was not in force on the date of suit (s. 69 Partnership Act) [only if true].
REPLY ON MERITS
2. Para 2 of the plaint is admitted to the extent that goods under invoices 101–118 were delivered; it is denied that all goods were of merchantable quality.
3. Para 3 is denied. The email dated 20 November 2025 did not acknowledge any balance; it recorded that goods worth ₹3,00,000 were defective and returned on 25 November 2025 under delivery challan No. 55.
4. Para 4 is denied. The amount due, if any, is ₹2,00,000 (6,40,000 − 1,40,000 − 3,00,000).
SET-OFF / COUNTER-CLAIM
5. The defendant claims ₹40,000 as cost of replacement of defective goods, to be set off.
Prayer: dismiss the suit beyond ₹1,60,000 (2,00,000 − 40,000), with costs.'

steps.title: Para-wise replies
steps.body: Reply to each paragraph of the plaint in order; use 'admitted', 'denied', 'not admitted – plaintiff to strict proof'.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Writing 'All allegations are denied' without specific denials. Under O. VIII R. 5 unspecified allegations may be taken as admitted.

quiz.why: Order VIII Rule 5 treats them as admitted, subject to the court's discretion.

scenes.text: Your client owns a plot; his cousin has started constructing a wall on it, claiming oral partition.
You file a suit for declaration and permanent injunction. You need an immediate stay.

steps.title: Order XXXIX Rules 1–3 and section 94
steps.body: Temporary injunction where property in dispute is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated, or the defendant threatens to dispossess or injure the plaintiff. **Three tests** (Dalpat Kumar v Prahlad Singh, 1992; Gujarat Bottling v Coca-Cola, 1995): (1) **prima facie case**; (2) **balance of convenience**; (3) **irreparable injury** not compensable in money. Ex parte injunction (R. 3): court must record reasons; plaintiff must send copies to defendant immediately; decide within 30 days. Disobedience: attachment and civil prison up to 3 months (R. 2A).

steps.title: Model application (extract)
steps.body:
'APPLICATION UNDER ORDER XXXIX RULES 1 AND 2 READ WITH SECTION 151 CPC
1. The applicant has filed the accompanying suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction regarding Plot No. 14, Survey No. 220, Village X.
2. Prima facie case: the applicant holds registered sale deed dated 12 June 2010, mutation entry No. 455 and property tax receipts up to 2025-26 (Annexures A-1 to A-3).
3. Balance of convenience: the applicant is in possession; the respondent has no document of title.
4. Irreparable injury: once the wall is built, the nature of the property changes and the applicant's possession is disturbed, causing loss not compensable in money.
PRAYER: (a) restrain the respondent from raising construction or interfering with the applicant's possession pending the suit; (b) ad interim ex parte injunction in the above terms.'

steps.title: Supporting affidavit
steps.body: Every injunction application must be supported by an affidavit verifying facts; annex photographs with dates.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Suppressing material facts (e.g. a pending earlier suit). Suppression disentitles the applicant to equitable relief.

quiz.why: Order XXXIX Rule 2A allows detention in civil prison up to three months and attachment of property.

quiz.q: An ex parte injunction application should be decided within
quiz.why: Rule 3A requires the court to endeavour to dispose of it within 30 days.

courses.summary: Drafting an FIR complaint and a private complaint to a Magistrate, regular and anticipatory bail applications, a petition for quashing under the High Court's inherent powers, and a reply to a criminal complaint, all with BNSS 2023 provisions.

lessons.title: FIR and complaint to the Magistrate

scenes.text: A shopkeeper's goods worth ₹2 lakh were stolen; the police station refuses to register an FIR.
What can his lawyer draft?

steps.title: BNSS provisions
steps.body:
- **Section 173**: information of a cognizable offence, oral or electronic (e-FIR, signed within 3 days), at any police station regardless of jurisdiction (**zero FIR**); preliminary enquiry within 14 days for offences punishable 3–7 years with DSP permission. Lalita Kumari v Govt of UP (2014): registration mandatory if information discloses a cognizable offence.
- **Section 173(4)**: if officer refuses, send the substance in writing to the Superintendent of Police.
- **Section 175(3)**: Magistrate may order investigation on an application supported by affidavit, after considering the SP application and the police officer's submissions.
- **Section 223**: Magistrate taking cognizance on complaint examines complainant and witnesses on oath; **no cognizance without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard** (proviso).

steps.title: Model application under s. 175(3)
steps.body:
'IN THE COURT OF THE JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS, NAGPUR
Application under Section 175(3) of the BNSS, 2023
Applicant: R.K., proprietor, Shop No. 5, Itwari, Nagpur.
1. On the night of 2–3 February 2026, goods worth ₹2,00,000 were stolen from the applicant's shop (CCTV footage in pen drive, Annexure A).
2. On 3 February 2026 the applicant approached P.S. Kotwali, which refused to register an FIR.
3. On 5 February 2026 the applicant sent a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police under s. 173(4) (Annexure B, postal receipt); no action followed.
4. The facts disclose theft, a cognizable offence under the BNS.
Prayer: direct the SHO, P.S. Kotwali to register an FIR and investigate.
Affidavit in support annexed.'

steps.title: Affidavit
steps.body: Priyanka Srivastava v State of UP (2015): s. 156(3) applications (now s. 175(3)) must be supported by affidavit, after approaching the SP.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Going straight to the Magistrate without first approaching the SP under s. 173(4). BNSS requires the applicant to have done so.

items: Give information at the police station
Send substance in writing to the SP under s. 173(4)
Application with affidavit to Magistrate under s. 175(3)

quiz.why: The Constitution Bench held the police must register an FIR when a cognizable offence is disclosed.

quiz.q: Zero FIR means
options: FIR may be lodged at any police station irrespective of jurisdiction
quiz.why: Section 173(1) BNSS allows information to be given at any police station, which then transfers it.

quiz.q: Under s. 223 BNSS, before taking cognizance on a complaint, the Magistrate must
options: Give the accused an opportunity of being heard
quiz.why: The proviso to section 223(1) is new and requires hearing the accused before cognizance.

scenes.text: A 23-year-old student has been in custody for 30 days on a cheating charge (punishable up to 7 years). Chargesheet has been filed.
Draft his bail application before the Sessions Court.

steps.title: Law
steps.body:
- **s. 478**: bail in bailable offences – a right.
- **s. 480**: bail in non-bailable offences by courts other than High Court/Sessions (with restrictions for offences punishable with death or life).
- **s. 483**: special powers of High Court and Court of Session.
- **s. 479**: undertrial who has served half the maximum sentence (one-third for first-time offenders) to be released on bond.
Principles: 'bail is the rule, jail the exception' (State of Rajasthan v Balchand, 1977; Satender Kumar Antil v CBI, 2022). Factors: nature and gravity, evidence, likelihood of absconding, tampering with witnesses, antecedents. Arnesh Kumar (2014) and Antil: for offences up to 7 years, arrest should be the exception.

steps.title: Grounds (extract)
steps.body:
'1. The applicant is a 23-year-old student with no criminal antecedents.
2. The offence is punishable up to 7 years and triable by a Magistrate; the chargesheet has been filed, so custodial interrogation is not required.
3. The evidence is documentary and already seized; no possibility of tampering.
4. The applicant has permanent residence at … and is not a flight risk.
5. Trial will take time; continued detention would violate Article 21 (Satender Kumar Antil).
6. The applicant undertakes to abide by any conditions, including surrender of passport and reporting to the police station.
Prayer: release on bail on such terms as the Court deems fit.'

steps.title: Previous applications
steps.body: State whether any earlier bail application was filed and its result – suppression is fatal.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Arguing innocence in detail on merits. At bail stage the court only takes a prima facie view.

items: Heading with court and provisions (s. 483 BNSS)
Particulars of FIR, offences and date of arrest

quiz.q: An undertrial first-time offender is to be released on bond after serving
quiz.why: Section 479 BNSS reduces the threshold to one-third for first-time offenders.

quiz.q: 'Bail is the rule, jail the exception' was stated in

scenes.text: A businessman learns that a former partner has filed a complaint alleging criminal breach of trust; police have called him to the station.
He wants protection before arrest.

steps.title: Section 482 BNSS
steps.body: A person with reason to believe he may be arrested for a non-bailable offence may apply to the High Court or Court of Session. Conditions may include availability for interrogation, not inducing or threatening witnesses, not leaving India without permission. **Sushila Aggarwal v State (NCT of Delhi) (2020)**: no fixed time limit; protection can continue till end of trial unless restricted. Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia (1980): wide discretion. Not available for certain offences (e.g. section 482(4) BNSS – rape of women under 18 and related offences).

steps.title: Grounds (extract)
steps.body:
'1. The dispute is essentially civil, arising from a partnership dissolution in which accounts are pending (civil suit No. 120/2025 pending).
2. The complaint was filed after the applicant refused to pay unverified sums – it is a pressure tactic.
3. The applicant has deep roots in the community, runs a business employing 40 people, and will cooperate with investigation.
4. Arrest would cause irreparable damage to reputation.
Prayer: in the event of arrest, release on bail; interim protection pending hearing.'

steps.title: Where to file
steps.body: Ordinarily first before the Sessions Court; then the High Court.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Filing for a bailable offence. Anticipatory bail is for non-bailable offences; bailable ones give bail as a right.

lessons.title: Lab: Quashing petition under section 528 BNSS

story.title: A civil dispute in criminal clothing

scenes.text: A buyer who failed to pay for goods has been charged with cheating, though the seller's real grievance is non-payment.
Can the High Court quash the FIR?

steps.title: Section 528 BNSS (former s. 482 CrPC)
steps.body: Saves the High Court's inherent power to make orders to give effect to any order under the Sanhita, to prevent abuse of process, or otherwise secure the ends of justice. **State of Haryana v Bhajan Lal (1992)** categories include: allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute an offence; uncontroverted allegations do not disclose a cognizable offence; allegations are absurd and inherently improbable; express legal bar; proceedings manifestly mala fide or maliciously instituted for vengeance. Also: compounding/settlement in non-heinous offences (Gian Singh, 2012; Parbatbhai Aahir, 2017).

steps.title: Grounds (extract)
steps.body:
'A. Because even taken at face value, the FIR shows only failure to pay the price after delivery; there is no allegation of dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, which is essential to cheating (Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v State of Bihar, 2000).
B. Because a purely civil dispute has been given a criminal colour to pressurise the petitioner, an abuse of process (Bhajan Lal, category 7).
C. Because a civil suit for recovery is pending, showing the true nature of the dispute.
Prayer: quash FIR No. 45/2026, P.S. …, and all consequential proceedings; stay further investigation pending hearing.'

steps.title: Annexures
steps.body: Attach FIR, chargesheet (if any), contract/invoices, civil suit papers and any settlement deed.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Asking the High Court to weigh disputed evidence. Quashing is decided on the face of the allegations.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Writ Petitions, Appeals, Affidavits and Family Pleadings
courses.summary: Drafting a writ petition under Article 226, a civil first appeal under section 96 and Order XLI CPC, affidavits under Order XIX, and family pleadings such as a divorce petition and maintenance application under section 144 BNSS.
outcomes: Draft a writ petition with synopsis, grounds and prayers
Draft memorandum of appeal grounds and compute limitation

scenes.text: A State university cancels a student's admission without notice, saying her caste certificate is 'doubtful'.
Draft a writ petition.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
1. Cause title: In the High Court of …, Writ Petition (Civil) No. … of 2026, under Article 226.
2. **Synopsis and list of dates**.
3. Parties (State, university as 'State' under Art. 12).
4. Facts in numbered paragraphs.
5. Statement that no alternative efficacious remedy exists (or why it is inadequate) and no other petition is pending.
6. **Grounds** – each starting with 'Because…'.
7. **Prayers**: writ of certiorari quashing the order, mandamus directing restoration; interim relief.
8. Affidavit, annexures marked P-1, P-2…

steps.title: Grounds
steps.body:
'A. Because the impugned order dated 15 January 2026 was passed without any show-cause notice or hearing, in violation of audi alteram partem.
B. Because verification of caste certificates must follow the procedure laid down in Kumari Madhuri Patil v Additional Commissioner (1994), through a scrutiny committee; the university has no power to cancel unilaterally.
C. Because the action is arbitrary and violates Article 14.
Prayers: (a) writ of certiorari quashing order dated 15.01.2026; (b) mandamus directing respondents to permit the petitioner to continue studies; (c) interim stay of the order.'

steps.title: Five writs
steps.body: Habeas corpus (unlawful detention), mandamus (compel public duty), prohibition (stop a lower court/tribunal exceeding jurisdiction), certiorari (quash order of lower body), quo warranto (challenge to holder of public office).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Omitting the statement about alternative remedy and other pending proceedings; registries return such petitions.
