scenes.text: The trial court dismissed your client's recovery suit on 10 January 2026, wrongly holding it time-barred despite a written acknowledgment.
How long to appeal, and how to draft it?

steps.title: Section 96 and Order XLI
steps.body: First appeal lies from an original decree on facts and law. Memorandum (O. XLI R. 1): signed by appellant/pleader, accompanied by a copy of the judgment, setting out **grounds of objection concisely under distinct heads**, numbered consecutively, without argument or narrative. Limitation (Article 116, Limitation Act): **90 days** for an appeal to a High Court and **30 days** for an appeal to any other court, from the date of the decree. Time requisite to obtain a certified copy is excluded (s. 12(2) Limitation Act).

steps.title: Grounds
steps.body:
'1. That the learned trial court erred in holding the suit barred by limitation, ignoring the written acknowledgment dated 20.11.2023 (Exh. P-7), which extends limitation under section 18 of the Limitation Act.
2. That the finding on Issue No. 3 is perverse, being contrary to the admitted documentary evidence.
3. That the trial court erred in not awarding interest under section 34 CPC.
Prayer: set aside the judgment and decree dated 10.01.2026 and decree the suit as prayed, with costs throughout.'

steps.title: Worked limitation
steps.body: Decree 10 January 2026; appeal to District Court (30 days). Certified copy applied 12 January, ready 22 January (10 days excluded). Last date = 10 January + 30 days (9 February) + 10 days = 19 February 2026.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Writing arguments instead of concise grounds. Order XLI R. 1(2) requires concise grounds without argument or narrative.

quiz.why: Article 116 of the Limitation Act allows 90 days for appeals to a High Court.

quiz.why: Section 12(2) excludes the time requisite for obtaining a copy of the decree or order.

quiz.q: Grounds of appeal must be
quiz.why: Order XLI Rule 1(2) requires concise grounds under distinct heads.

scenes.text: A registry returns an affidavit because it was attested by the deponent's own advocate and has no verification.
What makes an affidavit valid?

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Order XIX R. 3: affidavits confined to facts the deponent can prove from own knowledge, except interlocutory applications where statements of belief may be admitted with grounds. Parts: title; deponent's name, age, occupation, address; numbered paragraphs of facts; **verification** (which paras true to knowledge, which on information); signature of deponent; **jurat** – sworn/affirmed before an Oath Commissioner/Notary/Magistrate, with date and place. Many High Court rules bar an advocate from attesting an affidavit of his own client in the same matter. A false affidavit can amount to the offence of false evidence under the BNS.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
'AFFIDAVIT
I, Sunita Rao, aged 42, wife of Mohan Rao, residing at 7 Lake View, Bhopal, do hereby solemnly affirm and state as under:
1. That I am the petitioner in the above matter and well conversant with the facts.
2. That the contents of the accompanying petition have been drafted under my instructions and are true and correct.
DEPONENT
Verification: Verified at Bhopal on 12 March 2026 that the contents of paras 1–2 are true to my knowledge, no part is false and nothing material has been concealed.
DEPONENT
Sworn before me: Oath Commissioner, Seal, Date.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Including arguments or legal submissions in an affidavit. It should state facts only.

quiz.why: Order XIX deals with affidavits, especially Rule 3 on their contents.

options: The certificate by the attesting officer that it was sworn before him
quiz.why: The jurat records where, when and before whom the affidavit was sworn.

quiz.q: A false affidavit may amount to
quiz.why: A person bound by oath who makes a false statement commits the offence of giving false evidence.

lessons.title: Lab: Maintenance application and divorce petition outline

scenes.text: A wife and her 6-year-old daughter have been living with her parents since her husband stopped supporting them in 2025.
Draft a maintenance application.

steps.title: Section 144 BNSS (former s. 125 CrPC)
steps.body: A Magistrate First Class may order a person having sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain his wife (unable to maintain herself), legitimate or illegitimate minor child, adult child with disability, or parents, to pay a monthly allowance. No upper limit. Interim maintenance during proceedings; an interim application should be disposed of within 60 days of service of notice. Rajnesh v Neha (2020): mandatory disclosure of assets and liabilities affidavits in all maintenance proceedings.

steps.title: Model application (extract)
steps.body:
'IN THE FAMILY COURT, LUCKNOW
Application under Section 144 BNSS
1. Applicant No. 1 married the respondent on 5 May 2018 at Lucknow under Hindu rites; Applicant No. 2 is their daughter born 10 August 2019.
2. Since March 2025, the respondent has neglected and refused to maintain the applicants, who reside with Applicant No. 1's parents.
3. Applicant No. 1 has no independent income; the respondent earns about ₹90,000 per month as a software engineer.
4. Monthly needs: food and household ₹15,000; school fees and education ₹6,000; medical ₹3,000; rent share ₹6,000 = ₹30,000.
Prayer: (a) monthly maintenance of ₹30,000 for both applicants from the date of application; (b) interim maintenance; (c) costs.
Affidavit of assets and liabilities as per Rajnesh v Neha annexed.'

steps.title: Divorce petition outline (HMA s. 13)
steps.body: Court, parties, marriage date and place, children, residence for jurisdiction (s. 19), ground (e.g. cruelty s. 13(1)(ia) with particulars), no collusion (s. 23), no unnecessary delay, prayers (divorce, custody, permanent alimony s. 25), verification.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Vague allegations of 'cruelty' without dated incidents. Plead specific acts, dates and witnesses.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Conveyancing: Deeds, Will, Power of Attorney & Final Exam
courses.summary: Components of a deed; drafting a sale deed, lease deed, mortgage deed, gift deed, will, power of attorney and partnership deed; stamp duty and registration requirements; and a cumulative exam.
outcomes: Identify the standard parts of a deed
Draft a sale deed and lease deed with essential clauses
Apply the registration requirements of section 17 Registration Act and the Transfer of Property Act
Draft a valid will and a special power of attorney

lessons.title: Anatomy of a deed and the sale deed

scenes.text: Asha agrees to buy a flat in Pune from Mr Kulkarni for ₹75,00,000.
Draft the conveyance that will pass title.

steps.title: Parts of a deed
steps.body:
1. **Description/title** (Sale Deed).
2. **Date and place** of execution.
3. **Parties** (with parentage, age, address, PAN/Aadhaar as required).
4. **Recitals** ('WHEREAS…') – history of title and agreement.
5. **Testatum** ('NOW THIS DEED WITNESSETH…') – consideration and operative words.
6. **Operative part** – words of transfer ('hereby sells, conveys and transfers').
7. **Parcels** – description of the property (schedule with boundaries).
8. **Habendum** – 'TO HAVE AND TO HOLD' – extent of interest.
9. **Covenants** – title, encumbrances, indemnity, further assurance.
10. **Testimonium**, signatures and **attestation** by witnesses.
11. **Schedule(s)**.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: Sale (s. 54 TPA): transfer of ownership for a price paid or promised. For tangible immovable property of ₹100 or more, sale is made only by a **registered instrument**. Registration Act s. 17(1)(b) – compulsory registration; s. 23 – presentation within **four months** of execution; s. 49 – unregistered document does not affect the property. Stamp duty under the State Stamp Act on market value. Suraj Lamp & Industries v State of Haryana (2011): sale agreement + GPA + will transactions do not convey title. TDS 1% under s. 194-IA Income-tax Act for consideration ≥ ₹50 lakh.

steps.title: Model operative clause
steps.body: 'NOW THIS DEED WITNESSETH that in consideration of ₹75,00,000 (Rupees seventy-five lakh only) paid by the Purchaser to the Vendor (receipt whereof the Vendor hereby acknowledges as per the payment schedule below, after deduction of TDS of ₹75,000 under section 194-IA), the Vendor hereby sells, conveys and transfers unto the Purchaser ALL THAT Flat No. 702, 7th floor, 'Green Heights', Survey No. 45/2, Baner, Pune, more particularly described in the Schedule hereunder, TO HAVE AND TO HOLD the same absolutely and forever, free from all encumbrances.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Missing the four-month window for presentation for registration (s. 23), which can defeat the transaction.

activity.prompt: Order the parts of a sale deed

quiz.q: Sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires
quiz.why: Section 54 TPA requires a registered instrument for such sales.

quiz.q: TDS on ₹75 lakh property purchase at 1% equals
quiz.why: 1% of 75,00,000 = ₹75,000 under section 194-IA.

quiz.q: The 'habendum' clause
options: States the extent of the interest conveyed
quiz.why: 'To have and to hold' defines the estate taken by the transferee.

lessons.title: Lab: Lease deed and mortgage deed

scenes.text: A startup leases an office for 3 years at ₹1,20,000 per month with a 5% annual escalation.
Separately, its founder mortgages his house to a bank.

steps.title: Lease
steps.body: Section 105 TPA: transfer of a right to enjoy immovable property for a term, in consideration of rent. Lease from year to year or exceeding one year, or reserving yearly rent, only by registered instrument (s. 107 TPA; s. 17(1)(d) Registration Act). Key clauses: term and commencement, rent and due date, escalation, security deposit, maintenance, permitted use, repairs, subletting prohibition, lock-in, termination and notice, renewal, handover condition, stamp duty and registration costs.

steps.title: Mortgage
steps.body: Section 58 TPA: transfer of an interest in specific immovable property to secure a loan. Types: simple, conditional sale, usufructuary, English, **by deposit of title deeds** (equitable mortgage, s. 58(f), in notified towns – no registration of the deposit itself, though a memorandum recording terms may need registration), anomalous. Clauses: amount and interest, repayment schedule, right of redemption (s. 60 – cannot be clogged), insurance, events of default, power of sale (s. 69), SARFAESI enforcement for banks.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Drafting a 3-year lease on plain paper without registration. Under s. 49 Registration Act, it cannot be used as evidence of the lease terms (except for collateral purposes).

A lease exceeding one year must be

lessons.title: Lab: Gift deed, will and power of attorney

scenes.text: Mr Iyer, 78, wants to gift a flat to his daughter now, leave the rest of his estate by will, and let his son manage his bank work through a power of attorney.
Three documents, three sets of rules.

steps.title: Gift (ss. 122–123 TPA)
steps.body: Voluntary transfer without consideration, **accepted** by the donee during the donor's lifetime while the donor is still capable of giving. Immovable property: registered instrument signed by donor and **attested by at least two witnesses**. Gifts between specified relatives are exempt from income tax in the donee's hands (s. 56(2)(x)); stamp duty concessions often apply for family gifts.

steps.title: Will (Indian Succession Act 1925)
steps.body: Section 63: testator signs or affixes mark; signature placed so it appears intended to give effect as a will; **attested by two or more witnesses**, each of whom has seen the testator sign. Registration optional (s. 18 Registration Act). Revocable anytime; last will prevails. Probate mandatory for wills of Hindus in certain areas (Bombay, Calcutta, Madras original jurisdiction) – s. 57 and s. 213. A beneficiary should not be an attesting witness (s. 67 – the bequest to an attesting witness is void).

steps.title: Power of attorney
steps.body: Powers of Attorney Act 1882. General POA vs special POA (for a specific act). Authenticated before a notary or registered (registration required if it authorises sale of immovable property in many States). Does not survive the principal's death or incapacity (agency ends, s. 201 Contract Act) unless coupled with interest (s. 202).

steps.title: Will extract
steps.body: 'I, Venkatesh Iyer, aged 78, residing at 3 Temple Street, Chennai, being of sound mind, make this my last Will, revoking all earlier wills. 1. I appoint my son Ravi as executor. 2. I bequeath my fixed deposits with ABC Bank to my grandson Arjun. 3. All the rest of my property I give to my son Ravi and daughter Lakshmi in equal shares. Signed on 1 March 2026 at Chennai. [Signature]. Witnesses: (1) Dr P. Nair, (2) Mr K. Das – both present at the same time and signing in the presence of the testator.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Making a beneficiary sign as attesting witness. The bequest to that witness becomes void under s. 67.

Two attesting witnesses who saw the testator sign

quiz.why: Section 67 voids legacies to attesting witnesses or their spouses, though the will remains valid.

steps.title: Partnership deed essentials
steps.body: Name and business; place; partners' details; commencement and duration; capital contributions; profit-sharing ratio; interest on capital and drawings; salaries/remuneration (within s. 40(b) Income-tax Act limits); banking and signing authority; accounts and audit; admission, retirement, death; dissolution; arbitration clause. Registration with the Registrar of Firms is optional but an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties to enforce contract rights (s. 69 Partnership Act).

steps.title: Unit revision
steps.body: Sale – s. 54 TPA, registration compulsory; Lease > 1 year – s. 107; Mortgage – s. 58; Gift – ss. 122–123; Will – s. 63 ISA, two witnesses, registration optional; POA – 1882 Act; Registration – s. 17 compulsory, s. 18 optional, s. 23 four months, s. 49 effect of non-registration; Suraj Lamp – GPA sales do not pass title.

uni-llb-environmental-law.title: Environmental Law
uni-llb-environmental-law.description: Constitutional basis, pollution control statutes, forest and wildlife law, judicial principles, the NGT and international environmental law. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes. General education, not legal advice.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Concept, Constitution and Remedies
courses.summary: What environment and pollution mean in law, the constitutional provisions (Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g), 32, 226), common-law and criminal remedies, and the rise of environmental PIL.
outcomes: Define environment and pollution as used in the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
Explain how Article 21 was read to include a right to a wholesome environment
Distinguish Directive Principles (Art. 48A) from Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A(g))
Choose between writ, tort, public nuisance and criminal remedies for a pollution problem
Explain why PIL relaxed locus standi in environmental cases

lessons.title: Meaning of environment, pollution and the evolution of environmental law

scenes.text: Villagers along a river notice the water turning dark and fish dying after tanneries open upstream.
They ask a law student: is there any law that protects 'the environment' as such, or only our individual property?

steps.title: Statutory definitions
steps.body: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EPA) defines **environment** to include water, air and land and the inter-relationship among them and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property. **Environmental pollutant** is any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be injurious to the environment, and **environmental pollution** is the presence of any such pollutant in the environment.

steps.title: Phases of Indian environmental law
steps.body:
1. Pre-1972: scattered rules in the Indian Penal Code (public nuisance), the Indian Forest Act 1927, the Factories Act 1948 and municipal laws.
2. After the Stockholm Conference (1972): Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Water Act 1974, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Air Act 1981.
3. After the Bhopal gas leak (1984): the umbrella EPA 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991.
4. Judicial activism and specialised forums: PIL from the 1980s, National Green Tribunal Act 2010, Biological Diversity Act 2002.

steps.title: 42nd Amendment, 1976
steps.body: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 inserted Article 48A (State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife) and Article 51A(g) (duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures).

steps.title: Applying the definition
steps.body: Tannery effluent with chromium in the river: the chromium is an environmental pollutant because its concentration can injure fish, crops and people; its presence in the river is environmental pollution. So both the Water Act 1974 (specific) and the EPA 1986 (umbrella) are engaged.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Students often say Article 48A is enforceable in court on its own. Directive Principles are not enforceable by themselves (Article 37); courts use them to interpret Article 21 and statutes.

steps.title: Exam framing
steps.body: Open an answer on 'evolution' with Stockholm 1972 → 42nd Amendment 1976 → Bhopal 1984 → EPA 1986. Examiners look for this chronology.

activity.prompt: Put these milestones in chronological order
items: Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act

quiz.q: Which Act contains the definition of 'environment' as water, air and land and their inter-relationship with living beings and property?
quiz.why: The EPA 1986, enacted after Bhopal as an umbrella law, defines environment, environmental pollutant and environmental pollution.

quiz.q: Articles 48A and 51A(g) were inserted by the
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added Article 48A in the Directive Principles and Article 51A(g) in the Fundamental Duties.

quiz.q: The immediate trigger for the umbrella EPA 1986 was
quiz.why: The Bhopal disaster showed the gaps in sectoral laws, so Parliament enacted the EPA in 1986 using its Article 253 power to implement the Stockholm decisions.

quiz.q: Article 48A by itself is
options: Not enforceable in court but used to interpret other rights
quiz.why: Under Article 37 Directive Principles are non-justiciable, though courts read them together with Article 21.

lessons.title: Article 21 and the right to a healthy environment

scenes.text: Residents of a hill town complain that limestone quarrying has stripped the slopes and fouled their water.
They write a letter to the Supreme Court. Can a letter become a writ petition about the right to life?

steps.title: Judicial expansion of Article 21
steps.body:
After Maneka Gandhi (1978) read 'life' as life with dignity, the Supreme Court extended Article 21 to environmental quality. Key cases:
- **Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v State of UP (1985)** (Dehradun quarrying): mining in the Doon valley regulated/closed on ecological grounds; treated as an Article 32 petition.
- **Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar (1991)**: right to life includes the right to enjoy pollution-free water and air.
- **Virender Gaur v State of Haryana (1995)**: environmental, ecological, air and water pollution amounting to violation of Article 21.
- **M.C. Mehta v Union of India** series: Ganga pollution, Delhi vehicular pollution (CNG), Taj Trapezium.

steps.title: How DPSP and duties feed in
steps.body: Courts read Article 21 together with Article 48A and 51A(g): the State's duty and the citizen's duty give content to the right. Article 47 (public health) is also cited.

steps.title: Worked answer outline
steps.body:
Problem: a city dumps waste near a school, causing smoke and disease.
1. Right engaged: Article 21 (life includes a healthy environment – Subhash Kumar).
2. State obligation: Art. 48A plus statutory duties of the municipality.
3. Remedy: writ of mandamus under Art. 226 (High Court) or Art. 32 (Supreme Court) directing scientific waste management under the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016.
4. Conclusion: petition likely to succeed; court may also appoint a monitoring committee.

steps.title: Delhi CNG case
steps.body: In M.C. Mehta v Union of India (vehicular pollution) the Supreme Court in 1998 directed conversion of Delhi's public transport buses to CNG, monitoring compliance over several years.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not cite Article 21 against a private polluter as if it were directly enforceable by writ. Writs lie against the 'State' (Article 12); against a private factory you sue the regulator for failing to act, or use tort/statutory remedies.

activity.prompt: Which provision is the source?

State shall endeavour to protect forests and wildlife
Citizen must have compassion for living creatures
Life with dignity in a wholesome environment

Citizen must protect lakes, rivers and wildlife

options: Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar
quiz.why: In Subhash Kumar (1991) the Supreme Court said the right to pollution-free water and air is part of Article 21, though it dismissed that petition on its facts.

quiz.q: The Dehradun limestone quarrying case is
options: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v State of UP
quiz.why: RLEK v State of UP was among the first environmental cases where the Supreme Court closed quarries on ecological grounds.

quiz.q: A writ under Article 32 normally lies against
quiz.why: Fundamental rights are enforced against the State, so the petition usually targets the authorities who failed to stop the pollution.

quiz.q: The Delhi bus fleet was ordered to switch to
quiz.why: The Supreme Court's 1998 directions in the M.C. Mehta vehicular pollution case required CNG for Delhi's buses.

lessons.title: Common-law and criminal remedies: nuisance, negligence, strict liability

scenes.text: A brick kiln next to a housing colony emits thick smoke every night.
One resident wants damages and an injunction; another wants the kiln owner prosecuted. Which remedies exist apart from pollution statutes?

steps.title: Tort remedies
steps.body:
- **Private nuisance**: unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land (smoke, noise, smell). Remedy: damages and injunction.
- **Public nuisance**: interference with rights of the public generally; a private person may sue only on proof of special damage, or with leave under section 91 CPC.
- **Negligence**: duty, breach, damage.
- **Strict liability** (Rylands v Fletcher, 1868): one who brings a dangerous thing onto land and it escapes is liable even without negligence, subject to exceptions (act of God, plaintiff's fault, act of a stranger, consent, statutory authority).
- **Absolute liability** (M.C. Mehta v Union of India, Oleum gas leak, 1987): an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is absolutely liable, with no exceptions, and compensation is linked to its magnitude and capacity.

steps.title: Criminal and procedural remedies
steps.body: Public nuisance is an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (formerly section 268 IPC). The magistrate's power to order removal of a public nuisance by conditional order (formerly section 133 CrPC) continues in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023. In **Municipal Council, Ratlam v Vardhichand (1980)** the Supreme Court held the municipality could not plead lack of funds to escape its duty to remove a nuisance ordered under section 133 CrPC.

steps.title: Worked problem
steps.body:
Brick kiln smoke:
1. Civil: private nuisance (interference with enjoyment of homes) → injunction + damages.
2. Criminal: complaint to the Executive Magistrate for a conditional order to remove the public nuisance; prosecution for public nuisance.
3. Statutory: complaint to the State Pollution Control Board under the Air Act 1981 (consent to operate).
Best strategy: statutory complaint plus magistrate's order for speed; civil suit for compensation.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing up strict and absolute liability. Strict liability allows exceptions; the Oleum gas rule of absolute liability allows none for hazardous industries.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Ratlam = 'no money is no excuse'. Oleum = 'no exceptions'.

activity.prompt: Strict liability or absolute liability?

items.text: Act of God is a defence
Developed by the Supreme Court of India in 1987
Escape of a dangerous thing brought on land
Compensation linked to the enterprise's capacity to pay
Act of a stranger is a defence

quiz.q: Absolute liability for hazardous industries was laid down in
options: M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Oleum gas leak)
quiz.why: In the 1987 Oleum gas leak case the Supreme Court held hazardous enterprises absolutely liable without the Rylands exceptions.

quiz.q: In Ratlam Municipality the court rejected the plea of
quiz.why: Krishna Iyer J held that a statutory duty to remove nuisance cannot be avoided by pleading financial inability.

quiz.q: A private person can sue for public nuisance only if

quiz.why: Public nuisance affects everyone, so an individual needs special damage beyond the public's, or the procedure of section 91 CPC.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a defence to strict liability?
quiz.why: Strict liability does not depend on negligence, so proving you took care is not a defence.

lessons.title: Public interest litigation and environmental justice

scenes.text: An advocate with no personal stake writes to the Supreme Court about leather-industry effluent ruining Ganga water near Kanpur.
Can someone who is not personally harmed file the case?

steps.title: Relaxed locus standi
steps.body: Traditionally only an aggrieved person could sue. In S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981) the Supreme Court allowed any member of the public acting bona fide to approach the court for persons unable to do so. Environmental PILs followed: **M.C. Mehta v Union of India (Kanpur tanneries, 1987)** ordered tanneries without primary treatment plants to close.

steps.title: Tools courts use in PIL
steps.body:
- Epistolary jurisdiction (letters treated as petitions)
- Commissions and expert committees (e.g. NEERI reports)
- Continuing mandamus: the case stays open and the court issues periodic directions
- Amicus curiae to assist the court

steps.title: Drafting the core of a PIL
steps.body:
Parties: petitioner (public-spirited NGO) v Union of India, State, State Pollution Control Board, Municipal Corporation.
Facts: effluent discharge; Board's inaction despite complaints dated …
Grounds: violation of Art. 21; breach of statutory duty under Water Act ss. 24–25; polluter pays principle.
Prayers: mandamus to enforce consent conditions; closure of non-compliant units; compensation; monitoring committee.

steps.title: Limits of PIL
steps.body: Courts reject PILs filed for publicity, private or political motives, and may impose costs. The petitioner must show bona fides and usually prior representation to authorities.

steps.title: Since 2010
steps.body: Many environmental disputes are now directed to the National Green Tribunal, but writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 remains available.

options: S.P. Gupta v Union of India
quiz.why: S.P. Gupta (Judges' Transfer case, 1981) allowed public-spirited persons to sue on behalf of those unable to approach courts.

quiz.q: In the Kanpur tanneries case the Supreme Court
options: Ordered closure of tanneries without primary treatment plants
quiz.why: The court held that tanneries not setting up primary effluent treatment must stop, whatever the effect on employment.

quiz.q: 'Continuing mandamus' means
options: The court keeps the case pending and issues periodic directions to monitor compliance
quiz.why: Courts use continuing mandamus in environmental PILs to supervise implementation over time.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Water, Air and Environment (Protection) Acts
courses.summary: The regulatory machinery of the Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981 and EPA 1986: Pollution Control Boards, consent to establish and operate, standards, directions, citizen suits, offences and the 2024 decriminalisation changes, plus EIA and noise rules.
outcomes: Explain the constitution and functions of CPCB and SPCBs
Describe the consent mechanism under the Water and Air Acts
Use the Centre's powers under sections 3 and 5 of the EPA
Explain the citizen-suit provision and its 60-day notice
Outline the EIA Notification 2006 process

lessons.title: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

scenes.text: A dyeing unit plans to start production next to a canal in Gujarat.
Its consultant says: before you build, you need 'consent to establish'; before you run, 'consent to operate'. Why two?

steps.title: Scheme of the Act
steps.body: Enacted by Parliament under Article 252 (on resolutions of State legislatures), since water is a State subject. It creates the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** and **State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)**. Pollution means contamination or alteration of water properties likely to create a nuisance or render water harmful to health, safety, or legitimate uses, or to animal or aquatic life.

steps.title: Consent mechanism
steps.body: No person shall, without the previous consent of the SPCB, establish or take steps to establish an industry or process likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent into a stream, well, sewer or on land, or bring into use a new outlet (section 25). The Board may grant consent with conditions, or refuse with reasons. In practice: **Consent to Establish (CTE)** before construction, **Consent to Operate (CTO)** before production, renewed periodically. Industries are categorised Red, Orange, Green and White by pollution potential (white category generally exempt from consent).

steps.title: Enforcement powers
steps.body:
- Power to obtain information and take samples (sections 21–23)
- Emergency measures (section 32)
- Application to court to restrain apprehended pollution (section 33)
- Directions, including closure, prohibition or stoppage of electricity or water supply (section 33A)
- Citizen complaint after 60 days' notice to the Board (section 49)
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024 decriminalised many minor violations, replacing imprisonment with penalties adjudicated by an officer, and allows the Centre to exempt certain categories of industry from consent.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body:
The dyeing unit starts production without CTO and discharges coloured effluent:
1. Violation of section 25 (operating without consent).
2. SPCB can issue a section 33A direction for closure and disconnection of power.
3. Villagers can complain to the court after giving the Board 60 days' notice.
4. Under the polluter pays principle, remediation costs can be recovered.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying the Water Act was passed under Article 253. It was passed under Article 252 because 'water' is in the State List (Entry 17); the EPA was passed under Article 253.

activity.prompt: Order the regulatory life cycle of a new red-category industry
items: Apply for Environmental Clearance if listed in the EIA Notification
Apply to SPCB for Consent to Establish
Construct the plant with effluent treatment plant
Start production and meet discharge standards

quiz.q: The Water Act 1974 was enacted under Article
quiz.why: Water is a State subject, so Parliament legislated on resolutions of States under Article 252.

quiz.q: Which section of the Water Act empowers the Board to direct closure or stoppage of electricity?
quiz.why: Section 33A, inserted in 1988, gives the Board power to issue directions including closure and disconnection of utilities.

quiz.q: A citizen may complain to court under the Water Act after giving notice of
quiz.why: Section 49 lets a citizen complain after 60 days' notice of intention to the Board.

quiz.q: Consent to Operate is needed
quiz.why: Section 25 consent is in practice split into consent to establish and consent to operate, the latter before production begins.

lessons.title: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and noise

scenes.text: A State declares a district an air pollution control area. Stone crushers there must now get consent.
Meanwhile, residents complain of loudspeakers at midnight. Which law covers that?

steps.title: Key features
steps.body: Enacted under Article 253 to implement the Stockholm decisions. The Boards under the Water Act also act as Boards under the Air Act. The State Government may declare **air pollution control areas** (section 19); in such areas no person may establish or operate an industrial plant without SPCB consent (section 21). The Board may lay down emission standards, and vehicles must comply with standards under the Motor Vehicles Act. Section 31A gives directions power (closure, stoppage of power/water). 'Air pollutant' includes noise, by the 1987 amendment.

steps.title: Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000
steps.body: Made under the EPA. They prescribe ambient noise standards for industrial, commercial, residential and silence zones, and restrict loudspeakers and public address systems at night (10 pm to 6 am) except in closed premises or as permitted. In **In re Noise Pollution (2005)** the Supreme Court upheld strict limits and said no one can claim a right to create noise even in exercise of religion.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body:
Midnight loudspeaker at a wedding in a residential zone:
1. Rule: Noise Rules 2000 – no loudspeaker 10 pm–6 am except closed premises/permitted occasions.
2. Authority: police/District Magistrate as designated authority.
3. Remedy: complaint to the authority; seizure of equipment; Article 21 (right to sleep and peace).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Air Act consent applies within notified air pollution control areas; students often forget the notification requirement.

activity.prompt: Which instrument applies?

items.text: Chimney emissions in a notified control area

quiz.q: Under the Air Act, consent is required for industrial plants in
options: Air pollution control areas declared by the State
quiz.why: Sections 19 and 21 link consent to notified air pollution control areas.

quiz.q: Noise was included in 'air pollutant' by the amendment of
quiz.why: The 1987 amendment added noise to the definition of air pollutant.

quiz.q: The Noise Rules restrict loudspeakers at night between
quiz.why: Rule 5 restricts loudspeakers and public address systems between 10 pm and 6 am, subject to limited exceptions.

story.title: One law to fill the gaps

scenes.text: After Bhopal, Parliament found no single law dealing with hazardous substances, land contamination and coordination of agencies.
It passed a short Act that gives the Central Government very wide powers.

steps.title: Central Government powers
steps.body:
- **Section 3**: power to take all measures necessary to protect and improve the environment, including standards, restriction of areas for industries, procedures for hazardous substances; and to constitute authorities (s. 3(3)) – e.g. the Commission for Air Quality Management in the NCR is now under its own 2021 Act, earlier EPCA was under s. 3(3).
- **Section 5**: power to issue directions to any person, officer or authority, including closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry and stoppage of electricity, water or other service.
- **Section 6**: rules (e.g. Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016, Solid Waste Management Rules 2016, Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification 2019, EIA Notification 2006).
- **Section 19**: cognizance on complaint by the government or by any person after 60 days' notice.

steps.title: Penalties after 2023
steps.body: The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 replaced imprisonment for many EPA contraventions with monetary penalties adjudicated by an officer, with appeal to the NGT, and created an Environment Protection Fund. Check the current text of sections 15 and 15A–15K before writing exact amounts.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body:
A battery recycler dumps lead slag on open land in a State without any specific rule for that site:
1. No Water/Air Act consent issue directly about land, so use EPA.
2. Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016 apply to lead-bearing waste.
3. Centre/delegated SPCB issues a section 5 direction: stop dumping, remediate the site.
4. Polluter pays: costs of remediation recovered from the recycler.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: The EPA does not repeal the Water and Air Acts; it supplements them. Where a specific Act applies, it continues to operate alongside the EPA.

quiz.why: Section 5 empowers directions to any person or authority, including closure and stoppage of supply of electricity or water.

quiz.q: The EIA Notification 2006 was issued under the
quiz.why: It is a notification under section 3 of the EPA and rule 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules 1986.

quiz.why: Public consultation usually includes a public hearing conducted by the SPCB and written responses from affected people.

lessons.title: Lab: Advise the regulator – case scenario

scenes.text: An SPCB inspector finds a pharma unit bypassing its effluent treatment plant at night through a hidden pipe.
The Member Secretary asks you, the Board's legal officer, for a step-by-step action note.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: Unit: Red category, valid CTO with condition 'zero liquid discharge'. Sample from the hidden pipe shows COD far above standards. Downstream villagers report skin disease. Unit claims the pipe is for 'storm water'.

steps.title: Model action note
steps.body:
1. Draw samples in the statutory manner (notice to occupier, split sample, sealed) so the report is admissible.
2. Issue a show-cause notice citing breach of consent conditions and section 25.
3. Given emergency and health impact, issue a section 33A direction for immediate closure and disconnection of electricity, after a brief hearing where possible.
4. Assess environmental compensation using CPCB methodology (polluter pays) and direct remediation.
5. Initiate penalty/prosecution proceedings as applicable after the 2024 amendment.
6. Inform the District Collector and health department; arrange water supply for villagers.

steps.title: Natural justice
steps.body: Courts have upheld closure without a prior hearing in genuine emergencies, but a post-decisional hearing should then be given promptly.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Unsealed or casually taken samples can be challenged; procedure for sampling must be followed.

quiz.why: Polluter pays makes the polluter bear the cost of remedying the damage, as applied in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996).

quiz.q: Closure without prior hearing in an emergency should be followed by
quiz.why: Natural justice can be satisfied by a prompt post-decisional hearing when urgent action is needed.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Forests, Wildlife and Biodiversity
courses.summary: Indian Forest Act 1927, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 as amended in 2023, the Godavarman continuing mandamus, the Forest Rights Act 2006, Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and the Biological Diversity Act 2002.
outcomes: Distinguish reserved, protected and village forests
Explain prior approval for diversion of forest land
Explain the rights and procedure under the Forest Rights Act 2006
Describe protected areas and schedules under the Wildlife Act
Explain access and benefit sharing under the Biological Diversity Act

lessons.title: Forest laws and the Godavarman case

scenes.text: A State wants to widen a highway through 40 hectares of notified forest.
The forest department says the State cannot do it alone. Who must approve?

steps.title: Indian Forest Act, 1927
steps.body: Classifies forests as **reserved forests** (most restricted; rights settled by a Forest Settlement Officer, most activities prohibited), **village forests** (reserved forest assigned to a village community) and **protected forests** (fewer restrictions; specified acts prohibited by notification). It also regulates transit of forest produce and imposes duties on timber.

steps.title: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 – now 'Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980'
steps.body: Section 2 requires **prior approval of the Central Government** before a State de-reserves a forest, uses forest land for non-forest purpose, leases it to a private entity, or clears naturally grown trees for reafforestation. Approval comes with conditions such as compensatory afforestation and Net Present Value payment (managed by CAMPA under the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016). The 2023 amendment renamed the Act, clarified its application to land recorded as forest, and exempted some categories (e.g. certain strategic linear projects near borders, small roadside amenities).

steps.title: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v Union of India (1996 onward)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held that 'forest' must be understood in its dictionary sense, covering all forests regardless of ownership or classification, and kept the case open as a continuing mandamus, creating the Central Empowered Committee and directing NPV payments.

steps.title: Worked answer
steps.body: Highway widening through 40 ha of forest: State must apply through the user agency for Stage I (in-principle) and Stage II (final) approval under section 2 of the 1980 Act; conditions: compensatory afforestation on equivalent non-forest land, NPV deposit, wildlife mitigation (underpasses), plus Forest Rights Act consent of gram sabhas where rights are recognised. Without approval, the diversion is illegal.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking State ownership of the forest lets the State use it freely. Section 2 binds the State itself.

activity.prompt: Needs Central approval under the 1980 Act?

items.text: Leasing forest land to a mining company
Using forest land for a cement plant
Collecting fallen leaves under recognised rights

quiz.q: Which class of forest under the 1927 Act is most restrictive?
quiz.why: Reserved forests are notified after rights are settled, and most acts are prohibited in them.

quiz.q: Prior approval for using forest land for non-forest purposes is required by section
quiz.why: Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 requires prior Central approval.

quiz.q: In Godavarman the Supreme Court held 'forest' includes
options: Any forest in the dictionary sense, regardless of ownership
quiz.why: The 1996 order gave 'forest' its dictionary meaning irrespective of ownership or classification.

lessons.title: Forest Rights Act 2006 and community consent

scenes.text: A bauxite mine is proposed on a hill sacred to a tribal community in Odisha.
The Supreme Court asks: what do the gram sabhas say?

steps.title: The Act
steps.body: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006 recognises individual rights (land under occupation up to 4 hectares) and community rights (minor forest produce, grazing, fishing, community forest resource management). 'Other traditional forest dwellers' must show residence for three generations (75 years) before 13 December 2005. The **gram sabha** initiates claims, which go to the Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees.

steps.title: Orissa Mining Corporation v MoEF (Niyamgiri, 2013)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held that the gram sabhas must decide whether the mining would affect their religious and cultural rights. The gram sabhas rejected the project.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Before forest diversion, MoEFCC guidelines required certificates that FRA rights have been settled and gram sabha consent obtained. A diversion that ignores pending claims is open to challenge.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forest dwellers who are not Scheduled Tribes are not excluded; they qualify as other traditional forest dwellers on the 75-year test.

activity.prompt: Order the FRA claim process
items: Gram sabha constitutes Forest Rights Committee
Forest Rights Committee verifies on site
District Level Committee takes final decision and issues title

quiz.q: Other traditional forest dwellers must show residence for
quiz.why: Section 2(o) requires three generations, defined as 75 years, before 13 December 2005.

quiz.q: Who initiates the process for determining forest rights?
quiz.why: Section 6 makes the gram sabha the authority to initiate the process.

quiz.q: Niyamgiri (2013) is significant because
options: Gram sabhas were asked to decide on religious and cultural rights
quiz.why: The court left the decision on affected rights to the gram sabhas, who rejected the mine.

scenes.text: Customs officers seize pangolin scales at an airport.
The accused says he only 'possessed' them, he did not hunt. Is that an offence?

steps.title: Structure
steps.body:
- **Hunting** of animals in the Schedules is prohibited (section 9) except as permitted (e.g. danger to human life, scientific purposes).
- **Specified plants** protected from picking and uprooting.
- **Protected areas**: sanctuaries, national parks, conservation reserves and community reserves. National parks have stricter regime: no grazing, no rights except as allowed.
- **Trade**: dealing in trophies and animal articles of scheduled animals is prohibited; possession requires declaration/certificate of ownership.
- **Authorities**: National Board for Wildlife, National Tiger Conservation Authority (Chapter IVB, 2006), Wildlife Crime Control Bureau.
The 2022 amendment rationalised the schedules (now Schedule I and II for animals, III for plants, IV for CITES-listed specimens) and implemented CITES.

steps.title: Burden of proof
steps.body: In prosecutions for possession of animal articles or trophies, the Act presumes the accused was in unlawful possession unless the contrary is proved (section 57).

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: Pangolin (Indian pangolin is in Schedule I): possession without lawful certificate is an offence; the presumption of unlawful possession operates; trade is also a CITES Appendix I issue. Defence of 'mere possession' fails.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing sanctuary and national park. In a national park, rights cannot be retained in the way they sometimes can in a sanctuary, and grazing is prohibited.

activity.prompt: National park or sanctuary feature?

items.text: Some rights of people may continue as permitted by the Collector
Boundary alteration needs a resolution of the State legislature on NBWL recommendation

quiz.q: The National Tiger Conservation Authority was created by the 2006 amendment in Chapter
quiz.why: The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2006 inserted Chapter IVB on the NTCA and tiger reserves.

quiz.q: After the 2022 amendment, Schedule IV relates to
quiz.why: The 2022 amendment added a schedule for CITES-listed specimens to implement the Convention.

quiz.q: In a prosecution for possession of a trophy, the Act
options: Requires the State to prove intent
Presumes unlawful possession until the accused proves otherwise
quiz.why: Section 57 places the burden of proving lawful possession on the accused.

lessons.title: Biological Diversity Act 2002 and benefit sharing

scenes.text: In the 1990s a European patent on a neem-based fungicide was challenged because Indians had used neem for centuries.
How does Indian law now control foreign access to our biological resources?

steps.title: Three-tier structure
steps.body:
- **National Biodiversity Authority (NBA)**, Chennai
- **State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs)**
- **Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs)** at local body level, maintaining People's Biodiversity Registers
The Act implements the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and its Nagoya Protocol (2010) on access and benefit sharing (ABS).

steps.title: Approvals
steps.body: Foreign persons and entities need NBA approval to obtain biological resources or associated knowledge from India for research or commercial use. Applying for an IPR (e.g. a patent) based on research on Indian biological resources needs NBA approval (the 2023 amendment shifted this to before grant rather than before filing). Indian entities give prior intimation to the SBB for commercial use. Benefits shared may be monetary, joint ownership of IPR, technology transfer, etc. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 exempted cultivated medicinal plants and AYUSH practitioners in some respects and decriminalised offences into penalties.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: A foreign cosmetic company wants to use a Kerala tribe's traditional knowledge of a herb: needs NBA approval; NBA consults BMC/SBB; benefit-sharing agreement provides payment to the community (via the Biodiversity Fund). Using it without approval invites penalties and opposition to any patent.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming that the Patents Act alone governs. Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(D) of the Patents Act requires disclosure of the source of biological material, and section 25 allows opposition for non-disclosure or anticipation by traditional knowledge.

quiz.why: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) elaborates the CBD's third objective of fair and equitable sharing of benefits.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Judicial Principles and the National Green Tribunal
courses.summary: Sustainable development, precautionary principle, polluter pays, public trust doctrine, inter-generational equity and the jurisdiction and procedure of the National Green Tribunal.
outcomes: State and apply the precautionary and polluter pays principles with leading cases
Explain the public trust doctrine from M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath
Balance development and environment using sustainable development
Identify NGT jurisdiction under sections 14, 15 and 16 and limitation periods

lessons.title: Sustainable development, precautionary principle and polluter pays

scenes.text: Around 900 tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharge untreated effluent; agricultural land and groundwater are ruined.
The tanneries earn export income. How does the court balance jobs with the environment?

steps.title: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996)
steps.body:
Kuldip Singh J held that **sustainable development** is part of Indian law, and its essential features include the **precautionary principle** and the **polluter pays principle**, which are part of the law of the land via Articles 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g) and the statutes.
Precautionary principle, as stated: (i) the State must anticipate, prevent and attack the causes of environmental degradation; (ii) where there are threats of serious and irreversible damage, lack of scientific certainty should not be used as a reason for postponing measures; (iii) the **onus of proof** is on the actor or developer to show the action is environmentally benign.

steps.title: Polluter pays
steps.body: In **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India (1996)** (Bichhri, Rajasthan – H-acid sludge), the court held the polluting chemical units liable to pay for remedying the damage to soil and groundwater; the liability covers both compensation to victims and restoration of the environment (absolute liability applied).

steps.title: Applying the precautionary principle
steps.body:
A company wants to release a new genetically modified crop; data on long-term soil effects are uncertain.
1. Threat of serious/irreversible harm? Possibly to biodiversity.
2. Scientific uncertainty is not a reason to allow it freely.
3. Burden on the company to prove safety through field trials under regulatory supervision.
Result: approval only with safeguards or refusal.

steps.title: A.P. Pollution Control Board v M.V. Nayudu (1999)
steps.body: The Supreme Court elaborated the precautionary principle and the shift of burden of proof, and suggested referring scientific questions to expert bodies.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying the polluter pays principle only means compensating victims. It also includes cost of restoring the damaged ecology.

activity.prompt: Match each statement to the principle

items.text: Lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone protective measures
Polluter bears the cost of restoring damaged soil
Development that meets present needs without compromising future generations
Developer must prove the activity is benign
Compensation to victims and restoration of ecology

quiz.q: In Vellore Citizens, the onus of proof under the precautionary principle lies on
quiz.why: Kuldip Singh J held that the actor must show that the action is environmentally benign.

quiz.q: The Bichhri village H-acid pollution case is
options: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India
quiz.why: ICELA (1996) applied the polluter pays principle against chemical units in Bichhri.

quiz.q: The definition of sustainable development commonly cited comes from the
quiz.why: Our Common Future (Brundtland Report, 1987) defined it as meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.

lessons.title: Public trust doctrine and inter-generational equity

scenes.text: A motel in Himachal Pradesh diverts the course of the Beas river to protect its lawns.
The government had leased it riverbank land. Can the State give away a river?

steps.title: M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997)
steps.body: The Supreme Court adopted the **public trust doctrine**: certain resources like air, sea, waters and forests are of such great importance to the public that the State holds them as trustee for the public and cannot transfer them to private ownership for commercial use. The lease was quashed and the motel had to pay for restoration (later exemplary damages issue).

steps.title: Inter-generational equity
steps.body: Present generations hold the environment in trust for future generations (Principle 3 of the Rio Declaration: right to development must be fulfilled to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations). Indian courts cite it in cases on mining, forests and groundwater.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: A city allots a lake bed for a shopping mall: lake is a public trust resource; State as trustee cannot convert it for private commercial use that destroys its natural character; allotment liable to be quashed (see Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v State of AP, 2006).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: The doctrine does not freeze all use; it requires that use be consistent with the public purpose and not alienate the resource irreversibly.

activity.prompt: Structure a public trust argument
items: Identify the resource (river, lake, forest, seashore)
Show it is of public importance and held by the State as trustee
Show the impugned act transfers or degrades it for private benefit
Argue the act is inconsistent with the trust
Seek quashing and restoration at the private party's cost

quiz.q: The public trust doctrine was adopted in India in
quiz.why: The Span Motel case (1997) is the leading Indian authority on public trust.

quiz.q: Inter-generational equity is reflected in which Rio principle?
quiz.why: Principle 3 refers to the needs of present and future generations.

quiz.q: Under public trust, the State acts as
quiz.why: The State is a trustee and must protect the resource for public use.

scenes.text: An NGO wants to challenge an environmental clearance granted to a coal plant 25 days ago.
Should it go to the High Court or the NGT, and how soon?

steps.title: Constitution
steps.body: The NGT has a Chairperson (a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice), judicial members and expert members; principal bench at New Delhi with zonal benches (Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai). It is not bound by the CPC procedure or the Evidence Act but by principles of natural justice, and applies sustainable development, precautionary and polluter pays principles (section 20).

steps.title: Jurisdiction
steps.body:
- **Section 14**: original jurisdiction over civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment is involved and arises from implementation of the seven Schedule I enactments: Water Act 1974, Water Cess Act 1977, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Air Act 1981, EPA 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, Biological Diversity Act 2002. Limitation 6 months from when cause of action first arose (extendable by 60 days).
- **Section 15**: relief, compensation and restitution of property and environment. Limitation 5 years (extendable by 60 days).
- **Section 16**: appeals against orders under those Acts (e.g. environmental clearance): 30 days, extendable by 60 days.
- **Section 22**: appeal to the Supreme Court within 90 days.
Note: the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and Indian Forest Act 1927 are not in Schedule I.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: EC granted 25 days ago: appeal under section 16 to the NGT within 30 days; if delayed, ask condonation within the further 60 days showing sufficient cause. High Court writ is possible but the Supreme Court has said environmental clearance challenges should ordinarily go to the NGT.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Filing an NGT application about poaching under the Wildlife Act – that Act is outside Schedule I, so the NGT lacks jurisdiction on that ground alone.

activity.prompt: Within NGT Schedule I?

quiz.q: An appeal against an environmental clearance lies to the NGT under section
quiz.why: Section 16 provides the appellate jurisdiction, including against EC orders, within 30 days.

quiz.q: Appeal from the NGT lies to the
quiz.why: Section 22 provides an appeal to the Supreme Court within 90 days.

quiz.q: Which Act is NOT in Schedule I of the NGT Act?
quiz.why: Schedule I lists seven Acts; the Wildlife Act and the Indian Forest Act are not among them.

quiz.q: The NGT is bound by
quiz.why: Section 19 frees the NGT from CPC and Evidence Act rules but binds it to natural justice.

lessons.title: Lab: Argue before the NGT – scenario

scenes.text: Unregulated sand mining from a riverbed has collapsed a bridge pier and lowered groundwater.
You represent affected farmers seeking closure and compensation.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: Mining leases granted without environmental clearance for areas below 5 hectares, relying on an exemption later disapproved by the Supreme Court in Deepak Kumar v State of Haryana (2012), which required clearance even for small mining leases. Farmers' wells have dried; bridge damaged.

steps.title: Model argument outline
steps.body:
1. Jurisdiction: substantial question relating to environment from implementation of EPA (EIA Notification) – section 14; compensation and restitution – section 15 (within 5 years).
2. Violation: mining without EC contrary to EIA Notification and Deepak Kumar.
3. Principles: precautionary (irreversible river damage), polluter pays (restoration cost), public trust (riverbed).
4. Reliefs: halt mining; environmental compensation per unit volume; restoration plan with district survey report; compensation for wells and crops.

steps.title: Advocacy
steps.body: Ask for a joint committee (CPCB, SPCB, District Magistrate) to report on facts. The NGT frequently constitutes such committees.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting limitation. Plead the date the cause first arose and seek condonation if needed.

courses.title: Unit 5 · International Environmental Law, Revision & Exam
courses.summary: Stockholm, Rio and the major conventions (UNFCCC, Kyoto, Paris, CBD, Montreal, Basel, CITES, Ramsar), climate law in India, then a key-point sheet, problem-answer practice and a cumulative exam.
outcomes: Place the main international instruments on a timeline with their core obligations
Explain common but differentiated responsibilities and NDCs under Paris
Link each convention to its Indian implementing law
Answer problem questions using the IRAC structure with environmental cases

lessons.title: Stockholm to Rio: soft law foundations

scenes.text: In 1972, 113 countries met in Stockholm. Indira Gandhi was the only head of government other than the host to attend and spoke of poverty as a polluter.
Twenty years later, the Earth Summit in Rio produced 27 principles still quoted by courts.

steps.title: Stockholm Declaration 1972
steps.body: 26 principles; Principle 21: States have the sovereign right to exploit their resources and the responsibility to ensure activities within their jurisdiction do not cause damage to the environment of other States (echoing Trail Smelter arbitration, 1938/1941). Led to UNEP.

steps.title: Rio Declaration 1992
steps.body: Key principles: 2 (sovereignty and no-harm), 3 (inter-generational equity), 7 (common but differentiated responsibilities), 10 (public participation and access to information/justice), 15 (precautionary approach), 16 (internalisation of costs – polluter pays), 17 (EIA). Rio also produced Agenda 21, the UNFCCC and CBD (opened for signature) and the Forest Principles.

steps.title: Soft vs hard law
steps.body: Declarations are not binding treaties (soft law), but Indian courts have absorbed their principles into domestic law (Vellore Citizens).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling the Rio Declaration a treaty. The UNFCCC and CBD are treaties; the Declaration is not.

activity.prompt: Match the Rio principle

items.text: Developed countries bear greater responsibility given their pressures on the environment
Lack of full scientific certainty no reason to postpone cost-effective measures
Access to information and judicial proceedings

quiz.q: Principle 21 of Stockholm reflects which earlier arbitration?
quiz.why: Trail Smelter (US v Canada) held a State must not allow its territory to be used to cause serious transboundary fumes damage.

quiz.q: Precautionary approach is Rio Principle
quiz.why: Principle 15 states that lack of full scientific certainty shall not postpone measures where there is serious or irreversible damage.

quiz.q: Stockholm 1972 led to the creation of
quiz.why: The UN Environment Programme was established in 1972 following Stockholm.

lessons.title: Climate change and other key treaties

scenes.text: At COP21 in Paris in 2015, almost every country agreed to hold warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C.
India pledged targets through its Nationally Determined Contribution. Are these legally binding?

steps.title: Climate regime
steps.body:
- **UNFCCC (1992)**: framework; Annex I (developed) vs non-Annex I; CBDR-RC.
- **Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005)**: binding emission reduction targets only for Annex I parties; flexibility mechanisms – Clean Development Mechanism, Joint Implementation, emissions trading.
- **Paris Agreement (2015, in force 2016)**: all parties submit NDCs every five years; procedural obligations binding, achievement of NDC targets not; global stocktake every five years (first in 2023); enhanced transparency framework. India's updated NDC (2022) includes reducing emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from the 2005 level by 2030 and about 50% cumulative installed power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; India announced net zero by 2070.

steps.title: Other conventions and Indian law
steps.body:
- Montreal Protocol 1987 (ozone) → Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000; Kigali Amendment 2016 phases down HFCs.
- Basel Convention 1989 (transboundary hazardous waste) → Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016.
- CITES 1973 → Wildlife (Protection) Act (2022 amendment).
- Ramsar 1971 (wetlands) → Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017.
- CBD 1992 → Biological Diversity Act 2002.
- Stockholm Convention 2001 (persistent organic pollutants).

steps.title: M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024)
steps.body: The Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21, in a case about the Great Indian Bustard and power lines.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying India had binding Kyoto targets. India was non-Annex I and had none; it hosted many CDM projects.

quiz.why: India announced net zero by 2070 at Glasgow in 2021.

steps.body: Issue → Rule (statute + case) → Application (fact by fact) → Conclusion (remedy and forum).

scenes.text: A chemical plant in State X discharges into a river flowing into State Y, killing fish and harming farmers there.
Advise the farmers of State Y on remedies, forum and principles.

steps.title: Question (original)
steps.body: 'P Chemicals, a red-category unit in State X with valid consent, has been discharging effluent beyond prescribed standards for six months. Farmers 30 km downstream in State Y have lost crops and fish. State X's Board has taken no action. Advise the farmers.' (20 marks)

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Issues: (1) breach of standards; (2) regulator inaction; (3) compensation; (4) forum.
Rules: Water Act ss. 24–25, 33A; EPA ss. 5, 19; NGT Act ss. 14, 15; Art. 21; polluter pays (ICELA), precaution (Vellore), absolute liability (Oleum).
Application: consent does not license excess discharge; Board's inaction is a breach of statutory duty; harm is environmental and to property; cross-State nature makes CPCB's role relevant (it can direct SPCBs and, in effect, coordinate).
Conclusion: application to NGT under ss. 14 and 15 (within 6 months/5 years) for directions to stop discharge, environmental compensation and crop losses; alternatively writ under Art. 226 to State X's High Court; criminal/penalty proceedings through Board/court.

steps.title: Marks distribution
steps.body: Typically: identification of issues 3, law 6, application 7, conclusion 4. Always end with a clear remedy.

steps.title: Common mistake

uni-llb-evidence-bsa.title: Law of Evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
uni-llb-evidence-bsa.description: The law of evidence under the BSA 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024), mapped to the Indian Evidence Act, 1872: relevancy, admissions and confessions, dying declarations, expert opinion, documentary and electronic evidence, burden of proof, presumptions, estoppel and examination of witnesses. Section numbers are given only where well established; check the bare act. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB / BA LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Foundations: facts, evidence and relevancy
courses.summary: The scheme of the BSA, key definitions (fact, fact in issue, relevant, evidence, proved, disproved, not proved), relevancy vs admissibility, res gestae, motive and conduct, and statements of conspirators.
outcomes: Define and distinguish fact, fact in issue, relevant fact and evidence
Explain proved, disproved and not proved and the presumption terms
Apply the res gestae doctrine

lessons.title: Scheme of the BSA and basic definitions

scenes.text: In a murder trial, the prosecutor wants to show the accused bought a knife a week earlier and fled after the incident.
Are these facts 'evidence'? Are they 'relevant'?

steps.title: Background
steps.body: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 from 1 July 2024. It has 170 sections and largely retains the structure of the 1872 Act: Part I relevancy, Part II proof, Part III production and effect of evidence. Major changes concern electronic and digital records.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Fact**: anything capable of being perceived by the senses and any mental condition of which a person is conscious.
- **Fact in issue**: a fact from which, alone or with other facts, the existence, nature or extent of a right, liability or disability asserted or denied necessarily follows.
- **Relevant**: one fact is relevant to another when connected in any of the ways referred to in the relevancy provisions.
- **Evidence**: oral evidence (statements of witnesses, including those given electronically) and documentary evidence (including electronic or digital records).

steps.title: Proved, disproved, not proved
steps.body:
- **Proved**: after considering the matters before it, the court believes it to exist, or considers its existence so probable that a prudent man ought to act on the supposition that it exists.
- **Disproved**: the court believes it does not exist or considers its non-existence so probable.
- **Not proved**: neither proved nor disproved.
The 'prudent man' test underlies both civil (preponderance) and criminal (beyond reasonable doubt) standards.

steps.title: Presumptions
steps.body:
- **May presume**: court may regard the fact as proved unless disproved, or call for proof (discretionary).
- **Shall presume**: court shall regard it as proved unless disproved (rebuttable, mandatory).
- **Conclusive proof**: court shall regard it as proved and not allow evidence to disprove it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating relevancy with admissibility: relevancy is logical/legal connection; admissibility is whether the law permits it to be received
- Calling the accused's statement under examination 'evidence' – it is not on oath

activity.prompt: Tick statements that are correct under the BSA
items: Evidence includes electronic or digital records
A mental condition can be a fact
'Conclusive proof' cannot be disproved by evidence

quiz.q: The BSA replaced
quiz.why: The BSA replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

quiz.q: 'Conclusive proof' means
options: Court shall not allow evidence to disprove
quiz.why: Conclusive proof bars evidence to disprove the fact.

quiz.q: The test in 'proved' is that of
quiz.why: The definition uses whether a prudent man ought to act on the supposition.

lessons.title: Res gestae and facts forming part of the same transaction

scenes.text: As a man is stabbed, a bystander screams 'Ravi stabbed him!' and Ravi runs.
The bystander cannot be traced at trial. Can the scream be proved through others who heard it?

steps.title: Res gestae
steps.body: Facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the **same transaction**, are relevant whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places (old section 6). Statements made contemporaneously, as part of the transaction and without time for fabrication, are admissible.

steps.title: Cases
steps.body:
- Gentela Vijayavardhan Rao v State of AP (1996): statements must be contemporaneous with the act or immediately after, with no interval allowing fabrication.
- Sukhar v State of UP (1999): statement by an injured person immediately after the incident was held part of res gestae.

steps.title: Other connected facts
steps.body: Relevant also: facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue; facts showing opportunity; facts necessary to explain or introduce relevant facts (e.g. identity, time, place, relationship of parties).

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: The bystander's scream at the moment of stabbing is part of the same transaction → admissible through the witnesses who heard it. A statement made two hours later at the police station is not res gestae.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Extending res gestae to narratives given after reflection
- Forgetting that the transaction must be identified first

activity.prompt: Tick conditions for a statement to be part of res gestae
items: Connected to the fact in issue

quiz.q: Res gestae concerns facts
options: Forming part of the same transaction
quiz.why: Res gestae covers facts so connected as to form part of the same transaction.

quiz.q: A statement made hours later after reflection is
quiz.why: Time for fabrication breaks the contemporaneity required.

quiz.q: Gentela Vijayavardhan Rao stressed
quiz.why: The Court required statements to be contemporaneous with the act.

scenes.text: A week before the murder, the accused bought a knife; after it, he fled to another state.
Both facts may be relevant.

steps.title: Motive, preparation, conduct (old section 8)
steps.body: Any fact showing or constituting a motive or preparation for any fact in issue is relevant. The conduct of a party or agent, and of an accused, in reference to the proceeding, before or after the fact in issue, is relevant if it influences or is influenced by a fact in issue. Absconding is relevant conduct, though weak alone.

steps.title: Identification
steps.body: Facts establishing identity of anything or person are relevant (old section 9). Test identification parades (TIP) during investigation are used to test the memory of witnesses; the substantive evidence is the identification in court. Delay in holding a TIP reduces its value.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body:
1. Buying a knife – preparation.
2. Enmity over land – motive.
3. Fleeing – subsequent conduct.
4. Washing blood-stained clothes – conduct.
None alone proves guilt; they are links in circumstantial evidence.

steps.title: Circumstantial evidence
steps.body: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v State of Maharashtra (1984): the 'five golden principles' – circumstances fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive in nature, excluding every other hypothesis, and forming a complete chain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a TIP as substantive evidence
- Convicting on motive alone

lessons.title: Statements of conspirators and other relevant facts

scenes.text: One conspirator messages the group: 'Bring the cash to the godown tonight, as planned.'

steps.title: Things said or done by conspirators (old section 10)
steps.body: Where there are reasonable grounds to believe that two or more persons have conspired to commit an offence or an actionable wrong, anything said, done or written by any one of them in reference to their common intention, after the time when such intention was first entertained, is relevant against each, for proving the existence of the conspiracy and that any such person was a party to it.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Statements after the conspiracy ends (e.g. after arrest) are not covered. Kehar Singh v State (Delhi Admn) (1988, Indira Gandhi assassination) and State v Nalini (1999, Rajiv Gandhi assassination) discussed the scope.

steps.title: Other relevancy rules
steps.body:
- Facts inconsistent with or making probable a fact in issue (e.g. alibi) – old section 11
- In suits for damages, facts enabling the court to determine the amount
- Facts showing existence of a state of mind or body (intention, good faith, negligence)
- Facts bearing on whether an act was accidental or intentional (series of similar acts)

- Forgetting that prima facie grounds of conspiracy must first exist

courses.title: Unit 2 · Admissions, confessions and dying declarations
courses.summary: Admissions and their evidentiary value; confessions – voluntariness, bar on confessions to police and in police custody, the discovery exception, retracted and co-accused confessions; and statements of persons who cannot be called, especially dying declarations.
outcomes: Distinguish admission from confession
Apply the exclusion of confessions to police and the discovery proviso
Evaluate retracted and co-accused confessions
Test a dying declaration for admissibility and reliability

scenes.text: In a civil suit for unpaid rent, the tenant had emailed: 'I know I owe you three months' rent; I'll pay soon.'
Can the landlord rely on it?

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: An admission is a statement, oral or documentary or contained in electronic form, which suggests any inference as to a fact in issue or relevant fact, made by specified persons – a party, an agent authorised, persons with a joint proprietary interest, predecessors in interest, persons whose position must be proved against a party, and persons expressly referred to by a party.

steps.title: Value
steps.body: Admissions are not conclusive proof but may operate as estoppel. They are substantive evidence and can be explained. An admission may be proved against the maker; it cannot generally be proved by or on behalf of the maker except in limited situations (e.g. if it would be relevant as a dying declaration or res gestae).

steps.title: Civil without-prejudice rule
steps.body: In civil cases, an admission made upon an express condition that evidence of it is not to be given, or in circumstances showing the parties agreed it should not be given, is not relevant (settlement negotiations).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating admissions as conclusive
- Ignoring 'without prejudice' communications

activity.prompt: Tick persons whose statements can be admissions against a party
items: A person with joint proprietary interest

quiz.q: Admissions are
quiz.why: Admissions are not conclusive but may operate as estoppel.

quiz.q: Statements in settlement talks made without prejudice in civil cases are
quiz.why: The law excludes without-prejudice admissions in civil cases.

quiz.q: The tenant's email is
quiz.why: It is a statement by a party suggesting an inference about the fact in issue.

scenes.text: After two days in police custody, the accused tells the inspector he killed the victim and hid the knife under a well.
The police recover the knife from that well. What is admissible?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: A confession is an admission by an accused stating or suggesting the inference that he committed the crime. Pakala Narayana Swami v Emperor (1939): a confession must admit the offence or substantially all facts constituting it; an exculpatory statement is not a confession. Palvinder Kaur v State of Punjab (1952): a confession must be accepted or rejected as a whole.

steps.title: Exclusions
steps.body:
- Confession caused by inducement, threat, coercion or promise from a person in authority, relating to the charge, is irrelevant (old section 24).
- Confession to a police officer shall not be proved against the accused (old section 25).
- Confession made while in police custody is not provable unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate (old section 26).
In the BSA these are in sections 22 and 23.

steps.title: Discovery proviso (old section 27)
steps.body: When any fact is discovered in consequence of information received from an accused in police custody, so much of the information, whether a confession or not, as relates **distinctly** to the fact discovered may be proved. In the BSA this is the proviso to section 23. Pulukuri Kottaya v Emperor (1947): 'fact discovered' includes the place, the knowledge of the accused, and the object; only 'I hid it under the well' is admissible, not 'I killed him'.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Admissible: 'I hid the knife under the well' + recovery. Inadmissible: 'I killed the victim with this knife'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Admitting the whole confession because recovery followed
- Forgetting that confessions to a Magistrate under the procedure code are admissible if voluntary

Only the portion distinctly relating to the discovery is proved
