scenes.text: Accused A confesses before a Magistrate implicating himself and B; at trial A retracts.
Can the court convict A, and use the confession against B?

steps.title: Retracted confession
steps.body: A retracted confession may be relied upon if the court is satisfied it was voluntary and true; prudence requires general corroboration on material particulars (Subramania Goundan v State of Madras, 1958).

steps.title: Confession of a co-accused
steps.body: When persons are jointly tried for the same offence and a confession by one affecting himself and others is proved, the court may take it into consideration against the others (old section 30). It is not substantive evidence; it can only lend assurance to other evidence – Kashmira Singh v State of MP (1952); Haricharan Kurmi v State of Bihar (1964). The BSA explanation clarifies that trial of multiple persons where an accused has absconded or not responded to a proclamation is treated as a joint trial.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: A: conviction possible if confession found voluntary and corroborated. B: the confession cannot be the foundation; the court must first marshal other evidence against B and then use the confession to lend assurance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a co-accused's confession as substantive evidence
- Rejecting all retracted confessions automatically

activity.prompt: Order the Kashmira Singh approach against B
items: If other evidence is believable, use confession to lend assurance
Reach a conclusion on B's guilt

quiz.why: Kashmira Singh held it is not substantive evidence.

quiz.q: A retracted confession can be relied on if
quiz.why: Courts rely on retracted confessions that are voluntary and corroborated.

quiz.why: The rule applies to persons jointly tried for the same offence.

scenes.text: A woman with 80% burns tells the Magistrate her husband poured kerosene on her. She dies the next day.
The defence says she was not in a fit state to speak.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: Statements, written or verbal, of relevant facts made by a person who is dead, when the statement is as to the cause of his death or any circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, are relevant in cases where the cause of death is in question, whether or not the person expected death at the time, and in any proceeding (old section 32(1); BSA section 26).

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
- Khushal Rao v State of Bombay (1958): a dying declaration can be the sole basis of conviction if true and voluntary; no rule requires corroboration.
- Laxman v State of Maharashtra (2002): a doctor's certificate of fitness is a rule of prudence, not an absolute requirement; the Magistrate's satisfaction may suffice.
- Multiple declarations: if inconsistent, the court examines which is reliable.
- Indian law does not require expectation of death (unlike English law).

steps.title: Checklist for reliability
steps.body: Mental fitness; voluntary, not tutored; recorded preferably by a Magistrate in the declarant's words; question-answer form where possible; signature or thumb impression; consistency; opportunity to observe the assailant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Requiring corroboration as a rule
- Requiring the declarant to expect death

Recorded in her own words, preferably by a Magistrate
Consistency with other declarations and medical evidence

courses.title: Unit 3 · Opinion, character, documentary and electronic evidence
courses.summary: Expert and non-expert opinion; character evidence in civil and criminal cases; oral evidence and the hearsay rule; primary and secondary documentary evidence; and the admissibility of electronic records with the certificate under section 63 BSA.
outcomes: Explain when expert opinion is relevant and its evidentiary value
Apply rules on character evidence
Distinguish primary from secondary evidence
Prepare the certificate needed for electronic records under section 63

scenes.text: In a forged-will case, a handwriting expert says the signature is not the testator's.
The other side's expert says it is. What weight do such opinions carry?

steps.title: Expert opinion
steps.body: When the court has to form an opinion on foreign law, science, art, or any other field, or identity of handwriting or finger impressions, opinions of persons specially skilled are relevant. The BSA expressly includes 'any other field' and examiners of electronic evidence. Experts must give reasons; opinion is advisory and generally requires corroboration, especially handwriting opinion (Murari Lal v State of MP, 1980 – no rule that handwriting opinion can never be acted on without corroboration, but caution is needed).

steps.title: Non-expert opinion
steps.body: Opinions of persons acquainted with handwriting; opinions on existence of general customs or rights; on usages of bodies of men; on relationships, shown by conduct; and on electronic signatures by certifying authorities.

steps.title: Character evidence
steps.body:
- Civil cases: character to prove conduct imputed is irrelevant, except where character itself is in issue.
- Criminal cases: previous good character of the accused is relevant; previous bad character is irrelevant unless evidence of good character has been given (then rebuttal allowed), or bad character is itself a fact in issue.
- In sexual offences, evidence of the victim's character or previous sexual experience is not relevant on the issue of consent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating expert opinion as binding
- Leading bad character evidence of the accused in chief

activity.prompt: Tick when an accused's bad character becomes relevant
items: Accused has led evidence of good character
Bad character is itself a fact in issue
Previous conviction is relevant as evidence of bad character in such cases

quiz.why: Courts evaluate expert reasoning and are not bound by opinion.

quiz.q: In criminal cases, good character of the accused is
quiz.why: Previous good character of the accused is relevant.

quiz.q: Victim's previous sexual experience on consent in rape cases is
quiz.why: The law makes such character evidence irrelevant to consent.

scenes.text: A witness says: 'My neighbour told me he saw the accused climbing the wall.'
The judge stops the testimony. Why?

steps.title: Oral evidence must be direct
steps.body: If it refers to a fact which could be seen, it must be evidence of a witness who says he saw it; heard – who heard it; perceived by any other sense – who perceived it; an opinion – of the person holding that opinion. Hearsay is generally excluded because it is not on oath, not tested by cross-examination, and multiplies error.

steps.title: Exceptions
steps.body: Res gestae; admissions and confessions; statements of persons who cannot be called (dying declarations, statements in course of business, against interest); evidence in former proceedings when the witness is dead or unavailable; expert treatises in some cases.

steps.title: Oral evidence electronically
steps.body: The BSA allows oral evidence to be given electronically, supporting testimony through video conferencing as permitted by procedure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all out-of-court statements hearsay – some are relevant as facts (e.g. a threat)
- Ignoring statutory exceptions

activity.prompt: Tick reasons hearsay is excluded

quiz.why: Oral evidence must in all cases be direct.

quiz.why: Statements of persons who cannot be called, like dying declarations, are exceptions.

quiz.why: The witness did not perceive the fact himself.

scenes.text: The original sale deed was destroyed in a flood; only a certified copy from the registry remains.
Can the certified copy be used?

steps.title: Primary evidence
steps.body: The document itself produced for inspection. Each part of a document executed in several parts, and each counterpart against the party executing it, is primary. Documents made by a uniform process (printing, lithography) are primary of the rest. The BSA adds that an electronic or digital record is primary evidence, including where it is created or stored in multiple files simultaneously or sequentially, and where it is produced from proper custody.

steps.title: Secondary evidence
steps.body: Certified copies; copies by mechanical processes ensuring accuracy; copies made from or compared with the original; counterparts against non-executing parties; oral accounts of contents by someone who has seen it. The BSA adds oral and written admissions and evidence of a person skilled in examination of documents too voluminous to be examined in court.

steps.title: When secondary evidence is allowed
steps.body: Original in possession of the adverse party who does not produce it after notice; original destroyed or lost; original not easily movable; public document; certified copy permitted by law; voluminous accounts.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Original destroyed by flood → secondary evidence allowed; a certified copy of a registered deed is admissible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Producing a photocopy without laying foundation for secondary evidence
- Skipping notice to the adverse party holding the original

items: Produce the certified copy or other secondary evidence

quiz.why: Certified copies are listed as secondary evidence.

lessons.title: Lab: Admitting electronic evidence – the section 63 certificate

scenes.text: Police seize a CCTV DVR from a shop and copy the footage to a pen drive for court.
Defence objects: 'No certificate.' What is needed?

steps.title: Section 63 BSA (old section 65B)
steps.body: Information in an electronic record printed, stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory produced by a computer or any communication device is deemed a document and admissible without further proof of the original, if conditions are met: regular use of the device, information regularly fed in the ordinary course, device operating properly, and the information reproduces or is derived from such information fed in.

steps.title: The certificate
steps.body: A certificate must accompany the record each time it is submitted. The BSA prescribes a certificate in a Schedule with two parts: Part A filled by the party (person in charge of the device) and Part B by an expert. It identifies the record, describes the device and manner of production, and gives the hash value(s) of the record.

steps.title: Case law
steps.body:
- Anvar P.V. v P.K. Basheer (2014): certificate mandatory for secondary electronic evidence.
- Shafhi Mohammad (2018) relaxed it; overruled by Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020): certificate is a condition precedent; not needed only when the original device itself is produced and its owner testifies; court can direct production of certificate if refused by the custodian.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Pen drive copy = secondary → certificate (Part A by shop owner/person in charge of DVR; Part B by an expert) with hash values. If the DVR itself is produced and the owner testifies, it is primary evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filing printouts of WhatsApp chats with no certificate
- Not recording hash values at seizure, making integrity hard to show

courses.title: Unit 4 · Burden of proof, presumptions, estoppel and witnesses
courses.summary: Burden of proof and its shifting; special burdens and statutory presumptions including dowry death; estoppel; competency and privilege of witnesses; accomplice evidence; and examination-in-chief, cross-examination, leading questions, hostile witnesses and refreshing memory.
outcomes: Distinguish legal burden from evidential burden
Apply statutory presumptions in dowry death and other cases
State the elements and kinds of estoppel
Conduct examination of witnesses correctly, including handling hostile witnesses

scenes.text: The prosecution proves the accused was seen near the scene; the accused claims he was in another city.
Who bears the burden of the alibi?

steps.title: General rule
steps.body: Whoever desires a court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts he asserts must prove that those facts exist (old section 101). The burden lies on the person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side. The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on the person who wishes the court to believe in its existence (e.g. alibi on the accused).

steps.title: Legal vs evidential burden
steps.body: The legal burden (to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt) stays on the prosecution throughout. The evidential burden (onus) may shift during trial. Where the accused relies on a general or special exception, the burden is on him, on a preponderance of probabilities. Facts especially within knowledge of a person must be proved by him (old section 106) – used, for example, when a person was last seen with the deceased in a closed house (Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v State of Maharashtra, 2006).

steps.title: Statutory presumptions
steps.body:
- Abetment of suicide by a married woman within seven years of marriage where cruelty is shown – court **may** presume.
- Dowry death: when a woman was subjected to cruelty or harassment soon before death in connection with dowry, the court **shall** presume the person caused the dowry death.
- Absence of consent in certain rape prosecutions where the woman states she did not consent.
- Birth during marriage is conclusive proof of legitimacy (subject to non-access).
- Presumption of death when unheard of for seven years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the burden of proof shifts to the accused for guilt
- Using 'facts within special knowledge' to relieve the prosecution of its primary burden

scenes.text: A tenant who has paid rent for ten years suddenly claims the landlord never owned the house.
Can he deny the landlord's title?

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: When one person has, by declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between them, to deny the truth of that thing (old section 115).

steps.title: Elements and kinds
steps.body:
Elements: representation of an existing fact; intention or permission that the other believes it; the other acts on it to his detriment.
Kinds: estoppel by record (res judicata), by deed, by conduct (equitable), promissory estoppel (Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v State of UP, 1979). Tenant estoppel: a tenant cannot deny the landlord's title at the beginning of the tenancy; a licensee cannot deny the licensor's title.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: No estoppel against a statute; estoppel is a rule of evidence, not a cause of action; no estoppel on a question of law; a minor's misrepresentation of age does not create a contract by estoppel (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, 1903).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating estoppel as a cause of action
- Applying estoppel against statute

quiz.why: Tenant estoppel bars denial of the landlord's title at the commencement of tenancy.

quiz.why: Estoppel cannot override statutory provisions.

quiz.why: Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills applied promissory estoppel against the government.

scenes.text: A seven-year-old is the only eyewitness to her mother's murder.
Can she testify? Does her evidence need corroboration?

steps.title: Competency
steps.body: All persons are competent to testify unless the court considers they are prevented from understanding the questions or giving rational answers by tender years, extreme old age, disease of body or mind. A child witness may be examined after a preliminary test of understanding; corroboration is a rule of prudence (Dattu Ramrao Sakhare v State of Maharashtra, 1997). A witness unable to speak may give evidence by writing or signs, recorded with an interpreter's help and videographed.

steps.title: Privileged communications
steps.body:
- Communications during marriage (except in suits between spouses or prosecution for offence by one against the other)
- Affairs of State – unpublished official records
- Official communications in confidence
- Professional communications between client and advocate
- No witness is excused from answering on the ground the answer may incriminate, but such answer cannot be used to prosecute him except for false evidence

steps.title: Accomplice
steps.body: An accomplice is a competent witness and a conviction based on uncorroborated accomplice testimony is not illegal; yet the court may presume (illustration) that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless corroborated in material particulars – reconciled in Bhuboni Sahu v The King (1949) and later cases: corroboration is a rule of prudence that has hardened into practice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying children below a certain age cannot testify – no age bar exists
- Treating accomplice evidence as inadmissible

scenes.text: A prosecution eyewitness who supported the case in his police statement now says he saw nothing.
The prosecutor seeks permission to cross-examine his own witness.

steps.title: Order of examination
steps.body: Examination-in-chief by the party calling the witness → cross-examination by the adverse party → re-examination (only on matters arising in cross, unless court permits new matter, then further cross). Examination and cross must relate to relevant facts; cross need not be confined to facts stated in chief.

steps.title: Leading questions
steps.body: A leading question suggests the answer the questioner wishes. Not allowed in chief or re-examination if objected, except on introductory or undisputed matters or with court permission; allowed in cross-examination.

steps.title: Hostile witness
steps.body: The court may permit the person who calls a witness to put questions which might be put in cross-examination. The evidence of a hostile witness is not wiped off; the part found credible may be relied on (Sat Paul v Delhi Administration, 1976; Bhagwan Singh v State of Haryana, 1976). Previous police statements can be used to contradict, following the procedure of drawing attention to the parts to be used.

steps.title: Refreshing memory
steps.body: A witness may refresh memory by referring to a writing made by himself at the time of the transaction or soon after, or by another and read by him then and known to be correct; an expert may refresh from professional treatises. The adverse party may see the writing and cross-examine on it.

steps.title: Sample
steps.body:
Leading (bad in chief): 'You saw A stab B with a knife at 9 p.m., didn't you?'
Non-leading: 'What did you see at about 9 p.m.?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the entire testimony of a hostile witness as worthless
- Asking leading questions in chief on disputed facts

uni-llb-family-law.title: Family Law I & II: Marriage, Divorce, Adoption, Guardianship and Succession
uni-llb-family-law.description: Family Law I and II for Indian law students: sources and schools; Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Special Marriage Act marriages; matrimonial remedies and maintenance; domestic violence; adoption and guardianship; the Hindu joint family and succession; Muslim inheritance and wills; and the Indian Succession Act. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB / BA LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Sources of family law and Hindu marriage
courses.summary: Sources and schools of Hindu and Muslim law; who is a Hindu; the conditions and ceremonies of a valid Hindu marriage; void and voidable marriages; registration; and the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act.
outcomes: Identify sources and schools of Hindu and Muslim personal law
Determine to whom the Hindu Marriage Act applies
Apply sections 5 and 7 of the HMA to decide validity
Distinguish void (section 11) from voidable (section 12) marriages

lessons.title: Sources and schools; who is a Hindu

story.title: The Sikh groom and the Jain bride

scenes.text: A Sikh man marries a Jain woman with Hindu rites in Delhi.
Which law governs their marriage?

steps.title: Sources
steps.body:
Hindu law: Shruti (Vedas), Smritis (Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada), commentaries and digests (Mitakshara by Vijnaneshwara, Dayabhaga by Jimutavahana), custom, judicial decisions and legislation (the codifying Acts of 1955–56).
Muslim law: Quran, Sunna (traditions), Ijma (consensus), Qiyas (analogy); secondary – custom, judicial decisions, legislation (Shariat Application Act 1937, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939).

steps.title: Schools
steps.body: Hindu: Mitakshara (most of India) and Dayabhaga (Bengal, Assam). Muslim: Sunni (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and Shia (Ithna Ashari, Ismaili, Zaidi).

steps.title: Who is a Hindu
steps.body: The HMA, HSA, HAMA and HMGA apply to Hindus by religion in any form (including Virashaivas, Lingayats, followers of Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj), Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, and any other person domiciled in India who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless proved not governed by Hindu law. They do not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless the Central Government directs otherwise.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: The Sikh groom and Jain bride are both 'Hindus' for the HMA, so their marriage is governed by the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists are outside the HMA
- Forgetting the Scheduled Tribes exclusion

quiz.why: Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara commentary on Yajnavalkya Smriti.

quiz.why: Section 2(2) excludes Scheduled Tribes unless notified otherwise.

quiz.q: Qiyas means
quiz.why: Qiyas is reasoning by analogy, a source of Muslim law.

lessons.title: Conditions and ceremonies of a Hindu marriage (sections 5 and 7)

scenes.text: A 22-year-old man and 19-year-old woman marry in a temple; the saptapadi is performed.
Later the husband claims the marriage is invalid because it was not registered.

steps.title: Section 5 – conditions
steps.body:
(i) Neither party has a spouse living at the time (monogamy)
(ii) Neither party is incapable of valid consent due to unsoundness of mind, or suffers from mental disorder making them unfit for marriage and procreation, or recurrent insanity
(iii) Bridegroom has completed 21 years and bride 18 years
(iv) Parties not within degrees of prohibited relationship, unless custom permits
(v) Parties not sapindas of each other, unless custom permits

steps.title: Section 7 – ceremonies
steps.body: A Hindu marriage may be solemnised according to customary rites and ceremonies of either party. Where these include saptapadi (seven steps before the sacred fire), the marriage is complete and binding when the seventh step is taken. Section 7A recognises suyamariyathai/seerthiruththa marriages in Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Registration (section 8)
steps.body: Registration is evidence of marriage; failure to register does not affect validity. Seema v Ashwani Kumar (2006): the Supreme Court directed compulsory registration of marriages by States, without making unregistered marriages invalid.

steps.title: Ceremonies essential
steps.body: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v State of Maharashtra (1965): for bigamy, the second marriage must be proved to be solemnised with due ceremonies. Dolly Rani v Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024): a Hindu marriage needs the ceremonies; a mere certificate without solemnisation is not a valid marriage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating registration as essential for validity
- Forgetting that age violation does not make the marriage void under section 11

quiz.why: Registration is only evidence; validity depends on conditions and ceremonies.

scenes.text: Two months after marriage, Asha discovers her husband had a living wife when he married her.
Is her marriage void or voidable, and are any children legitimate?

steps.title: Void marriages (section 11)
steps.body: A marriage solemnised after the Act is null and void, and may be declared so by a decree on a petition by either party, if it contravenes section 5 clause (i) (spouse living), (iv) (prohibited degrees) or (v) (sapindas).

steps.title: Voidable marriages (section 12)
steps.body: Annullable by decree on grounds: (a) non-consummation owing to impotence of the respondent; (b) contravention of section 5(ii) (mental capacity); (c) consent obtained by force or by fraud as to the nature of ceremony or any material fact or circumstance concerning the respondent; (d) respondent pregnant by someone else at the time of marriage. Time limits and bars apply to (c) and (d) (e.g. petition within one year of discovering fraud or force ceasing).

steps.title: Legitimacy (section 16)
steps.body: Children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate. Revanasiddappa v Mallikarjun (2023, Constitution Bench): such children are entitled to their parent's share in coparcenary property, determined by a notional partition, but not to rights in others' property.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Asha's marriage contravenes section 5(i) – void ab initio under section 11; a decree of nullity can be obtained. Any child is legitimate under section 16. The husband may face bigamy prosecution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating child-marriage age violation as a ground under section 11
- Saying children of void marriages are illegitimate

steps.title: Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
steps.body: A 'child' means a male below 21 and a female below 18. A child marriage is **voidable** at the option of the contracting party who was a child, by petition within two years of attaining majority. It is void in specified cases – where the child is enticed, taken by force, sold or trafficked.

steps.title: Offences
steps.body: Punishable: a male adult above 18 marrying a child; persons who perform, conduct, direct or abet a child marriage; parents or guardians promoting or permitting it. Offences are cognizable and non-bailable. Child Marriage Prohibition Officers are appointed by States.

steps.title: Courts
steps.body: Independent Thought v Union of India (2017): sexual intercourse with a wife below 18 is rape; the exception was read down. Society for Enlightenment and Voluntary Action v Union of India (2024) issued guidelines for preventing child marriages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all child marriages are void
- Forgetting the two-year limitation after attaining majority

courses.summary: Restitution of conjugal rights, judicial separation, divorce on fault and other grounds, divorce by mutual consent, irretrievable breakdown, bars to relief, and maintenance and alimony under the HMA and HAMA.

lessons.title: Restitution of conjugal rights and judicial separation

story.title: The wife who left for a job

scenes.text: A wife takes a job in another city; the husband files for restitution of conjugal rights.
Is taking a job a 'reasonable excuse' for withdrawal from society?

steps.title: Section 9 – restitution
steps.body: When either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved spouse may petition for restitution. The burden of proving reasonable excuse is on the person who has withdrawn. Saroj Rani v Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) upheld section 9 as constitutional, though the Andhra Pradesh High Court in T. Sareetha (1983) had struck it down. Non-compliance with a decree for one year is a ground for divorce.

steps.title: Section 10 – judicial separation
steps.body: Either spouse may seek judicial separation on any ground for divorce (and the wife on the additional grounds in section 13(2)). After the decree, cohabitation is not obligatory. If no resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after the decree, either party may seek divorce.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a decree of restitution is enforced physically
- Treating judicial separation as dissolution of marriage

activity.prompt: Order the path from restitution to divorce
items: Spouse withdraws from society without reasonable excuse
Aggrieved spouse obtains decree of restitution
No restitution for one year after decree

quiz.why: Section 9 places it on the person who has withdrawn.

quiz.why: The Supreme Court upheld it in 1984.

quiz.why: The decree relieves the parties from the duty to cohabit.

scenes.text: A husband constantly humiliates his wife before relatives and files false complaints against her parents.
No physical violence – can she get divorce for cruelty?

steps.title: Section 13(1) – either spouse
steps.body:
(i) voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than spouse after marriage (adultery)
(ia) cruelty
(ib) desertion for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the petition
(ii) conversion to another religion
(iii) incurable unsoundness of mind or mental disorder
(v) venereal disease in communicable form
(vi) renounced the world by entering a religious order
(vii) not heard of as alive for seven years
The leprosy ground was omitted in 2019.

steps.title: Section 13(1A) and 13(2)
steps.body:
13(1A): no resumption of cohabitation for one year after judicial separation; no restitution for one year after restitution decree.
13(2) – wife's additional grounds: husband's other wife living (pre-Act bigamy); husband guilty of rape, sodomy or bestiality; non-resumption of cohabitation for one year after maintenance order; marriage solemnised before she was 15 and she repudiated it after 15 but before 18.

steps.title: Cruelty cases
steps.body:
- Dastane v Dastane (1975): standard is preponderance of probabilities; cruelty need not be physical.
- Samar Ghosh v Jaya Ghosh (2007): illustrative list of mental cruelty.
- K. Srinivas Rao v D.A. Deepa (2013): false criminal complaints can be mental cruelty.

steps.title: Desertion
steps.body: Requires factum of separation, animus deserendi (intention to end cohabitation permanently), absence of consent and of reasonable cause, and the two-year period. Bipinchandra Shah v Prabhavati (1957) is the classic case.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing leprosy as a current ground
- Requiring physical violence for cruelty

scenes.text: A couple separated for three years agree to divorce and settle all claims.

steps.title: Section 13B
steps.body: Joint petition on the ground that they have been living separately for one year or more, cannot live together and have mutually agreed to dissolve the marriage. A second motion is made not earlier than six months and not later than eighteen months after the first. No petition within one year of marriage except under section 14 for exceptional hardship.

steps.title: Cooling period waiver
steps.body: Amardeep Singh v Harveen Kaur (2017): the six-month period is directory and may be waived if: separation of 18 months already before the first motion; mediation and reconciliation failed; parties settled all issues; waiting would prolong agony.

steps.title: Irretrievable breakdown
steps.body: Not a statutory ground under the HMA. Shilpa Sailesh v Varun Sreenivasan (2023, Constitution Bench): the Supreme Court can dissolve a marriage on irretrievable breakdown under Article 142 and dispense with the 13B waiting period, considering factors like period of separation and attempts at reconciliation. Consent can be withdrawn before the second motion (Sureshta Devi v Om Prakash, 1991).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming lower courts can grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown
- Assuming consent cannot be withdrawn

scenes.text: A non-earning wife needs money for the litigation and her living while the divorce case is pending.
Her husband earns ₹1,20,000 net per month.

steps.title: HMA sections 24 and 25
steps.body:
Section 24: maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings to either spouse with no independent income sufficient for support; application to be disposed of within 60 days of service of notice as far as possible.
Section 25: permanent alimony and maintenance at the time of the decree or later, to either spouse, considering income, property and conduct; may be varied or rescinded on change of circumstances, remarriage or unchastity.

steps.title: HAMA, 1956
steps.body: Section 18: a Hindu wife is entitled to be maintained by her husband during her lifetime, and may live separately without forfeiting maintenance on grounds such as desertion, cruelty, another wife living, conversion. Section 20: maintenance of children and aged or infirm parents. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law from father-in-law in certain cases.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Husband's net income ₹1,20,000/month; wife has no income. Using the commonly cited 25% benchmark from Kalyan Dey Chowdhury (2017): 0.25 × 1,20,000 = **₹30,000/month** for the wife, adjustable for child expenses, liabilities and standard of living. Rajnesh v Neha (2020): affidavits of disclosure, maintenance from date of application, and adjustment of amounts awarded under different statutes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only wives can claim under sections 24 and 25 – they are gender-neutral
- Treating the 25% figure as statutory

courses.title: Unit 3 · Muslim law: marriage, mahr, divorce and maintenance
courses.summary: Nikah as a contract, its essentials and classification (valid, void, irregular), mahr, iddat, modes of divorce including talaq, khula, mubarat and judicial divorce under the 1939 Act, the triple talaq decision and the 2019 Act, and maintenance of Muslim women.
outcomes: State the essentials of a valid nikah and classify marriages
Explain kinds of mahr and the wife's remedies
Distinguish modes of talaq and the effect of Shayara Bano and the 2019 Act
List grounds under the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939
Explain maintenance after Shah Bano, Danial Latifi and later decisions

scenes.text: A widow marries again one month after her husband's death.
Is the marriage void, irregular or valid?

steps.title: Nature and essentials
steps.body: Nikah is a civil contract (Abdul Kadir v Salima, 1886, Mahmood J) with religious significance. Essentials: proposal (ijab) and acceptance (qubul) at one meeting; competence – Muslims of sound mind who have attained puberty (presumed at 15 in the absence of evidence); free consent; absence of prohibitions; under Sunni law two adult Muslim male witnesses (or one male and two females); no witnesses needed under Shia law.

steps.title: Classification (Sunni law)
steps.body:
- **Valid (sahih)**: all conditions met.
- **Void (batil)**: absolute prohibitions – consanguinity, affinity, fosterage; marrying another's wife. No legal effects; children illegitimate.
- **Irregular (fasid)**: relative prohibitions – no witnesses; fifth wife; marriage during iddat; difference of religion (Muslim man with non-kitabia); unlawful conjunction (two sisters). Can be regularised; children legitimate; wife entitled to mahr if consummated.
Shia law recognises only valid and void.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Marriage during iddat (widow's iddat is 4 months 10 days) → irregular under Sunni law; void under Shia law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Muslim marriage as a sacrament only
- Classifying all prohibited marriages as void under Sunni law

activity.prompt: Tick grounds that make a Sunni marriage irregular (fasid)
items: Unlawful conjunction such as two sisters

quiz.why: Mahmood J called it a civil contract.

quiz.why: The widow's iddat is four months and ten days.

quiz.q: A fifth marriage while four wives live is, in Sunni law,
quiz.why: It is a relative prohibition, making the marriage fasid.

scenes.text: A wife's mahr of ₹5 lakh was 'deferred' and never paid. Her husband dies.
She remains in possession of his house. Can she keep it?

steps.title: Mahr
steps.body: Mahr is a sum of money or property the wife is entitled to receive from the husband in consideration of marriage, an obligation imposed by law as a mark of respect (Mahmood J in Abdul Kadir). Kinds: **specified** (fixed by agreement) – prompt (payable on demand) or deferred (payable on dissolution by death or divorce); and **proper/customary** (mahr-ul-misl), when not fixed, determined by the mahr of her paternal female relatives and her qualities.

steps.title: Wife's remedies
steps.body:
- Refuse cohabitation until prompt mahr is paid (before consummation)
- Sue as a debt
- Right of retention: a widow lawfully in possession of the husband's property in lieu of unpaid mahr may retain it until paid; it is not a title and cannot be transferred (Maina Bibi v Chaudhri Vakil Ahmad, 1924).

steps.title: Iddat
steps.body: Waiting period during which the woman cannot remarry: on divorce, three menstrual courses (or three lunar months); on death, 4 months 10 days; if pregnant, until delivery. No iddat on divorce if marriage was not consummated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating retention as ownership
- Forgetting that unpaid mahr is a debt against the husband's estate

Widow is lawfully in possession of his property

lessons.title: Divorce: talaq, khula, mubarat and the 1939 Act

scenes.text: A husband sends 'talaq talaq talaq' to his wife on WhatsApp.
Is the marriage dissolved? Has he committed an offence?

steps.title: Talaq by husband
steps.body:
- **Talaq-ul-sunnat** (approved): ahsan – single pronouncement in a tuhr (period of purity) followed by abstinence during iddat; hasan – three pronouncements in three successive tuhrs.
- **Talaq-ul-biddat** (disapproved): three pronouncements at once – instantly irrevocable.
Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017): talaq-e-biddat set aside. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 declares instant triple talaq in any form (spoken, written, electronic) void and illegal, punishable with up to three years and fine; the wife can claim subsistence allowance and custody of minor children.

steps.title: Other modes
steps.body:
- **Ila** and **zihar** (historic forms)
- **Talaq-e-tafweez**: delegated divorce – wife exercises a power delegated to her
- **Khula**: divorce at the wife's instance, usually returning mahr or other consideration
- **Mubarat**: mutual divorce where both desire it
- **Lian**: on false charge of adultery by husband

steps.title: Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939 (section 2)
steps.body: A wife may obtain a decree on grounds including: husband's whereabouts unknown for 4 years; failure to maintain for 2 years; imprisonment for 7 years or more; failure to perform marital obligations without reasonable cause for 3 years; impotence; insanity for 2 years, leprosy or virulent venereal disease; option of puberty – married before 15, repudiated before 18 if not consummated; cruelty, including unequal treatment of co-wives; any other ground recognised under Muslim law.

steps.title: Shamim Ara v State of UP (2002)
steps.body: A mere plea of talaq in a written statement does not effect divorce; talaq must be for a reasonable cause and preceded by attempts at reconciliation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all talaq is abolished – only instant talaq-e-biddat
- Forgetting the wife's statutory route under the 1939 Act

quiz.why: Instant triple talaq was set aside.

scenes.text: A 62-year-old woman divorced after 40 years of marriage receives only mahr and iddat maintenance.
Can she claim more?

steps.title: The line of cases
steps.body:
- Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985): divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself can claim under the secular provision (then CrPC 125).
- Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986: reasonable and fair provision and maintenance within the iddat period, mahr, and properties.
- Danial Latifi v Union of India (2001): upheld the 1986 Act, reading it to require a reasonable and fair provision for her future, to be made within iddat; not limited to the iddat period.
- Mohd. Abdul Samad v State of Telangana (2024): a divorced Muslim woman can also claim under the secular provision (now BNSS section 144); the 1986 Act does not exclude it.

steps.title: Structure an answer
steps.body:
1. Personal law position (iddat maintenance, mahr)
2. Shah Bano
3. 1986 Act
4. Danial Latifi
5. Abdul Samad (2024)
6. Conclusion on current law

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying maintenance ends with iddat
- Ignoring the 2024 decision

courses.title: Unit 4 · Special Marriage Act, domestic violence, adoption and guardianship
courses.summary: Inter-faith and civil marriages under the Special Marriage Act; an overview of Christian and Parsi marriage laws; protection under the Domestic Violence Act 2005; adoption under HAMA and the Juvenile Justice Act; guardianship and custody.
outcomes: Describe the SMA notice and solemnisation procedure

lessons.title: Special Marriage Act and other personal laws

scenes.text: A Hindu woman and a Christian man want to marry without either converting.
They approach the Marriage Officer.

steps.title: Special Marriage Act, 1954
steps.body: A civil marriage available to any two persons regardless of religion. Conditions: neither has a living spouse; capacity to consent and mental fitness; male 21, female 18; not within prohibited degrees (unless custom permits for at least one party).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Notice of intended marriage to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one party has resided for 30 days
2. Notice published; objections within 30 days
3. Officer inquires into objections (decides within 30 days)
4. Solemnisation with three witnesses and declaration; certificate entered in the Marriage Certificate Book – conclusive evidence
Supriyo Chakraborty v Union of India (2023): the Supreme Court declined to read same-sex marriage into the SMA, leaving it to Parliament.

steps.title: Other personal laws
steps.body:
- Christians: Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872; Divorce Act, 1869 (amended 2001 to equalise grounds, with mutual consent after two years' separation).
- Parsis: Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936.
- Succession of persons married under the SMA is governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (with an exception for two Hindus marrying under the SMA).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking conversion is needed for inter-faith marriage
- Forgetting the 30-day residence and notice periods

Notice published; objection period of 30 days

Certificate entered in the Marriage Certificate Book

quiz.why: Three witnesses sign along with the parties.

quiz.why: The Divorce Act, 1869 applies to Christians.

lessons.title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

scenes.text: A daughter-in-law is thrown out of her in-laws' house where she lived with her husband.
Can she claim a right to reside there?

steps.title: Scope
steps.body: Domestic violence includes physical, sexual, verbal and emotional, and economic abuse. An 'aggrieved person' is a woman in a domestic relationship with the respondent – by consanguinity, marriage, a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, or joint family. Hiral P. Harsora (2016) struck 'adult male' from the definition of respondent, so women can also be respondents.

steps.title: Reliefs
steps.body: Protection orders; residence orders; monetary relief; custody orders; compensation orders; interim and ex parte orders. A Protection Officer assists and files a Domestic Incident Report. Breach of a protection order is an offence.

steps.title: Shared household
steps.body: Satish Chander Ahuja v Sneha Ahuja (2020): a shared household includes a household where the woman lived in a domestic relationship, including one belonging to in-laws; it overruled S.R. Batra v Taruna Batra (2007) on this point. The right is to reside, not ownership.

steps.title: Live-in relationships
steps.body: D. Velusamy v D. Patchaiammal (2010): a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' requires holding out as spouses, legal age, qualified to marry, voluntary cohabitation for a significant period.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only husbands can be respondents
- Equating right of residence with ownership

lessons.title: Adoption under HAMA and the JJ Act

scenes.text: A 35-year-old unmarried Hindu woman wants to adopt a 4-year-old girl.
She already has a biological daughter.

steps.title: Section 6 – valid adoption
steps.body: The person adopting has capacity and right; the person giving has capacity; the child is capable of being adopted; and the adoption complies with the Act (actual giving and taking).

steps.title: Capacity
steps.body:
- Hindu male of sound mind, not a minor; if he has a living wife, her consent is needed unless she is incapable (section 7).
- Hindu female of sound mind, not a minor; a married woman needs her husband's consent (section 8, as amended in 2010).
- Child: Hindu, not already adopted, not married (unless custom), below 15 (unless custom) (section 10).

steps.title: Section 11 conditions
steps.body:
- Adopting a son: adopter must not have a living Hindu son, son's son or son's son's son.
- Adopting a daughter: adopter must not have a living Hindu daughter or son's daughter.
- Male adopting a female, or female adopting a male: age difference of at least 21 years.
- Same child cannot be adopted by two persons simultaneously.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: She has a living daughter → she cannot adopt a daughter under HAMA (section 11(ii)). She could adopt a son if at least 21 years older. Alternatively, under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 and the Adoption Regulations (through CARA), adoption is secular and not subject to the HAMA restriction – Shabnam Hashmi v Union of India (2014) recognised the right of any person to adopt under the JJ framework.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 21-year age gap for opposite-sex adoptions
- Applying HAMA restrictions to JJ Act adoptions

scenes.text: Separated parents both want custody of a 6-year-old.
Who is the natural guardian, and how does the court decide?

steps.title: HMGA, 1956 – natural guardians
steps.body:
- Boy or unmarried girl: the father, and after him the mother; custody of a child below five ordinarily with the mother.
- Illegitimate child: mother, then father.
- Married girl: husband.
Githa Hariharan v RBI (1999): 'after' means 'in the absence of' the father, so the mother can act as natural guardian when the father is not taking interest or is unable.

steps.title: Welfare is paramount
steps.body: Section 13 HMGA: the welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration. Under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, the court appoints guardians considering age, sex, religion, character and capacity of the proposed guardian, the minor's wishes if old enough. Courts may order joint custody, visitation and video calls.

steps.title: Muslim law
steps.body: Hizanat (custody) belongs to the mother for young children – under Hanafi law, a son till 7 years and a daughter till puberty – but guardianship of property rests with the father. Courts still apply the welfare principle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the father's preferential right as absolute
- Confusing custody with guardianship of property

courses.summary: The Mitakshara joint family and coparcenary, the karta and alienation, partition, the 2005 amendment and daughters as coparceners, succession to a Hindu male (Class I and II heirs, agnates and cognates), succession to a Hindu female, and women's absolute property.

lessons.title: Joint family, coparcenary and the 2005 amendment

scenes.text: A father died in 2001 owning ancestral agricultural land with his sons. His daughter claims a coparcenary share in 2020.
Does it matter that the father died before 2005?

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: A Hindu joint family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, including wives and unmarried daughters. A coparcenary is a narrower body within it, holding joint family property with a right by birth. Under classical Mitakshara law, it included the holder and three generations of male descendants. Under Dayabhaga, sons have no right by birth.

steps.title: Section 6 HSA as amended in 2005
steps.body: From 9 September 2005, the daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right in the same manner as a son, with the same rights and liabilities. Partitions effected before 20 December 2004 by registered deed or court decree are saved.

steps.title: Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020)
steps.body: A three-judge bench held the daughter's right is by birth; it is not necessary that the father be alive on 9 September 2005. Prakash v Phulavati (2016) and Mangammal (2018), to the extent of requiring a living father, were overruled. Oral partitions are not accepted as a defence unless supported by public documents.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: The daughter is a coparcener despite the father's death in 2001, unless a partition had been effected before 20 December 2004 by registered deed or decree.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Requiring the father to be alive in 2005
- Treating joint family and coparcenary as identical

activity.prompt: Tick what the daughter must check before claiming
items: She is a daughter of a coparcener
No partition by registered deed or decree before 20 Dec 2004
Claim is not barred by a completed partition

quiz.why: The right arises by birth.

quiz.q: The 2005 amendment came into force on
quiz.why: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 commenced on 9 September 2005.

quiz.why: Dayabhaga gives rights only on the father's death.

scenes.text: The karta sells a joint family plot to pay for his sister's wedding.
His nephew challenges the sale.

steps.title: The karta
steps.body: The senior-most member (now including a daughter who is the senior-most coparcener) manages the family. He can alienate joint family property only for **legal necessity** (marriage of members, maintenance, family debts, litigation, taxes), **benefit of the estate**, or **indispensable religious duties**. Hanooman Persaud Pandey v Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree (1856): the purchaser must make bona fide inquiry into the necessity.

steps.title: Partition
steps.body: Partition is severance of status – an unequivocal declaration of intention to separate suffices. Division by metes and bounds may follow. Members entitled to a share: coparceners; on partition between father and sons, the father's wife and the mother get shares under classical Mitakshara; unborn child in womb. Reopening is allowed in limited cases such as fraud.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Marriage of a sister is a recognised legal necessity → the sale binds the family if the purchaser made bona fide inquiries.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the karta as owner
- Thinking partition needs physical division to sever status

lessons.title: Lab: Succession to a Hindu male (sections 8–13)

scenes.text: Ramesh dies intestate leaving separate property worth ₹12 lakh, a widow, mother, son and daughter.
Who gets what?

steps.title: Order of succession
steps.body: Section 8: property devolves first on **Class I** heirs; if none, on **Class II** heirs (in order of entries); if none, on **agnates**; then **cognates**. Class I includes son, daughter, widow, mother, son/daughter of predeceased son, son/daughter of predeceased daughter, widow of predeceased son, and further specified grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

steps.title: Section 10 – distribution among Class I
steps.body: Rule 1: widow (or widows together) take one share. Rule 2: surviving sons, daughters and mother take one share each. Rule 3: heirs in the branch of each predeceased son or daughter take one share between them. Rule 4: within a branch, the share is divided equally (per stirpes then per capita).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Heirs: widow, mother, son, daughter → 4 shares. ₹12,00,000 ÷ 4 = **₹3,00,000 each**.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Heirs: widow, one son, and the widow and son of a predeceased son. Shares: widow 1/3, son 1/3, predeceased son's branch 1/3 → split equally between his widow and son = 1/6 each. On ₹12,00,000: widow ₹4,00,000; son ₹4,00,000; predeceased son's widow ₹2,00,000; grandson ₹2,00,000. Total ₹12,00,000.

steps.title: Agnates and cognates
steps.body: An agnate is related wholly through males; a cognate is related not wholly through males. Preference rules in section 12: fewer degrees of ascent preferred; then fewer degrees of descent; otherwise share equally.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving the father a Class I share – the father is a Class II heir
- Splitting per capita across branches instead of per stirpes

lessons.title: Women's property and succession to a Hindu female

scenes.text: In 1965 a widow was given a house for her maintenance in a family settlement.
Was it a limited estate or her absolute property?

steps.title: Section 14 – absolute property
steps.body: Any property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act, is held by her as full owner, not limited owner. Section 14(2): it does not apply to property acquired by gift, will or instrument prescribing a restricted estate. V. Tulasamma v Sesha Reddy (1977): property given in lieu of a pre-existing right to maintenance falls under 14(1) and becomes absolute.

steps.title: Stridhan
steps.body: Property given to a woman before, at or after marriage (jewellery, gifts) is her stridhan, absolutely hers. Pratibha Rani v Suraj Kumar (1985): husband or in-laws holding stridhan hold it as trustees; refusal to return can be criminal breach of trust.

steps.title: Section 15 – female intestate
steps.body:
(a) sons and daughters (including children of predeceased ones) and husband; (b) heirs of the husband; (c) mother and father; (d) heirs of the father; (e) heirs of the mother.
Exceptions (if no son, daughter or children of predeceased ones): property inherited from her father or mother goes to the heirs of the father; property inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes to the heirs of the husband.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: The 1965 house was given in recognition of her maintenance right → absolute under section 14(1) (Tulasamma). If she dies intestate leaving no children or husband but her husband's brother, and the house came from the husband's family, it goes to the husband's heirs.

steps.body:
- Ignoring the source-of-property exceptions in section 15(2)
- Applying 14(2) to maintenance settlements

Explain the doctrine of return (radd) and its limit on spouses
State the essentials of a valid hiba and the bequeathable third
Distribute a Christian intestate's estate under the Indian Succession Act

scenes.text: A Muslim son asks his living father for his 'share' of the family house.
Under Muslim law, does a son have any right while his father is alive?

steps.title: General principles
steps.body:
- No right by birth; inheritance opens on death (spes successionis cannot be transferred).
- No distinction between movable and immovable, ancestral and self-acquired property.
- No joint family concept.
- Males generally take double the share of females of the same degree.
- A child in the womb inherits if born alive.
- Homicide bars inheritance (Hanafi: intentional or accidental; Shia: only intentional).

steps.title: Classes (Hanafi)
steps.body:
1. **Sharers** (Quranic heirs): 12 – husband, wife, father, true grandfather, mother, true grandmother, daughter, son's daughter, full sister, consanguine sister, uterine brother, uterine sister.
2. **Residuaries** (agnates) – e.g. son, son's son, father (as residuary), brother.
3. **Distant kindred** – all others related by blood.

steps.title: Key shares
steps.body:
- Husband: 1/4 with child or son's child; else 1/2
- Wife (wives together): 1/8 with child or son's child; else 1/4
- Father: 1/6 with child or son's child
- Mother: 1/6 with child or son's child, or two or more siblings; else 1/3
- Daughter (alone, no son): 1/2; two or more: 2/3 together; with a son she becomes a residuary taking half a son's share

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying coparcenary ideas to Muslim law
- Giving a daughter a fixed share when a son exists

steps.title: Case 1 – wife, son, daughter; estate ₹24,00,000
steps.body:
Wife: 1/8 = 3/24.
Residue: 7/8 = 21/24 to son and daughter in 2:1 → son 14/24, daughter 7/24.
Amounts: wife ₹3,00,000; son ₹14,00,000; daughter ₹7,00,000. Check: 3 + 14 + 7 = 24 lakh.

steps.title: Case 2 – father, mother, son; estate ₹6,00,000
steps.body:
Father 1/6, mother 1/6 (a child exists). Son takes residue: 1 − 1/6 − 1/6 = 2/3.
Amounts: father ₹1,00,000; mother ₹1,00,000; son ₹4,00,000.

steps.title: Case 3 – husband and daughter only; estate ₹8,00,000
steps.body: Husband 1/4 (child exists); daughter 1/2. Residue 1/4 with no residuary → **return (radd)** to sharers other than spouse under Hanafi law, so the daughter takes it. Final: husband 1/4 = ₹2,00,000; daughter 3/4 = ₹6,00,000.

steps.title: Increase (aul)
steps.body: If fixed shares exceed unity, each share is proportionately reduced by raising the denominator. Example: husband 1/2 and two full sisters 2/3 → 3/6 + 4/6 = 7/6; shares become 3/7 and 4/7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Returning surplus to a spouse when blood sharers exist
- Forgetting to verify the total equals the estate

scenes.text: A Muslim man orally gifts his house to his daughter and hands her the keys; later he wills half his estate to a friend.
Are both valid?

steps.title: Hiba (gift)
steps.body: Essentials: (1) declaration by the donor, (2) acceptance by the donee, (3) delivery of possession (actual or constructive). Writing and registration are not essential for an oral hiba under Muslim law; the Transfer of Property Act's registration rule does not apply to Muslim gifts (section 129 TPA). Mushaa (undivided share) gifts of divisible property are irregular but validated on delivery.

steps.title: Wills (wasiyat)
steps.body: A Muslim may bequeath up to **one-third** of the net estate (after funeral expenses and debts). Bequests beyond one-third, or to an heir (Sunni law), need consent of the heirs after the testator's death. Shia law allows bequests to heirs within one-third without consent. Wills may be oral or written.

steps.title: Applying it
steps.body: Gift: declaration, acceptance and handing over keys → valid hiba. Will to a friend of half the estate: valid only to one-third unless heirs consent to the excess.

steps.title: Wakf
steps.body: Permanent dedication of property by a Muslim for purposes recognised by Muslim law as religious, pious or charitable. Once constituted, it is irrevocable and inalienable; ownership vests in God; a mutawalli manages it. Wakf-alal-aulad (family wakf) is valid under the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913. Wakfs are regulated by the Waqf Act, 1995 as amended.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Requiring registration for an oral hiba
- Applying the one-third limit to gifts made during lifetime

quiz.why: Possession completes the gift.

quiz.why: The 1913 Act validated wakf-alal-aulad.

lessons.title: Indian Succession Act: Christian intestate succession

scenes.text: A Christian man dies intestate leaving a widow and two children; estate ₹9 lakh.
How is it divided?

steps.title: Scope
steps.body: The Indian Succession Act, 1925 governs intestate succession of Christians and others not covered by personal codes (Parsis have a separate chapter), and testamentary succession of most communities other than Muslims. Mary Roy v State of Kerala (1986): the ISA applied to Travancore Christians, overriding the discriminatory Travancore Christian Succession Act.

steps.title: Rules for Christians
steps.body:
- Widow with lineal descendants: 1/3; the remaining 2/3 to lineal descendants.
- Widow with no lineal descendants but kindred: 1/2 to widow, 1/2 to kindred.
- Widow with no kindred: whole estate.
- Children share equally, regardless of sex.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Estate ₹9,00,000, widow and two children: widow 1/3 = ₹3,00,000; remaining ₹6,00,000 split equally → ₹3,00,000 each child.

steps.title: Wills under the ISA
steps.body: Any person of sound mind not a minor may make a will; it must be signed by the testator and attested by two witnesses (privileged wills of soldiers excepted). A will is revocable and takes effect on death. Probate is required in certain cases (e.g. in the presidency towns).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Hindu Class I rules to Christians
- Forgetting attestation by two witnesses

steps.title: Outline
steps.body:
1. Court: Family Court / District Court having jurisdiction (where marriage solemnised, respondent resides, parties last resided together, or wife resides)
2. Parties: Petitioner 1 (husband) and Petitioner 2 (wife), with addresses
3. Facts: date and place of marriage, ceremonies, children
4. Separation since a date, at least one year before filing
5. Statement that they cannot live together and have mutually agreed to dissolve the marriage

uni-llb-ip-law.title: Intellectual Property Law
uni-llb-ip-law.description: Nature of IP, international treaties, copyright, patents, trademarks, designs, geographical indications and enforcement under Indian law. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes. General education, not legal advice.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of IP and the International Framework
courses.summary: What intellectual property is, why the law protects it, the kinds of IP rights in India, and the Paris, Berne and TRIPS framework including the TRIPS flexibilities.
outcomes: Classify subject matter into the correct IP right
Explain the justifications for IP protection (labour, incentive, personality)
State the core principles of national treatment and minimum standards
Explain TRIPS flexibilities such as compulsory licensing and the Doha Declaration

scenes.text: A smartphone maker launches a new phone in India.
Its chip design, its name, its shape, its software and its ringtone are each protected by a different law. Which is which?

steps.title: Definition and character
steps.body: Intellectual property is a bundle of exclusive, territorial, time-limited (mostly) rights over creations of the mind. It is intangible movable property: it can be assigned, licensed and inherited. Rights are **negative**: they allow the owner to exclude others from using the subject matter without consent.

steps.title: Indian IP statutes
steps.body:
- Copyright Act 1957 – literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, films, sound recordings, software (as literary work)
- Patents Act 1970 – inventions (new, inventive step, industrial application)
- Trade Marks Act 1999 – marks distinguishing goods/services
- Designs Act 2000 – shape, configuration, pattern, ornament applied to articles
- Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999
- Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000
- Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001
- Trade secrets: no statute; protected by contract and equity (breach of confidence).

steps.title: Justifications
steps.body:
- Locke's labour theory: one is entitled to the fruits of one's labour.
- Utilitarian/incentive theory: temporary monopoly encourages creation and disclosure.
- Hegel's personality theory: a work is an extension of the author's personality (basis of moral rights).

steps.title: Classifying the phone
steps.body: Chip layout → Semiconductor IC Layout-Design Act; brand name → Trade Marks Act; outer shape → Designs Act (if new and original) and possibly trademark (shape mark); software code → Copyright (literary work); new battery chemistry → Patents Act; ringtone → Copyright (musical work and sound recording).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying 'I patented my book' or 'copyrighted my logo name'. Books are copyright; brand names are trademarks; copyright in a logo protects it as artistic work, not as a brand.

items.text: Novel ornamental shape of a bottle

quiz.why: An IP owner's core right is to prevent others from exploiting the subject matter without permission.

quiz.q: Moral rights are most closely linked to
quiz.why: Personality theory sees the work as an extension of the author, supporting rights of attribution and integrity.

scenes.text: An Indian startup filed a patent in India in January and wants protection in Germany too.
Has it lost novelty by publishing in March? Not if it uses 'priority'.

steps.title: Paris Convention 1883 (industrial property)
steps.body:
- **National treatment**: each member gives nationals of other members the same protection as its own nationals.
- **Right of priority**: an application in one member gives a priority period – 12 months for patents and utility models, 6 months for trademarks and industrial designs – during which later filings elsewhere are treated as filed on the first date.
- **Independence of patents**: a patent granted in one country is independent of others.
- Article 6bis: protection of well-known marks.

steps.title: Berne Convention 1886 (literary and artistic works)
steps.body:
- National treatment.
- **Automatic protection**: no formalities such as registration may be required.
- Minimum term: life of the author plus 50 years for most works.
- Article 6bis: moral rights of paternity and integrity.
India is a member of both; the Copyright Act's International Copyright Order extends protection to works of Berne countries.

steps.title: Priority worked
steps.body: Indian patent filed 10 January 2026; startup publishes 1 March 2026; German application filed 5 December 2026 claiming priority. Since 5 December is within 12 months of 10 January, novelty is judged as of 10 January, so the March publication does not destroy novelty. Filing on 15 January 2027 would be outside priority.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using 12 months for trademarks. Trademark and design priority is 6 months.

quiz.why: Article 4C gives 6 months for trademarks and designs and 12 for patents.

scenes.text: In 2012 India's Controller of Patents granted a compulsory licence on an expensive cancer drug to a generic maker.
Was this allowed under the WTO's TRIPS Agreement?

steps.title: TRIPS (1994, WTO)
steps.body: Binds all WTO members to minimum standards for all major IP types and enforcement, with WTO dispute settlement. Key: national treatment and **most-favoured-nation** (Arts. 3–4); patents for products and processes in all fields of technology (Art. 27); 20-year patent term (Art. 33); copyright per Berne (excluding moral rights, Art. 9); exceptions must meet the **three-step test**. India got a transition until 1 January 2005, using a 'mailbox' for pharma product applications, and introduced product patents by the Patents (Amendment) Act 2005.

steps.title: Flexibilities
steps.body:
- Compulsory licences (Art. 31) – India: section 84 Patents Act (after 3 years from grant, if reasonable requirements of public unmet, not available at reasonably affordable price, or not worked in India).
- Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (2001): members may protect public health and determine grounds for CLs and what is a national emergency.
- Parallel imports / exhaustion left to members (Art. 6).
- Strict patentability standards, e.g. India's section 3(d).

steps.title: Bayer v Natco (2012)
steps.body: The Controller granted Natco a compulsory licence for sorafenib tosylate (Nexavar) since Bayer priced it around ₹2.8 lakh per month, available to a tiny fraction of patients; royalty set at 6% (upheld by the IPAB and the Bombay High Court).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying TRIPS bans compulsory licences. Article 31 expressly allows them with conditions (case-by-case, prior negotiation except emergencies, adequate remuneration).

2. Trade secret: keep the recipe confidential via NDAs and limited access; do not patent (disclosure, and recipes rarely meet inventive step).
