courses.title: Unit 2 · Copyright and Related Rights
courses.summary: Subject matter and originality, authorship and ownership, economic and moral rights, term, infringement, fair dealing under section 52, and remedies under the Copyright Act 1957.
outcomes: Apply the originality standard from Eastern Book Company v Modak
Identify the first owner of copyright in employment and commissioned works
Compute the term of copyright for different works
Test an alleged infringement and apply fair dealing defences

scenes.text: A law publisher adds paragraph numbers, headnotes and corrections to Supreme Court judgments.
A software company copies the corrected text into its database. Does the publisher own copyright in public judgments?

steps.title: Works protected (section 13)
steps.body: Original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works; cinematograph films; sound recordings. 'Literary work' includes computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer databases (section 2(o)).

steps.title: Originality
steps.body: UK 'sweat of the brow' (labour and skill) vs US 'modicum of creativity' (Feist, 1991). In **Eastern Book Company v D.B. Modak (2008)** the Supreme Court adopted a middle path: the work must show **skill and judgment** with a minimal degree of creativity. Copy-edited judgments as such were not protected, but the headnotes, footnotes and editorial paragraph numbering involving judgment were.

steps.title: Idea-expression dichotomy
steps.body: Copyright protects expression, not ideas, facts or plots. **R.G. Anand v Delux Films (1978)**: no infringement where the later film used the same theme (provincialism) but expressed it differently; test – would an ordinary viewer get the unmistakable impression that the later work is a copy? Merger doctrine: where an idea can be expressed only in limited ways, expression merges with idea.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: Two cookbooks with 'butter chicken' recipes: the list of ingredients and method (functional facts) is not protected; the author's narrative introduction, photos and particular arrangement may be. Copying the photos and introduction is infringement; independently writing the same recipe is not.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying registration is required. Copyright exists on creation; registration under section 45 is only prima facie evidence (section 48).

activity.prompt: Protected expression or unprotected idea/fact?

items.text: Plot idea of a boy wizard at a school
The exact text of a novel chapter
An original photograph of a monument
Raw text of a Supreme Court judgment

quiz.q: The originality standard in India after EBC v Modak is
options: Skill and judgment with minimal creativity
quiz.why: The Supreme Court in 2008 required skill and judgment with a flavour of minimal creativity.

quiz.q: R.G. Anand v Delux Films established that
options: Themes and ideas are not protected; similarity in expression is the test
quiz.why: The court laid down the lay-observer test and held that the same theme expressed differently is not infringement.

quiz.q: Computer programmes are protected as
quiz.why: Section 2(o) includes computer programmes in literary works.

scenes.text: A lyricist writes a song for a film; the producer pays her; a label releases the soundtrack.
Years later the song plays on radio. Who gets royalties?

steps.title: First owner (section 17)
steps.body: The author is the first owner, except: work by an employee in the course of employment under a contract of service → employer; photograph, painting, portrait, engraving or film made for valuable consideration at the instance of a person → that person; journalists' work for a newspaper → proprietor for publication in the paper. 2012 amendment provisos protect authors of lyrics and music in films: they cannot be deprived of the right to share royalties equally for uses other than communication in the cinema hall (sections 18 and 19).

steps.title: Rights (section 14) and moral rights (section 57)
steps.body: Economic: reproduce, issue copies, perform/communicate to the public, make films or translations or adaptations; for software, also sell or rent. Moral: paternity (claim authorship) and integrity (restrain distortion, mutilation prejudicial to honour or reputation) – Amar Nath Sehgal v Union of India (2005), mural removal case.

steps.title: Term
steps.body:
- Literary, dramatic, musical, artistic (published in lifetime): life of author + 60 years (from the beginning of the calendar year after death).
- Films, sound recordings, photographs, anonymous/pseudonymous, posthumous, government and international organisation works: 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following publication.

steps.title: Worked numerical
steps.body:
A novelist died on 10 August 1970. Term = 60 years counted from 1 January 1971 → copyright expires at the end of 31 December 2030; the work enters public domain on 1 January 2031.
A film published on 3 March 2000: term runs from 1 January 2001 for 60 years → expires 31 December 2060.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Counting 60 years from the date of death. Count from the beginning of the next calendar year.

activity.prompt: Who is the first owner?

items.text: Freelance novelist writing her own book
Employee programmer writing code at work
Portrait painted for a fee at a client's request

quiz.q: An author died in 1990. When does his copyright in a published novel expire?
quiz.why: Sixty years are counted from 1 January 1991, so it expires at the end of 2050.

quiz.q: Amar Nath Sehgal concerned
options: Moral right of integrity in a mural
quiz.why: The Delhi High Court protected the sculptor's integrity right after his mural at Vigyan Bhawan was damaged and stored away.

quiz.q: Term for a sound recording is
quiz.why: Section 27 gives sound recordings 60 years from the year following publication.

scenes.text: A photocopy shop near Delhi University prepares course packs with chapters from Oxford and Cambridge books.
The publishers sue. Is copying for education infringement?

steps.title: Infringement (section 51)
steps.body: Copyright is infringed when a person without licence does anything exclusively conferred on the owner, or permits a place to be used for communication to the public for profit knowingly, or sells/distributes/imports infringing copies. Test: substantial copying (quality, not just quantity) plus access.

steps.title: Fair dealing (section 52)
steps.body: Fair dealing with any work (other than a computer programme in some respects) for private or personal use including research, criticism or review, reporting current events; reproduction by a teacher or pupil in the course of instruction (s. 52(1)(i)); performance in educational institutions; making back-up copies of software; transient storage. In **University of Cambridge v Rameshwari Photocopy (Delhi HC Division Bench, 2016)** the court held that reproduction for course packs 'in the course of instruction' can fall within section 52(1)(i), subject to the test of necessity for the purpose of instruction; publishers later withdrew the suit.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body: Civil: injunction (including John Doe/Ashok Kumar orders against unknown infringers, and dynamic injunctions against mirror websites), damages or account of profits, delivery up. Criminal: section 63 – imprisonment 6 months to 3 years and fine ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. Section 65A/65B: circumvention of technological measures and rights management information.

steps.title: Worked fair dealing analysis
steps.body: A YouTuber uses 40 seconds of a 2-hour film to critique its portrayal of farmers. Purpose: criticism/review. Amount: small and necessary for criticism. Effect: no substitute for the film. Likely fair dealing. If she uploads the whole climax with a few comments, it is a substitute → infringement.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Acknowledging the source does not by itself make copying fair.

activity.prompt: Likely fair dealing or infringement?

items.text: Quoting two paragraphs in a book review
Uploading a full new film to a website
News channel showing a clip of a speech while reporting it
Selling photocopies of a whole textbook to the public
Teacher reproducing a poem in a question paper

quiz.q: The DU photocopy case relied on section
quiz.why: Section 52(1)(i) permits reproduction by a teacher or pupil in the course of instruction.

quiz.q: A 'John Doe' order is
quiz.why: Indian courts grant Ashok Kumar/John Doe injunctions against unidentified infringers, especially for film piracy.

quiz.q: Minimum imprisonment for a first offence under section 63 is
quiz.why: Section 63 prescribes 6 months to 3 years, with fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh, subject to reduction for adequate special reasons.

lessons.title: Lab: Licensing, societies and the digital world

scenes.text: A café in Pune plays Bollywood songs from a streaming app for customers.
It receives a legal notice from a music label. Is a personal subscription enough?

steps.title: Licences and copyright societies
steps.body: Licences must be in writing (section 30). Copyright societies registered under section 33 (e.g. IPRS for authors/composers, PPL and RMPL for sound recordings, though their status has changed over time) issue public performance licences. Personal streaming subscriptions are for private use; playing to customers is communication to the public.

steps.title: Statutory licences
steps.body: Section 31D allows broadcasting organisations to broadcast published works and sound recordings on royalty rates fixed by the Commercial Court/Appellate Board successor authority; whether it covers internet streaming has been litigated (Bombay HC in Tips Industries v Wynk, 2019, held it did not).

steps.title: Advice to the café
steps.body:
1. Stop or obtain public performance licences from the relevant owners/societies for musical works and sound recordings.
2. Check whether the label's representative is a registered society or the owner itself.
3. Keep licence copies at the premises.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking buying a CD or subscription allows public play. Section 14 rights include communication to the public, which needs a separate licence.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to respond to the notice
items: Read the notice and identify the claimant's rights
Check whether claimant owns or administers the repertoire
Reply to the notice with licence details

quiz.q: A copyright licence must be
quiz.why: Section 30 requires a licence to be in writing signed by the owner or authorised agent.

quiz.q: Playing music to café customers is
quiz.why: It is an exclusive right of the owner under section 14, so it requires a licence.

quiz.q: Section 31D deals with
quiz.why: Section 31D, added in 2012, provides a statutory licence for broadcasting literary, musical works and sound recordings.

questions.q: Copyright registration is under section
Novelist dies 15 June 2000. Copyright expires
Feist (US, 1991) required
First owner of a portrait commissioned for payment is
Moral rights are in section
The lay observer test comes from
Back-up copy of a lawfully held programme is
Term for photographs
Circumventing DRM is addressed by section
Merger doctrine applies when
options: Idea can be expressed in very few ways

questions.q: Lyricists' right to equal royalty share was strengthened in
Acknowledging the source makes copying
questions.why: Fairness depends on purpose, amount and effect.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Patents
courses.summary: Patentability (novelty, inventive step, industrial application), exclusions under sections 3 and 4 including 3(d), procedure from filing to grant, oppositions, rights, infringement and defences under the Patents Act 1970.
outcomes: Test an invention against the three patentability criteria
Apply section 3(d) as interpreted in Novartis v Union of India
Order the stages of patent prosecution with time limits
Identify infringement and defences such as the Bolar exemption

scenes.text: An engineer designs a pressure cooker valve that cuts gas use by 20% using a new spring mechanism.
A similar valve was described in a 2019 Japanese journal, but without the spring. Can she get a patent?

steps.title: Invention (section 2(1)(j))
steps.body:
A new product or process involving an **inventive step** and **capable of industrial application**.
- **Novelty**: not anticipated by publication anywhere in the world or prior use before the priority date (absolute novelty).
- **Inventive step** (s. 2(1)(ja)): technical advance over existing knowledge or economic significance or both, making it **not obvious to a person skilled in the art**.
- **Industrial application** (s. 2(1)(ac)): capable of being made or used in an industry.

steps.title: Obviousness test
steps.body: Courts in India (e.g. Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam v Hindustan Metal Industries, 1979) asked whether the invention would be obvious to a skilled person given the state of the art. A structured approach: (1) identify the person skilled in the art and common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept; (3) identify differences from prior art; (4) ask whether those differences would be obvious steps.

steps.title: Applying to the valve
steps.body: Novelty: the 2019 article lacks the spring, so claim is novel. Inventive step: if a skilled engineer would not obviously add this spring mechanism to achieve 20% savings, and it gives a technical advance, inventive step is met. Industrial application: cookers are manufactured. Patentable, subject to section 3 exclusions (none apply).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking novelty is judged only in India. Indian law uses worldwide publication as prior art.

activity.prompt: Order the inventive-step analysis
items: Identify the person skilled in the art
Identify common general knowledge and closest prior art
Identify the inventive concept of the claim
Ask whether the differences would be obvious to the skilled person

quiz.q: Novelty in Indian patent law is assessed against prior art
quiz.why: Indian law applies absolute novelty, so publication anywhere before the priority date anticipates.

quiz.q: Inventive step requires that the invention be
options: Not obvious to a person skilled in the art
quiz.why: Section 2(1)(ja) defines inventive step by non-obviousness plus technical advance or economic significance.

quiz.q: Bishwanath Prasad Radhey Shyam is a leading case on
quiz.why: The Supreme Court in 1979 discussed novelty, utility and inventive step in revoking a utensil-making patent.

lessons.title: What is not patentable: sections 3 and 4

scenes.text: Novartis sought a patent on the beta-crystalline form of imatinib mesylate, a leukaemia drug.
The Supreme Court in 2013 refused. Why?

steps.title: Key exclusions in section 3
steps.body:
- 3(b): inventions contrary to public order or morality or causing serious prejudice to life or environment
- 3(c): mere discovery of a scientific principle or of a living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature
- **3(d)**: mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of known efficacy; salts, esters, polymorphs, isomers etc. are the same substance unless they differ significantly in efficacy
- 3(e): mere admixture resulting only in aggregation of properties
- 3(i): methods of treatment of humans or animals
- 3(j): plants and animals (other than micro-organisms), essentially biological processes
- 3(k): mathematical or business methods, computer programmes per se, algorithms
- 3(p): traditional knowledge or aggregation of known properties of traditionally known components
Section 4: inventions relating to atomic energy.

steps.title: Novartis AG v Union of India (2013)
steps.body: The Supreme Court held that for medicines 'efficacy' means **therapeutic efficacy**; better bioavailability or flow properties alone are not enough. The beta-crystalline form failed section 3(d).

steps.title: Software
steps.body: Section 3(k) excludes 'computer programme per se'. Under the CRI Guidelines and decisions like Ferid Allani v Union of India (Delhi HC, 2019), inventions involving software that produce a technical effect or contribution may be patentable.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Section 3(d) does not ban all incremental pharma patents; it requires proof of enhanced therapeutic efficacy.

activity.prompt: Patentable subject matter or excluded?

items.text: New salt of a known drug with no efficacy gain
Method of surgery on a patient
A business method for online sales as such
Software-controlled braking system with technical effect

quiz.q: In Novartis, 'efficacy' under section 3(d) for drugs means
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held efficacy must mean therapeutic efficacy for medicines.

quiz.q: Methods of treatment of human beings are excluded by section
quiz.why: Section 3(i) excludes medicinal, surgical, curative and similar processes for treating humans or animals.

quiz.q: A computer programme per se is excluded under
quiz.why: Section 3(k) excludes mathematical or business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithms.

lessons.title: Procedure: filing to grant, oppositions and term

scenes.text: A university lab files a provisional specification on 1 February 2026.
What deadlines must its tech-transfer office track?

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. Application with provisional or complete specification (s. 7, 9). Complete specification within **12 months** of provisional (s. 9(1)), or it is deemed abandoned.
2. Publication after **18 months** from priority date (s. 11A), earlier on request.
3. Request for examination (s. 11B) – currently within **31 months** from priority date (rule 24B, as amended in 2024).
4. First examination report; response period (6 months, extendable by 3).
5. **Pre-grant opposition** by any person after publication and before grant (s. 25(1)).
6. Grant and publication.
7. **Post-grant opposition** by a person interested within **1 year** of publication of grant (s. 25(2)).
8. Term: **20 years from filing date** (s. 53), subject to annual renewal fees.

steps.title: Worked dates
steps.body:
Provisional filed 1 Feb 2026 (priority date).
- Complete specification due by 1 Feb 2027.
- Publication ~ 1 Aug 2027 (18 months).
- Examination request by 1 Sep 2028 (31 months).
- If the complete specification is filed 15 Jan 2027, the patent term runs 20 years from the date of filing of the application, i.e. from 1 Feb 2026 (the provisional filing date is the date of the application) → expires 1 Feb 2046.

steps.title: Working statement
steps.body: Patentees must file a statement of working in India (Form 27) – after 2024 rules, once every three financial years.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing who can oppose: pre-grant – 'any person'; post-grant – 'person interested'.

activity.prompt: Order the patent prosecution stages

quiz.q: Complete specification must follow a provisional within
quiz.why: Section 9(1) deems the application abandoned if the complete specification is not filed within 12 months.

quiz.q: Pre-grant opposition can be filed by
quiz.why: Section 25(1) lets any person file a representation by way of opposition after publication.

quiz.q: Patent term is 20 years from
options: Date of filing of the application
quiz.why: Section 53 counts the term from the date of filing of the application.

scenes.text: A generic company prepares trial batches of a patented drug to seek regulatory approval before the patent expires.
The patentee sues. Is preparation for approval infringement?

steps.title: Rights (section 48)
steps.body: Product patent: prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product in India. Process patent: prevent using the process and using, offering, selling or importing products obtained directly by that process.

steps.title: Infringement
steps.body: Literal infringement: every element of a claim is taken. Doctrine of equivalents/pith and marrow: insubstantial changes performing the same function in the same way. Reversal of burden for process patents in some cases (s. 104A).

steps.title: Defences
steps.body:
- **Bolar exemption** (s. 107A(a)): acts reasonably related to development and submission of information required under any law (e.g. drug approval).
- **Parallel imports** (s. 107A(b)): importing products from a person duly authorised to sell them.
- Experimental/research use and use by government (s. 47).
- Invalidity counter-claim (s. 64 grounds) – revocation in the High Court.
- Innocent infringer: damages may be refused if defendant proves he was not aware and had no reasonable grounds for believing the patent existed (s. 111).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Generic's trial batches for regulatory submission are protected by section 107A(a). Commercial sale before expiry would infringe; the patentee can seek injunction and damages or account of profits in a suit filed in the District Court or High Court (s. 104).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking the Bolar exemption allows stockpiling for sale. It covers only acts reasonably related to regulatory submissions.

activity.prompt: Infringement or defence available?

items.text: Making test batches for a drug-approval dossier
Selling copies of a patented machine in India
Importing products bought from the patentee's authorised seller abroad
Using the patented process to make goods for export sale
Purely experimental research on the invention

quiz.q: The Bolar exemption is in section
quiz.why: Section 107A(a) protects acts reasonably related to obtaining regulatory approval.

quiz.q: Parallel import of goods from an authorised seller abroad is
quiz.why: India follows international exhaustion for patents through section 107A(b).

quiz.q: A revocation counter-claim in a patent infringement suit is heard by
quiz.why: Under section 104 proviso, where a counter-claim for revocation is made, the suit is transferred to the High Court.

Novartis v UoI was decided in
Plants and animals except micro-organisms are excluded under
Post-grant opposition period
Rights of a patentee are in section
Atomic energy inventions are excluded by section
Patent filed 10 May 2020 expires
Mere admixture with aggregated properties is excluded by
Ferid Allani (2019) concerned
A compulsory licence application can be made after
Absolute novelty means
Innocent infringer protection against damages is in section

courses.title: Unit 4 · Trademarks and Passing Off
courses.summary: Definition and functions of marks, absolute and relative grounds of refusal, registration procedure, well-known marks, infringement, passing off and remedies under the Trade Marks Act 1999.
outcomes: Test whether a sign is capable of registration and distinctive
Apply absolute (s. 9) and relative (s. 11) grounds
Distinguish infringement from passing off
Apply the deceptive similarity tests from Cadila v Cadila

lessons.title: What is a trademark and what can be registered

scenes.text: A shampoo maker wants to register 'BEST SHAMPOO'.
The examiner objects. Another wants to register the sound of a lion's roar. That is accepted. Why?

steps.title: Definition (section 2(1)(zb))
steps.body: A mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing goods or services of one person from those of others; includes shape of goods, packaging and combination of colours. 'Mark' includes device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral. Sound marks are accepted when represented as MP3 with notation (Trade Marks Rules 2017).

steps.title: Absolute grounds (section 9)
steps.body: Refused if: devoid of distinctive character; consists exclusively of descriptive indications (kind, quality, quantity, purpose, origin) – e.g. 'BEST'; customary in the trade; deceptive; hurts religious susceptibilities; scandalous/obscene; prohibited under the Emblems and Names Act 1950; shapes resulting from the nature of goods, necessary for technical result, or giving substantial value. **Proviso**: acquired distinctiveness through use (secondary meaning) can overcome descriptiveness.

steps.title: Relative grounds (section 11)
steps.body: Refused if identical/similar to an earlier mark for identical/similar goods with likelihood of confusion; or if identical/similar to an earlier **well-known mark** even for dissimilar goods where use would take unfair advantage or be detrimental to its distinctiveness or repute; or if use is liable to be prevented by passing off or copyright.

steps.title: Spectrum of distinctiveness
steps.body: Generic ('Shampoo' for shampoo) – never; descriptive ('Best Shampoo') – only with secondary meaning; suggestive ('Sunsilk' for hair care) – registrable; arbitrary ('Apple' for computers) – strong; fanciful/coined ('Kodak') – strongest.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking a famous word cannot be used by anyone. Trademark rights are linked to goods/services; ordinary words remain usable descriptively.

activity.prompt: Place each mark on the distinctiveness spectrum

quiz.q: Absolute grounds of refusal are in section
quiz.why: Section 9 covers inherent defects like lack of distinctiveness and descriptiveness.

quiz.q: A descriptive mark may be registered if
options: It has acquired distinctiveness through use
quiz.why: The proviso to section 9(1) allows registration where the mark has acquired distinctive character.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest type of mark?
quiz.why: Invented words have no meaning apart from the brand, so they are inherently most distinctive.

lessons.title: Registration procedure, term and well-known marks

scenes.text: A bakery uses 'TM' next to its brand while its application is pending.
When can it switch to ®?

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. Search and file application (Form TM-A) in the correct NICE class(es) – section 18.
2. Examination report; reply within 1 month (practice) and hearing.
3. Acceptance and advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal (s. 20).
4. Opposition within **4 months** of advertisement (s. 21).
5. Counter-statement within 2 months; evidence; hearing.
6. Registration certificate (s. 23) – registration dates back to the date of application.
7. Term **10 years**, renewable indefinitely for 10 years at a time (s. 25).

steps.title: Well-known marks
steps.body: Section 2(1)(zg) and section 11(6)–(9): factors include public knowledge, duration and extent of use and promotion, registrations, successful enforcement. The Registrar can determine a mark as well-known on request (rule 124, 2017 Rules). Courts have declared marks like 'Google', 'Bata', 'Whirlpool' well-known. **N.R. Dongre v Whirlpool (1996)**: transborder reputation of Whirlpool protected in India even without much local sale.

steps.title: Symbols
steps.body: ® may be used only for registered marks; falsely representing a mark as registered is an offence (section 107).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying the opposition period is 3 months. Under the 1999 Act and 2017 Rules it is 4 months (not extendable).

activity.prompt: Order the trademark registration steps
items: File application in the right class
Advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal

quiz.q: Trademark registration lasts
quiz.why: Section 25 gives 10 years with renewals for further 10-year periods indefinitely.

quiz.q: Opposition must be filed within
quiz.why: Section 21 and the rules fix four months from advertisement.

quiz.q: Whirlpool's case is important for
quiz.why: The Supreme Court protected Whirlpool's reputation in India based on advertisements and limited sales.

scenes.text: Two companies sell anti-malarial drugs named Falcigo and Falcitab.
In medicines, confusion can kill. How strict should the test be?

steps.title: Section 29
steps.body: A registered mark is infringed by a person not entitled who uses in the course of trade a mark identical or deceptively similar for identical/similar goods causing likelihood of confusion; identity of mark and goods → confusion presumed (s. 29(3)); dissimilar goods if the mark has a reputation in India and use takes unfair advantage or is detrimental (dilution, s. 29(4)). Use as trade name, in advertising and in comparative advertising contrary to honest practices are also covered (s. 29(5), (8)).

steps.title: Cadila Health Care v Cadila Pharmaceuticals (2001) factors
steps.body:
1. Nature of the marks (word, label, composite)
2. Degree of resemblance – phonetic, visual, idea
3. Nature of goods
4. Similarity in character and performance of goods
5. Class of purchasers, their education and degree of care
6. Mode of purchasing goods
7. Other surrounding circumstances
For medicines, a stricter approach: even a small possibility of confusion matters.

steps.title: Worked application
steps.body: 'Falcigo' vs 'Falcitab': common prefix 'Falci' (from Plasmodium falciparum, descriptive) – but overall phonetic similarity with prescription medicines handled by busy chemists → Supreme Court remanded applying stricter test. Marks are compared as a whole (anti-dissection rule), with the test of an average consumer of imperfect recollection (Amritdhara Pharmacy v Satya Deo Gupta, 1962: Amritdhara vs Lakshmandhara).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Comparing marks side by side letter-by-letter. The test is the impression on a person of average intelligence and imperfect recollection.

activity.prompt: Order your deceptive similarity analysis
items: Identify both marks and the goods
Compare marks as a whole: sound, look, idea
Assess similarity of goods and trade channels
Consider class of purchasers and care exercised

quiz.q: Which case laid down the seven factors for deceptive similarity?
options: Cadila Health Care v Cadila Pharmaceuticals
quiz.why: The Supreme Court in 2001 listed these factors and urged strictness for medicines.

quiz.q: The test consumer has
quiz.why: Amritdhara and later cases use the ordinary purchaser with imperfect recollection.

quiz.q: Dilution of a mark with reputation even for dissimilar goods is in section
quiz.why: Section 29(4) covers unfair advantage or detriment to a reputed mark used on dissimilar goods.

lessons.title: Lab: Passing off and remedies – draft a cease-and-desist

scenes.text: An unregistered biscuit brand 'Crunchy Moon' in a blue moon wrapper is copied by 'Crunchy Noon' in near-identical packaging.
No registration exists. Your client wants to act.

steps.title: Passing off
steps.body: A common-law action preserved by section 27(2). The classical trinity (Reckitt & Colman v Borden, 'Jif lemon', 1990): **goodwill**, **misrepresentation** likely to deceive the public, **damage** or likelihood of damage. In India: **S. Syed Mohideen v P. Sulochana Bai (2016)** held passing off rights are superior to registration rights. No registration needed.

steps.title: Remedies
steps.body: Injunction (interim and permanent), damages or account of profits, delivery up and destruction (s. 135). Criminal: falsifying or falsely applying a trademark (ss. 102–104) – imprisonment 6 months to 3 years and fine. Jurisdiction: suits for infringement/passing off in a District Court or above; section 134 allows plaintiff to sue where it carries on business.

steps.title: Draft cease-and-desist (key paragraphs)
steps.body:
'1. Our client has, since 2015, manufactured biscuits under the mark CRUNCHY MOON in a distinctive blue wrapper with a crescent device, enjoying substantial goodwill (sales of ₹… in FY 2025-26).
2. You have recently launched CRUNCHY NOON in packaging that slavishly imitates our client's trade dress.
3. This constitutes passing off and is likely to deceive consumers.
4. You are called upon within 7 days to: (a) cease manufacture and sale; (b) recall stock; (c) disclose sales; (d) give a written undertaking.
5. Failing which our client will initiate civil and criminal proceedings without further notice.'

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Threatening criminal action without basis can backfire; groundless threats of infringement proceedings are actionable under section 142.

activity.prompt: Order the parts of the cease-and-desist letter
items: Introduce your client and its mark with dates of use

quiz.why: Lord Oliver in the Jif Lemon case set out goodwill, misrepresentation and damage.

quiz.q: Passing off is saved by section
quiz.why: Section 27(2) preserves the common-law action for passing off.

quiz.q: Groundless threats of infringement proceedings are addressed by section
quiz.why: Section 142 gives the aggrieved person a remedy against groundless threats.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Designs, GI, Plant Varieties, Revision & Exam
courses.summary: Industrial designs under the Designs Act 2000, geographical indications, plant varieties and farmers' rights, then a comparison sheet, a problem answer and a cumulative exam.
outcomes: Explain registrable designs and the design–copyright overlap
Explain GI registration and the extra protection for wines and spirits
Describe farmers' rights under the PPV&FR Act
Compare terms, registration and remedies across IP rights

scenes.text: A company registers the curved body design of its new scooter.
A rival launches a nearly identical body. Design piracy?

steps.title: What is a design (section 2(d))
steps.body: Features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to an article by an industrial process, which in the finished article appeal to and are judged solely by the eye. Excludes mode or principle of construction, mere mechanical devices, trademarks and artistic works under section 2(c) of the Copyright Act.

steps.title: Registrability and term
steps.body: Must be new or original, not previously published in India or elsewhere, significantly distinguishable from known designs, and not contrary to public order or morality (s. 4). Term: **10 years** from registration, extendable once by **5 years** (total 15) (s. 11). Infringement is called **piracy** (s. 22): remedy damages up to ₹25,000 per contravention as a debt (total cap ₹50,000 for one design) or suit for damages and injunction.

steps.title: Design–copyright overlap
steps.body: Section 15(2) Copyright Act: copyright in a design capable of registration but not registered ceases once the article has been reproduced more than **50 times** by industrial process by the owner or licensee. Microfibres Inc v Girdhar (Delhi HC, 2009) applied this to fabric designs.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling a functional feature a design. Designs protect eye appeal; functional mechanisms belong to patents.

Distinctive shape of a perfume bottle
The principle of a folding chair

scenes.text: Darjeeling tea became India's first registered GI in 2004.
Meanwhile a farmer is sued for growing a potato variety. Can a plant-variety owner sue a farmer?

steps.title: GI Act 1999
steps.body: A GI identifies goods (agricultural, natural or manufactured, including handicrafts and foodstuffs) as originating in a territory where a given quality, reputation or characteristic is essentially attributable to geographical origin. Registry at Chennai. **Registered proprietor** (association/organisation of producers) and **authorised users**. Term 10 years, renewable. Section 22(2) gives additional protection to notified goods (based on TRIPS Art. 23 wines and spirits). GIs cannot be assigned or licensed (s. 24). Examples: Darjeeling tea, Mysore silk, Kanchipuram silk, Basmati (registered 2016 for specified states), Banarasi saree.

steps.title: PPV&FR Act 2001
steps.body: Registers new, extant and farmers' varieties if they meet **DUS** (distinctness, uniformity, stability) and, for new varieties, novelty. Term: 15 years (field crops), 18 years (trees and vines). **Farmers' rights** (s. 39): a farmer may save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange, share or sell farm produce including seed of a protected variety, but not as branded seed. Innocent infringement by farmers is protected (s. 42). In 2019 PepsiCo withdrew suits against Gujarat farmers over FL-2027 potatoes, and in 2021 the PPV&FR Authority revoked its registration (upheld by the Delhi HC Single Judge in 2024, later partly reversed in appeal regarding procedure – check current status).

steps.title: Applying farmers' rights
steps.body: A farmer grows a registered potato variety from saved seed and sells potatoes in the local market without branding: protected by section 39(1)(iv). If he packs and sells seed under the breeder's brand name, he infringes.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating a GI like a trademark owned by one company. A GI is a collective right of producers of the region.

quiz.why: Darjeeling tea was registered in 2004–05 as the first GI under the 1999 Act.

quiz.q: Can a GI be assigned?
options: No, section 24 prohibits assignment and licensing
quiz.why: A GI is tied to the region and its producers, so it cannot be assigned, transmitted or licensed.

quiz.why: New plant varieties must be distinct, uniform and stable to be registered.

scenes.text: A common short note asks you to compare IP rights.
Learn this table and you can answer any comparison question.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- **Copyright**: automatic; life + 60 (author works), 60 from publication (films, sound recordings); Copyright Office registration optional.
- **Patent**: registration compulsory; 20 years from filing; novelty, inventive step, industrial application.
- **Trademark**: registration optional (passing off protects unregistered); 10 years renewable indefinitely.
- **Design**: registration required; 10 + 5 years.
- **GI**: registration; 10 years renewable; collective.
- **Plant variety**: 15/18 years; DUS.
- **Trade secret**: no registration; lasts while secret.

steps.title: Forums
steps.body: The Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 abolished the Intellectual Property Appellate Board; its jurisdiction moved to High Courts (Delhi HC created an IP Division). Commercial Courts Act 2015 applies to IP suits as commercial disputes (pre-institution mediation under s. 12A unless urgent relief is sought).

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: In problem answers, always identify ALL rights in play – most fact patterns involve two or more.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Citing IPAB as a current forum. It was abolished in 2021.

quiz.why: Section 12A mandates pre-institution mediation except where urgent interim relief is claimed.

scenes.text: A developer launches 'YogaGuru' app with original illustrations of asanas, a new algorithm-based posture correction feature using phone sensors, and a logo.
A rival copies the illustrations and uses 'YogGuroo'. Advise.

steps.title: Question (original)
steps.body: Advise the developer on (a) protection available, (b) remedies against the rival, (c) whether the posture-correction method can be patented. (20 marks)

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
(a) Copyright: illustrations (artistic works), code (literary). Trademark: 'YogaGuru' – suggestive, registrable in classes 9 and 41. Patent: posture-correction method using sensors may be patentable if it shows technical effect beyond a 'computer programme per se' (s. 3(k), Ferid Allani); asanas themselves are traditional knowledge (s. 3(p)) and not patentable.
(b) Rival: copyright infringement (s. 51) for copied illustrations; trademark infringement if registered (s. 29, deceptive similarity: phonetic similarity YogaGuru/YogGuroo, same goods, Cadila factors) or passing off if unregistered. Remedies: interim injunction, damages/account of profits, takedown from app stores. Commercial Court suit with s. 12A exemption if urgent.
(c) Yes, possibly, if claimed as a technical system/method producing technical effect; not if claimed as an algorithm alone.

steps.title: Answer structure
steps.body: Use sub-headings (a), (b), (c), each with law, case and application.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Claiming copyright in yoga poses themselves. Poses are ideas/traditional knowledge; only the original illustrations are protected.

quiz.why: The two names sound almost the same, which is central to deceptive similarity.

uni-llb-jurisprudence.title: Jurisprudence (Legal Theory)
uni-llb-jurisprudence.description: Meaning and scope of jurisprudence; natural law, analytical positivism (Bentham, Austin, Hart, Kelsen), historical, sociological and realist schools; theories of justice; sources of law – custom, precedent, legislation; and legal concepts – rights and duties, Hohfeld, persons, possession, ownership, liability and theories of punishment, with Indian case illustrations. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB (3-year and 5-year) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature of Jurisprudence, Natural Law and Analytical Positivism
courses.summary: Definitions and scope of jurisprudence; natural law from the Greeks to Aquinas, the social-contract thinkers and its revival (Fuller, Finnis); Bentham and Austin's command theory; Hart's concept of law with primary and secondary rules; and Kelsen's pure theory with the Grundnorm.
outcomes: Compare definitions of jurisprudence by Salmond, Austin, Holland and Paton
Trace the development of natural law and its influence on Indian constitutional law
Explain and criticise Austin's command theory
Explain Hart's union of primary and secondary rules and the rule of recognition
Explain Kelsen's hierarchy of norms and apply the Grundnorm to revolutions

scenes.text: A first-year student asks: why study 'what law is' when I just need sections and cases?
Because judges deciding Kesavananda or Puttaswamy were really answering theoretical questions about the nature and limits of law.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- Cicero: knowledge of law (juris prudentia – 'knowledge or skill in law')
- Ulpian: knowledge of things divine and human, the science of the just and unjust
- Austin: philosophy of positive law
- Holland: the formal science of positive law
- Salmond: the science of the first principles of the civil law; generic (whole body of legal doctrine) and specific (first principles)
- Paton: a particular method of study, of the general notion of law rather than the law of one country

steps.title: Scope and kinds
steps.body:
Salmond's division: analytical (structure and concepts of law), historical (growth of law), ethical (law as it ought to be).
Other approaches: sociological, economic, feminist, critical legal studies.
Uses: clarity of concepts, interpretation of statutes, critical evaluation, law reform.

steps.title: Indian thought
steps.body: Ancient Indian sources treated law as dharma – duty-centred, with the king bound by dharma. Sources included Shruti, Smriti, custom (sadachara) and conscience (atmatushti), discussed by Manu and Yajnavalkya.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing that jurisprudence is just 'philosophy': Holland and Austin saw it as a science of positive law; give both views.

activity.prompt: Match the definition to the jurist

items.text: Science of the first principles of the civil law

quiz.q: 'Formal science of positive law' – who?
quiz.why: Holland defined jurisprudence in these words.

quiz.q: Salmond divided jurisprudence into
quiz.why: These are Salmond's three kinds.

quiz.q: Juris prudentia literally means
quiz.why: It comes from juris (law) and prudentia (knowledge or skill).

scenes.text: In Sophocles' play, Antigone buries her brother against King Creon's order, appealing to a higher, unwritten law.
This idea – that human law must answer to a higher law – runs through natural law thought to modern human rights.

steps.title: Ancient and medieval
steps.body:
- Greeks: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle – natural justice vs conventional justice
- Stoics and Romans: Cicero – 'true law is right reason in agreement with nature'; jus naturale, jus gentium, jus civile
- Aquinas (Summa Theologica): four kinds of law – eternal, divine, natural, human. An unjust human law is 'not law but a corruption of law' (lex iniusta non est lex)

steps.title: Social contract thinkers
steps.body:
- Grotius: natural law exists even if God did not exist; father of international law
- Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651): life in nature 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short' → absolute sovereign
- Locke (1690): rights of life, liberty and property; limited government; right to resist
- Rousseau (1762): general will; popular sovereignty

steps.title: Revival in 20th century
steps.body: After the Nazi era: Radbruch's formula (extremely unjust law is not valid law); Lon Fuller's 'inner morality of law' – 8 desiderata (generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity, clarity, non-contradiction, possibility of compliance, constancy, congruence between rules and official action); John Finnis – basic goods and practical reasonableness; Stammler – 'natural law with a variable content'.

steps.title: In Indian law
steps.body: Natural justice principles (audi alteram partem, nemo judex in causa sua) – A.K. Kraipak (1969), Maneka Gandhi (1978); the basic structure doctrine and 'right, just and fair' procedure reflect natural law thinking; Puttaswamy treated privacy as natural and inalienable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing Fuller's procedural natural law with religious natural law: Fuller's desiderata are about how law is made and applied, not about God.

quiz.why: These are Aquinas's four kinds of law.

quiz.why: Lon Fuller set out eight procedural desiderata.

quiz.why: Hobbes wrote this in Leviathan.

quiz.q: 'Natural law with a variable content' was proposed by

lessons.title: Bentham and Austin: the command theory

story.title: The gunman and the tax collector

scenes.text: A gunman says 'hand over your money or I shoot'. A tax officer says 'pay tax or face a penalty'.
Both are commands backed by threats. Hart asked: is law just 'the gunman situation writ large'?

steps.title: Austin's theory (The Province of Jurisprudence Determined, 1832)
steps.body:
Law properly so called is a **command** of the **sovereign** backed by a **sanction**.
- Command: expression of wish with power to inflict evil if not obeyed
- Sovereign: a determinate human superior who receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society and is not in habitual obedience to any other
- Sanction: the evil incurred on disobedience
Laws not properly so called: laws by analogy (fashion, honour), laws by metaphor (laws of science). Positive morality and international law are not law in the strict sense.
Bentham (Of Laws in General) earlier proposed a similar but more refined imperative theory and separated 'law as it is' from 'law as it ought to be' (expositorial vs censorial jurisprudence).

steps.title: Criticisms
steps.body:
1. Customary law and judge-made law are not commands of a sovereign
2. Power-conferring rules (making a will, contract) do not command anything
3. Indivisible, illimitable sovereign does not fit federal or constitutional states like India (where the Constitution is supreme)
4. Continuity: on a sovereign's death, laws do not lapse
5. International law is denied the status of law
6. Ignores the moral and social dimension

steps.title: Applying to India
steps.body: Who is the Austinian sovereign in India? Parliament is limited by Fundamental Rights and basic structure; the President acts on advice; the people are not a determinate body. The theory struggles – a classic 15-mark point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Austin denied all morality: he separated law and morality analytically but did not say morality is unimportant.

activity.prompt: Tick the criticisms that apply to Austin's theory
items: Cannot locate an illimitable sovereign in a constitutional democracy
Cannot explain continuity of law on change of sovereign
Denies international law the status of law

quiz.q: Austin's three elements of law are
quiz.why: These are the elements of Austin's imperative theory.

quiz.q: International law for Austin is
quiz.why: Lacking a sovereign, it is only positive morality in his scheme.

quiz.q: Bentham distinguished expositorial and
quiz.why: Expository is law as it is; censorial is law as it ought to be.

scenes.text: In State v Dosso (1958) Pakistan's Supreme Court used Kelsen to validate a successful military revolution.
In Asma Jilani (1972) it overruled Dosso, rejecting that use of Kelsen.

steps.title: Hart – The Concept of Law (1961)
steps.body:
Law is a union of **primary rules** (duty-imposing) and **secondary rules** (power-conferring).
Secondary rules cure defects of a primitive system:
- Rule of **recognition** – cures uncertainty
- Rules of **change** – cure static quality
- Rules of **adjudication** – cure inefficiency
Internal point of view: officials accept rules as standards. Minimum content of natural law: human vulnerability, approximate equality, limited altruism, limited resources, limited understanding.
Hart–Fuller and Hart–Devlin debates; Dworkin's criticism (rules vs principles, Riggs v Palmer, 'right answer' thesis).

steps.title: Kelsen – Pure Theory of Law
steps.body:
Law should be studied free of ethics, politics, sociology and psychology.
Law is a hierarchy of norms (Stufenbau); each norm gets validity from a higher norm, up to the **Grundnorm** (basic norm), which is presupposed, not posited.
A norm is an 'ought' (sollen) – if X, then sanction Y ought to follow.
Efficacy: the Grundnorm must be by and large effective; when a revolution succeeds, a new Grundnorm emerges.
In India one may say the Grundnorm is that the Constitution ought to be obeyed; Kesavananda and basic structure test where that norm's limits lie.

steps.title: Hierarchy example
steps.body: Grundnorm → Constitution → Act of Parliament (e.g. Motor Vehicles Act) → Rules under the Act → a traffic police officer's challan. Each is valid because authorised by the higher level.

steps.title: Hart vs Austin
steps.body: Hart rejected the gunman model: obligation ('being obliged' vs 'having an obligation'), the habit of obedience vs rule acceptance, and the variety of laws (power-conferring).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling the Grundnorm 'the Constitution': it is the presupposed norm that the first constitution ought to be obeyed.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Historical, Sociological and Realist Schools; Theories of Justice
courses.summary: Savigny's Volksgeist and Maine's 'from status to contract'; sociological jurisprudence of Ehrlich, Duguit, Ihering and Roscoe Pound's social engineering; American and Scandinavian realism; and theories of justice – Aristotle, utilitarianism, Rawls, Nozick, Sen – with Indian applications.
outcomes: Explain Savigny's Volksgeist and its criticism
State Maine's thesis and its relevance to Indian personal law
Apply Pound's classification of interests to a public-interest case
Contrast American and Scandinavian realism
Compare Rawls, Nozick and Sen on justice

scenes.text: In 1814 Thibaut proposed a single civil code for the German states, modelled on the Code Napoléon.
Savigny replied that law, like language, grows from the spirit of the people and cannot be made in a hurry.

steps.title: Savigny
steps.body:
Law is found, not made. It grows with the growth and strengthens with the strength of the people, and dies away as the nation loses its nationality.
Volksgeist: the common consciousness of the people. Stages: customary law → juristic law (lawyers give it technical form) → codification only when law is mature.
Criticisms: ignores conscious legislation and reform; Volksgeist is vague; many customs come from a minority; borrowing of laws (reception of Roman law) contradicts it; later misused by nationalist ideologies.
Puchta developed the theory further.

steps.title: Sir Henry Maine – Ancient Law (1861)
steps.body:
'The movement of the progressive societies has hitherto been a movement from **Status to Contract**.'
Used comparative and historical method, including Indian material from his time as Law Member in India. Stages: commands of rulers (themistes) → custom → codes; progressive societies then use legal fictions, equity and legislation to change law.
Relevance: caste and family status giving way to individual choice, yet welfare and labour laws show a partial return from contract toward status.

steps.title: Indian illustration
steps.body: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 gave daughters coparcenary rights by birth (Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma, 2020) – legislation changing custom, which shows the limits of Savigny's view that law should simply follow existing popular custom.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Maine's thesis holds without qualification: modern employment and consumer protection laws re-introduce status-based protections.

activity.prompt: Savigny or Maine?

quiz.why: Savigny's term for the people's common consciousness.

quiz.q: 'From Status to Contract' appears in
quiz.why: Maine's Ancient Law (1861).

quiz.q: Savigny opposed
quiz.why: He rejected Thibaut's call for a quick German code.

scenes.text: Tanneries poured untreated effluent into a river used by villages.
In Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) the Supreme Court balanced industrial interest against public health – Pound's social engineering in action.

steps.title: Founders
steps.body:
- Ihering: law as a means to a social end; purpose (Zweck) in law; reward and coercion as levers
- Ehrlich: 'living law' – the centre of gravity of legal development lies in society itself, not in legislation, juristic science or judicial decision
- Duguit: social solidarity; the State is subject to law; rejected sovereignty and individual rights as fictions
- Max Weber: types of legal authority and rationality

steps.title: Pound's social engineering
steps.body:
The task of law is to satisfy the maximum of human wants with the minimum of friction and waste – balancing interests.
Interests: (1) **individual** – personality, domestic relations, substance; (2) **public** – interests of the State as a juristic person; (3) **social** – general security, security of social institutions, general morals, conservation of social resources, general progress, individual life.
Jural postulates of a civilised society.

steps.title: Applying Pound
steps.body:
Vellore Citizens' case:
- Individual interest: tannery owners' property and trade
- Social interest: conservation of resources, public health
- Balance: polluter pays, precautionary principle, compensation and closure of non-compliant units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Pound's interests have fixed priorities: he left balancing to the facts of each case.

story.title: What did the judge have for breakfast?

scenes.text: Realists joked that a decision may depend on what the judge had for breakfast.
The serious point: to understand law, study what courts actually do, not only the rules in books.

steps.title: American realism
steps.body:
- Holmes: 'The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience'; law is 'prophecies of what the courts will do in fact'; the 'bad man' perspective (The Path of the Law, 1897)
- John Chipman Gray: law is what courts lay down; statutes are only sources
- Jerome Frank: rule-sceptic and fact-sceptic; the 'basic legal myth' of certainty
- Karl Llewellyn: law-jobs theory; 'paper rules' vs 'real rules'

steps.title: Scandinavian realism
steps.body: Hägerström, Olivecrona, Lundstedt, Alf Ross: rejected metaphysics; rights and duties are psychological facts; law as 'independent imperatives' (Olivecrona); validity explained by the psychology of judges and citizens.

steps.title: Indian relevance
steps.body: Studies of judicial behaviour, judicial activism (PIL era) and the role of the Chief Justice as 'master of the roster' (Shanti Bhushan v Supreme Court, 2018) show realist questions are live in India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying realists rejected all rules: they were sceptical of rules as the only determinant of decisions.

quiz.why: Holmes wrote it in The Common Law (1881).

quiz.q: Fact-scepticism is associated with
quiz.why: Frank doubted the reliability of fact-finding.

quiz.q: Scandinavian realists treated rights as
quiz.why: They rejected metaphysical rights.

scenes.text: Imagine designing society without knowing whether you will be rich or poor, able or disabled.
Rawls argued that you would choose principles protecting the least advantaged.

steps.title: Classical
steps.body:
- Aristotle: distributive justice (according to merit, proportional equality) and corrective justice (restoring balance after wrongs)
- Utilitarianism: Bentham – greatest happiness of the greatest number; felicific calculus; J.S. Mill – quality of pleasures, harm principle

steps.title: Rawls – A Theory of Justice (1971)
steps.body:
Original position behind a veil of ignorance.
Principles (in lexical order):
1. Equal basic liberties for all
2. Social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if (a) attached to offices open to all under fair equality of opportunity, and (b) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (difference principle)
Indian echo: Articles 14–16 with Articles 38, 39 and 46; reservations as fair equality of opportunity (cited in N.M. Thomas, 1976 reasoning on substantive equality).

steps.title: Nozick and Sen
steps.body:
Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974): entitlement theory – justice in acquisition, transfer and rectification; minimal State; redistribution violates rights.
Amartya Sen (The Idea of Justice, 2009): niti (rules, institutions) vs nyaya (realised justice in people's lives); capability approach; comparative rather than transcendental justice.

steps.title: Applying the theories
steps.body:
A State gives free laptops only to students from families below a certain income.
- Utilitarian: does it maximise total welfare?
- Rawls: benefits the least advantaged → justified by difference principle.
- Nozick: taxation to fund it is coerced transfer → suspicious.
- Sen: does it expand real capabilities (internet access, skills)?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Rawls allows liberty to be traded for economic gain: the first principle has lexical priority.

quiz.why: It is the second part of Rawls's second principle.

quiz.why: Sen uses these Sanskrit terms in The Idea of Justice.

quiz.why: Aristotle distinguished distributive and corrective justice.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Sources of Law: Custom, Precedent and Legislation
courses.summary: Formal, material, legal and historical sources; custom and the tests of a valid custom; precedent – ratio decidendi, obiter dicta, stare decisis, Article 141 and per incuriam; legislation – supreme and subordinate, delegated legislation and its control, and the main rules of statutory interpretation.
outcomes: Classify sources of law using Salmond's scheme
Test whether a custom is valid using the established requirements
Find the ratio of a case using Wambaugh's and Goodhart's methods
Apply Article 141, per incuriam and the binding force of benches

scenes.text: A community has, for generations, allowed divorce by a panchayat decision.
Hindu Marriage Act s.29(2) saves rights recognised by custom to obtain a divorce – if the custom is proved.

steps.title: Salmond's classification
steps.body:
- **Formal** source: from which law derives force and validity (will of the State)
- **Material** source: from which law derives its matter
  - Legal sources: legislation, precedent, custom, agreement (conventional law)
  - Historical sources: writings, foreign law, unauthoritative works which influence law but lack legal authority
Allen and Paton criticised this division as artificial in parts.

steps.title: Requisites of a valid custom
steps.body:
1. Antiquity – immemorial (in England from 1189); in India no fixed date, but ancient and established
2. Continuity – uninterrupted
3. Peaceable enjoyment
4. Certainty and clarity
5. Reasonableness
6. Conformity with statute law (cannot be contrary to an Act)
7. Not opposed to public policy or morality
8. Obligatory force (opinio necessitatis)
Burden of proof lies on the party asserting the custom (Ramalakshmi Ammal v Sivanantha Perumal, 1872 PC: custom must be ancient, certain, reasonable, and not opposed to public policy).
Hindu Marriage Act s.3(a) defines custom and usage.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body: Legal custom (general and local) vs conventional custom (usage incorporated into contracts). Custom vs prescription: custom is a long practice creating a law for a class; prescription creates a right for an individual.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming a custom can override a statute: a custom contrary to an Act is invalid unless the Act saves it.

lessons.title: Precedent: ratio, obiter and stare decisis

scenes.text: A 100-page judgment discusses history, foreign cases and hypothetical examples.
Only the ratio decidendi – the principle necessary for the decision – binds lower courts.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Ratio decidendi**: the principle of law on which the decision is based.
**Obiter dicta**: observations not necessary for the decision; persuasive (though Supreme Court obiter is treated with great respect – often followed by High Courts).
**Stare decisis**: stand by what has been decided.

steps.title: Finding the ratio
steps.body:
Wambaugh's reversal test: reverse the proposition; if the decision would still be the same, the proposition is not the ratio.
Goodhart's material facts test: ratio = material facts as seen by the judge + the decision on them.
Divided Benches: majority ratio binds.

steps.title: Precedent in India
steps.body:
- Art. 141: law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India (not on the Supreme Court itself – Bengal Immunity v State of Bihar, 1955)
- Larger Bench binds smaller; a Bench of equal strength should refer doubts to a larger Bench (Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community, 2005)
- High Court decisions bind subordinate courts in that State; persuasive elsewhere
- Per incuriam: decision given in ignorance of a binding statute or precedent – not binding
- Sub silentio: point not argued
- Prospective overruling (Golaknath, 1967)

steps.title: Reversal test
steps.body: Case: a tenant was evicted because he sublet without consent. The judgment says, 'Also, tenants must keep premises clean.' Reverse: 'tenants need not keep premises clean' – would the eviction still follow from unauthorised subletting? Yes → cleanliness remark is obiter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the Supreme Court is bound by its own decisions: it can overrule itself through a larger Bench.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to extract the ratio
items: Read the facts found by the court
Identify which facts the court treated as material
Identify the decision on those facts

options: Only High Courts in that State
quiz.why: It binds all courts within India, but the Supreme Court can depart from its own precedents.

scenes.text: An Act says 'the Central Government may make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act'.
The ministry's rules are law – but only within the limits the Act permits.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body:
Supreme legislation: by the sovereign legislature (in India, Parliament and State Legislatures within constitutional limits).
Subordinate legislation: executive (rules, regulations), judicial (rules of court), municipal (bye-laws), autonomous (universities), colonial.

steps.title: Delegated legislation and control
steps.body:
Essential legislative functions cannot be delegated (In re Delhi Laws Act, 1951); the legislature must lay down policy and guidelines.
Controls:
- Parliamentary: laying before the House; Committee on Subordinate Legislation
- Judicial: ultra vires the parent Act or the Constitution; excessive delegation (Hamdard Dawakhana, 1960)
- Procedural: publication, consultation

steps.title: Legislation vs precedent vs custom
steps.body:
Legislation: abrogative power, prospective, deliberate, in advance, clear form.
Precedent: arises from disputes, retrospective in effect, gradual.
Custom: grows from practice; slow; local.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating rules as valid merely because published: they must stay within the parent Act.

steps.title: Main rules
steps.body:

- **Golden rule**: modify literal meaning to avoid absurdity (R v Allen, 1872; Lee v Knapp)
- **Mischief rule** (Heydon's Case, 1584): what was the law before, what was the mischief, what remedy did Parliament adopt, and the reason
- **Purposive** approach (modern)
- Harmonious construction (Venkataramana Devaru, 1958), ejusdem generis, noscitur a sociis, reading down

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A statute penalises 'any person who impersonates a person entitled to vote'. X impersonates a dead voter.
Literal rule: a dead person is not 'entitled to vote' → acquittal (Whiteley v Chappell).
Mischief rule: the law targets electoral fraud → impersonating the dead is the mischief → conviction would better serve the purpose.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Legal Rights, Duties, Hohfeld's Analysis and Legal Personality
courses.summary: Theories of rights (will and interest), Salmond's elements and kinds of rights, duties and their kinds, Hohfeld's jural correlatives and opposites, and legal personality – natural and juristic persons, theories of corporate personality, idols, unborn persons, the dead, animals and rivers.
outcomes: Compare the will and interest theories of rights

Apply Hohfeld's four pairs of correlatives to facts
Explain the theories of corporate personality and lifting the veil

scenes.text: Ravi lends Sita ₹20,000 repayable in a month.
Ravi has a right to be repaid; Sita has a duty to repay. Every right has a correlative duty.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
**Will theory** (Kant, Hegel, Savigny, Hart): a right is an individual's will or choice protected by law.
**Interest theory** (Ihering, Bentham, MacCormick): a right is a legally protected interest.
Salmond: a right is an interest recognised and protected by a rule of right; Holland: capacity of one man to control the acts of another with the assent and assistance of the State.

steps.title: Salmond's five elements
steps.body:
1. Person of inherence (subject/owner of the right)
2. Person of incidence (who bears the duty)
3. Content – the act or forbearance
4. Object – the thing over which the right exists
5. Title – facts by which the right came to its owner
Example: Ravi (inherence), Sita (incidence), repayment (content), ₹20,000 (object), loan contract (title).

steps.title: Kinds of rights
steps.body: Perfect (enforceable) vs imperfect (e.g. time-barred debt); positive vs negative; real (in rem – against the world) vs personal (in personam); proprietary vs personal; vested vs contingent; principal vs accessory; legal vs equitable; corporeal vs incorporeal; rights in re propria vs in re aliena (encumbrances such as lease, servitude, security).

steps.title: Duties
steps.body: Positive or negative; absolute (no corresponding right in an individual, e.g. duties to the public – Austin) or relative; primary or secondary (sanctioning).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing up 'object' and 'content': the object is the thing; the content is the act or omission.

quiz.why: The right exists but cannot be enforced by action.

scenes.text: Lawyers use 'right' loosely – for claims, liberties, powers and immunities.
Wesley Hohfeld (1913, 1917) separated them into eight fundamental conceptions.

steps.title: Correlatives
steps.body:
Right (claim) ↔ Duty
Privilege (liberty) ↔ No-right
Power ↔ Liability
Immunity ↔ Disability

steps.title: Opposites
steps.body:
Right ↔ No-right
Privilege ↔ Duty
Power ↔ Disability
Immunity ↔ Liability

steps.title: Applying
steps.body:
1. A landowner may walk on his own land: privilege; others have no-right to stop him.
2. A landowner can sell the land: power; the buyer's position changes – liability.
3. Article 20(3): accused has immunity from compelled self-incrimination; the State has disability.
4. Tenant's claim that landlord not disturb possession: right; landlord's duty.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing correlatives with opposites: correlatives exist between two persons; opposites describe the absence of a position in the same person.

quiz.why: Having a privilege means having no duty to the contrary.

scenes.text: In 2017 the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and Yamuna to be legal persons.
The Supreme Court stayed that order later that year – but the question of who is a 'person' remains alive.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
A legal person is any being capable of rights and duties (Salmond). Natural persons (human beings) and legal/juristic persons (companies, idols, universities, States).
Unborn child: law protects interests (Transfer of Property Act s.13, s.20; Hindu Succession Act s.20 on a child in the womb).
Dead persons: limited protection – reputation (criminal defamation of the deceased), body (dignity of the dead under Art. 21 – Parmanand Katara and later Ashray Adhikar Abhiyan), and wishes (wills).

steps.title: Theories of corporate personality
steps.body:
1. Fiction theory (Savigny, Salmond): personality is a fiction of law
2. Concession theory: it exists by State concession
3. Realist theory (Gierke, Maitland): corporation is a real entity with its own will
4. Bracket theory (Ihering): the members are the real persons; the corporate form is a bracket
5. Purpose theory (Brinz): property dedicated to a purpose
Salomon v Salomon (1897): company separate from members. Lifting the veil: fraud, evasion of tax (Juggilal Kamlapat), enemy character (Daimler, 1916), public interest (LIC v Escorts, 1986).

steps.title: Idols and others
steps.body:
Hindu idol is a juristic person capable of holding property, acting through a shebait (Pramatha Nath Mullick v Pradyumna Kumar Mullick, 1925 PC). Ram Janmabhoomi (M. Siddiq v Mahant Suresh Das, 2019): Ram Lalla Virajman a juristic person; the land itself not a juristic person.
Animal Welfare Board v A. Nagaraja (2014): animals have rights to live with dignity under Art. 21 read with the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act; jallikattu restrictions (later legislative changes were upheld in 2023).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the Supreme Court upheld the Ganga as a legal person: it stayed the High Court order.

2. Rights: idol's beneficial ownership (in rem); company's lease (right in re aliena).
3. Hohfeld: lessor's power to terminate on breach ↔ lessee's liability; lessee's claim to quiet possession ↔ lessor's duty.

courses.summary: Possession – corpus and animus, Savigny, Ihering and Salmond, kinds of possession and possessory remedies; ownership – Austin's definition, incidents and kinds; property theories; liability – mens rea, negligence, strict and vicarious liability; and theories of punishment with Indian sentencing law.

story.title: The bracelet on the shop floor

scenes.text: In Bridges v Hawkesworth (1851) a customer found banknotes on a shop floor.
The finder won against the shopkeeper, who did not know of the notes and had not shown an intention to control things on the public part of the floor.

steps.title: Elements
steps.body:
**Corpus possessionis**: physical control or the power to exclude others.
**Animus possidendi**: intention to possess and exclude others.
Savigny: both corpus and animus domini (intention to hold as owner) are needed; possession is the foundation of ownership.
Ihering: possession is the outward visibility of ownership; animus is inferred from corpus; protects possession to protect ownership.
Salmond: possession is continuing exercise of a claim to the exclusive use of a material object; corpus + animus possidendi.
Pollock: physical control.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body: Corporeal (of things) vs incorporeal (of rights, e.g. easement); mediate (through another – agent, bailee) vs immediate; constructive (keys to a godown); adverse possession (Limitation Act 1963 – 12 years for private immovable property, 30 years against the Government; Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur, 2019: the possessor can also sue to protect title acquired by adverse possession); concurrent possession.

steps.title: Finders
steps.body:
- Armory v Delamirie (1722): finder has better title than all except the true owner
- Bridges v Hawkesworth: finder of goods on public part of a shop wins over shopkeeper
- South Staffordshire Water v Sharman (1896): things found in or attached to land belong to the landowner
- Parker v British Airways Board (1982): occupier needs a manifest intention to control
India: s.71 Contract Act treats the finder as a bailee.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body:
A cleaner employed by a hotel finds a ring under a mattress in a guest room.
Corpus: hotel controls private rooms. Animus: hotel shows intention to control items in its rooms (lost-property policy).
Result: hotel's claim is better than the employee-cleaner's (employee finds on behalf of employer), subject to the true owner.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating possession with ownership: a thief has possession but not ownership.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Austin: a right indefinite in point of user, unrestricted in point of disposition and unlimited in point of duration over a determinate thing.
Salmond: the relation between a person and a right vested in him; ownership in its widest sense is the whole of a person's proprietary rights.
Honoré's incidents: right to possess, use, manage, income, capital, security, transmissibility, absence of term, prohibition of harmful use, liability to execution, residuary character.

steps.title: Kinds
steps.body: Corporeal vs incorporeal; sole vs co-ownership (joint – survivorship; in common – shares pass to heirs); trust (legal) vs beneficial; legal vs equitable; vested vs contingent; absolute vs limited (e.g. Hindu woman's limited estate before s.14 Hindu Succession Act 1956).

steps.title: Possession vs ownership
steps.body: Possession is de facto; ownership is de jure. Possession is prima facie evidence of ownership. Ownership can exist without possession and vice versa. Possession is 'nine points of the law'.

steps.body: Saying ownership is unlimited today: constitutional and statutory limits apply (Art. 300A, land ceilings, zoning).

lessons.title: Liability: mens rea, negligence and strict liability

scenes.text: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea – an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is guilty.
But a dairy owner selling adulterated milk may be liable even without knowledge – strict liability offences.

steps.title: Conditions of liability
steps.body:
Act (positive or negative; voluntary) + mental element + causation + absence of a legal excuse.
Mental elements: intention (purpose and foresight), recklessness, negligence (failure to take care), knowledge.

steps.title: Strict and vicarious
steps.body:
Strict liability in crime: public welfare offences – food adulteration, environmental laws (Ranjit D. Udeshi on knowledge; State of Maharashtra v M.H. George, 1965 – gold smuggling: mens rea excluded by necessary implication). Mens rea is presumed unless excluded expressly or by necessary implication (Sweet v Parsley, 1970).
Vicarious liability: master for servant in tort; in crime, generally not, except by statute (e.g. company officers under special laws).

steps.title: Theories of negligence
steps.body:
Subjective (Salmond, Austin): negligence is a state of mind – indifference.
Objective (Pollock, Winfield): negligence is conduct falling below the standard of a reasonable person – modern view.

steps.title: M.H. George
steps.body: A German passenger on transit through Bombay carrying gold was unaware of a recent RBI notification. Held: liable under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act – the scheme excluded mens rea by necessary implication; ignorance of law is no excuse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling motive and intention the same: motive is the reason behind intention, generally irrelevant to liability.

scenes.text: In Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) the Supreme Court upheld the death penalty but limited it to the 'rarest of rare' cases.
Life imprisonment is the rule; death the exception, after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Deterrent**: punish to deter the offender and others (Bentham)
- **Retributive**: punishment as deserved; 'an eye for an eye' (Kant, Hegel)
- **Preventive**: disable the offender – imprisonment, disqualification
- **Reformative**: rehabilitate the offender – probation, parole, open prisons (Probation of Offenders Act 1958)
- **Expiatory**: offender atones
- **Restorative justice**: victim–offender reconciliation; compensation (BNSS provisions on victim compensation)

steps.title: Indian sentencing
steps.body:

- Community service is a new form of punishment in BNS 2023 (s.4(f)) for some petty offences

steps.title: Applying
steps.body:
A first-time 19-year-old offender steals a phone.
- Reformative: probation and counselling
- Deterrent: a short term to signal to others
- Restorative: return the phone, compensate
Indian practice for petty first offences leans reformative (probation).

uni-llb-labour-law.title: Labour & Industrial Law
uni-llb-labour-law.description: Constitutional framework and the four Labour Codes, industrial disputes and their settlement, strikes and lock-outs, lay-off, retrenchment and closure, trade unions and standing orders, wages, bonus and social security (gratuity, EPF, ESI, maternity), and occupational safety, contract labour and workplace protections, with worked computations. General education, not legal advice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian LLB programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Constitutional framework, Labour Codes and industrial disputes
courses.summary: Constitutional basis of labour law, the consolidation into four Labour Codes, and the core concepts of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 carried into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020: industry, workman/worker, industrial dispute, and the dispute-settlement machinery.
