lessons.title: Constitutional basis and the four Labour Codes

scenes.text: A law student finds her textbook cites the Industrial Disputes Act, but her internship firm talks about the 'IR Code'.
How do the old Acts and the new Codes fit together?

steps.title: Constitutional framework
steps.body:
- **Labour** is in the **Concurrent List** (entries 22, 23, 24 of List III) – both Parliament and States legislate.
- Fundamental rights: **Art 19(1)(c)** (form unions), **Art 23** (forced labour/begar banned), **Art 24** (no child under 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work).
- Directive Principles: **Art 38, 39** (adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work – 39(d)), **Art 41** (right to work, assistance in unemployment), **Art 42** (just and humane conditions, maternity relief), **Art 43** (living wage), **Art 43A** (workers' participation in management).

steps.title: The four Labour Codes
steps.body:
1. **Code on Wages, 2019** – minimum wages, payment of wages, bonus, equal remuneration.
2. **Industrial Relations Code, 2020** – Industrial Disputes Act, Trade Unions Act, Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act.
3. **Code on Social Security, 2020** – EPF, ESI, gratuity, maternity benefit, employees' compensation, building workers' cess, and more, plus gig/platform workers.
4. **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020** – Factories, Mines, Contract Labour, Inter-State Migrant Workmen and others.
The Codes were brought into force with effect from **21 November 2025**, with rules being framed by the Centre and States. Older case law under the repealed Acts remains highly relevant for interpreting similar provisions.

steps.title: Mapping old to new
steps.body:
A retrenchment question: old law – ID Act ss.25F, 25N; new – IR Code chapter on lay-off, retrenchment and closure.
A gratuity claim: old – Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972; new – Code on Social Security chapter on gratuity.
Always state which regime applies by the date of the event, and note any transition rules.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming old case law is irrelevant – courts still rely on precedents interpreting identical words.

activity.prompt: Tick the laws consolidated into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020

quiz.why: Article 39(d) directs equal pay for equal work for both men and women.

lessons.title: Meaning of 'industry' — the Bangalore Water Supply test

scenes.text: Nurses at a charitable hospital raise a demand for wage revision; management says a hospital is not an 'industry'.
The same question arose for a city's water supply board decades ago.

steps.title: The triple test
steps.body:
**Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v A. Rajappa (1978, 7 judges)**: 'industry' is any (1) **systematic activity**, (2) organised by **co-operation between employer and employee**, (3) for **production or distribution of goods and services** calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes (not spiritual or religious). Absence of profit motive or capital is irrelevant. The **dominant nature** test applies to mixed activities.
Excluded: **sovereign functions** strictly understood (defence, justice, legislation), and certain activities as the statute excludes.

steps.title: Statutory exclusions
steps.body: The amended definition (and the IR Code definition) expressly excludes, among others: institutions owned/managed by organisations wholly or substantially engaged in **charitable, social or philanthropic service**; **sovereign functions** of the Government including defence research, atomic energy and space; **domestic service**; and activities where the number of employees is below thresholds prescribed in some definitions. The precise exclusions should be read from the Code text.

steps.title: Applying to the hospital
steps.body:
1. Systematic activity: running wards, OPDs ✔.
2. Employer–employee co-operation ✔.
3. Services satisfying human wants (health care) ✔.
Under Bangalore Water Supply, it is an industry despite no profit motive. But if the statutory exclusion for charitable institutions applies on facts, the result can change – so check the Code definition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 'no profit, so no industry' – profit motive is irrelevant under the triple test.

activity.prompt: Order the analysis of whether an activity is an 'industry'
items: Is it a systematic, organised activity?
Is there co-operation between employer and employees?
Does it produce or distribute goods or services for human wants?
Is it a sovereign function or statutorily excluded?
Apply the dominant-nature test if activities are mixed

quiz.q: The triple test for industry comes from
options: Bangalore Water Supply v A. Rajappa
quiz.why: The seven-judge bench laid down the triple test in 1978.

quiz.q: Is profit motive necessary for an industry?
quiz.why: Bangalore Water Supply held profit motive and capital are irrelevant.

quiz.q: Strict sovereign functions like defence are
quiz.why: Sovereign functions are outside the definition of industry.

scenes.text: A shift supervisor earning ₹16,000 a month is dismissed; he raises a dispute alone, without a union.
Is he a 'workman', and is it an 'industrial dispute'?

steps.title: Workman (ID Act s.2(s)) / worker (IR Code)
steps.body: Any person employed in an industry to do manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward. Excluded: persons in armed forces/police/prison service; those employed mainly in **managerial or administrative** capacity; those in a **supervisory** capacity drawing wages above a ceiling (₹10,000 per month under the ID Act; the IR Code raises the supervisory ceiling to **₹18,000** per month or as notified). The test is the **main/dominant duties**, not designation (S.K. Maini v Carona Sahu, 1994).

steps.title: Industrial dispute
steps.body:
Any dispute between employers and employers, employers and workmen, or workmen and workmen, connected with employment, non-employment, terms of employment or conditions of labour.
Individual disputes: generally must be **espoused** by a union or substantial number of workmen (Central Provinces Transport Services v Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, 1957), **except** disputes on **discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination** of an individual, which are deemed industrial disputes (**s.2A** ID Act; similar in IR Code), and he may directly approach the Labour Court/Tribunal after conciliation (within the prescribed time).

steps.title: The supervisor
steps.body:
1. Duties mainly supervisory; wages ₹16,000.
2. Under the ID Act ceiling of ₹10,000 → he would be excluded.
3. Under the IR Code ceiling of ₹18,000 → he is a 'worker'.
4. Dismissal of an individual → deemed industrial dispute (s.2A), no espousal needed.
The applicable regime (date of dismissal) decides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Deciding 'workman' status by job title – courts look at the dominant nature of duties.

activity.prompt: Tick categories excluded from 'workman/worker'
items: Persons employed mainly in managerial capacity
Supervisors drawing wages above the prescribed ceiling

quiz.q: Individual dismissal disputes are industrial disputes under
quiz.why: Section 2A deems discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination disputes to be industrial disputes.

quiz.q: Workman status depends on
quiz.why: Courts look at the main duties actually performed.

quiz.q: Supervisory wage ceiling under the IR Code
quiz.why: The IR Code excludes supervisors drawing wages above ₹18,000 per month or as notified.

scenes.text: A union serves a charter of demands for wage revision; management refuses.
How does the dispute move through the system?

steps.title: Authorities
steps.body:
- **Works Committee** (ID Act) for establishments with 100+ workmen.
- **Grievance Redressal Committee** for establishments with 20+ workers (IR Code / ID Act s.9C).
- **Conciliation Officers** and **Boards of Conciliation** – mediate; settlement in conciliation binds all parties (s.18(3)).
- **Courts of Inquiry**.
- **Labour Courts** (Second Schedule matters: dismissal, legality of strike) and **Industrial Tribunals** (Third Schedule: wages, hours, bonus, retrenchment) – under the IR Code, **Industrial Tribunals** with judicial and administrative members, and a **National Industrial Tribunal**.
- **Voluntary arbitration** (s.10A).

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
1. Demand → bilateral negotiation.
2. Conciliation: if settlement – binding; if failure – failure report.
3. **Reference** by the appropriate Government (ID Act s.10) to Labour Court/Tribunal (under the IR Code, parties may approach the Tribunal directly after failure of conciliation within the prescribed period).
4. Award; publication; enforceability after 30 days (s.17A).
5. Writ jurisdiction of High Courts remains.

steps.title: The wage-revision demand
steps.body: Union demand → management refusal → conciliation officer calls meeting → no settlement → failure report → reference/application to Industrial Tribunal → award fixing new scales → published and enforced; any violation punishable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking a settlement reached privately binds all workmen – only a conciliation settlement (s.18(3)) binds all; a private one binds only the parties (s.18(1)).

activity.prompt: Order the life of an industrial dispute
items: Reference/application to Labour Court or Tribunal

quiz.q: Settlement in conciliation binds
quiz.why: Section 18(3) makes it binding on all parties to the dispute and those employed later.

quiz.q: Voluntary arbitration under the ID Act is in
quiz.why: Section 10A provides for voluntary reference to arbitration.

quiz.q: Grievance Redressal Committee is required for establishments with
quiz.why: It is required in establishments employing twenty or more workers.

questions.q: Art 23 prohibits
questions.why: Article 23 bans traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour.

questions.q: Art 24 bars employment of children below
questions.why: Article 24 prohibits children below fourteen in factories, mines or hazardous employment.

questions.q: Workers' participation in management is in
questions.why: Article 43A was added by the 42nd Amendment.

questions.q: Number of Labour Codes
questions.why: Four Codes consolidate 29 central labour laws.

questions.q: Dominant nature test applies to
questions.why: Where an organisation has several activities, the predominant one decides its character.

questions.q: Espousal is needed for
questions.why: Individual grievances other than termination must be espoused to become industrial disputes.

questions.q: S.K. Maini v Carona Sahu concerned
questions.why: The Court held that main duties determine workman status.

questions.q: Award becomes enforceable
questions.why: Section 17A provides enforceability on expiry of thirty days from publication.

questions.q: Labour Courts deal with matters in
questions.why: Under the ID Act, Second Schedule matters like dismissal go to Labour Courts.

questions.q: Living wage is a Directive under
questions.why: Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage.

questions.q: Workers' right to form unions comes from
questions.why: Article 19(1)(c) guarantees freedom to form associations or unions.

questions.why: Supervisors drawing more than ₹10,000 per month were excluded under s.2(s).

courses.title: Unit 2 · Strikes, lock-outs, lay-off, retrenchment and closure
courses.summary: Strikes and lock-outs and their legality, wages for strike period, continuous service, lay-off compensation, retrenchment conditions and compensation, closure, and prior-permission thresholds, with worked computations.
outcomes: Determine whether a strike is legal under notice and pendency rules
Compute lay-off compensation
Apply conditions precedent to retrenchment and compute compensation
Explain 'last come, first go' and re-employment preference
Know the prior-permission thresholds under the ID Act and the IR Code

scenes.text: Bus depot workers walk out without notice during pending conciliation over bonus.
Management cuts wages for the strike days and charge-sheets leaders.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Strike**: cessation of work by a body of persons acting in combination, or concerted refusal to work (IR Code also includes **concerted casual leave** by 50% or more workers on a given day). **Lock-out**: temporary closing of a place of employment, suspension of work, or refusal by the employer to continue to employ persons.

steps.title: Legality
steps.body:
- **Notice** (ID Act s.22 for public utility services; IR Code extends to **all industrial establishments**): strike only after notice within **60 days** before striking, and not within **14 days** of giving notice, nor before the date specified.
- **During pending proceedings** (s.23): not during conciliation before a Board and **7 days** after; not during adjudication and **2 months** after; not during arbitration; not during the period a settlement/award is in operation for matters covered.
- Contravention = **illegal strike/lock-out** (s.24), penalties.
- There is **no fundamental right to strike** (T.K. Rangarajan v Govt of Tamil Nadu, 2003; All India Bank Employees' Assn, 1962), though the right to form unions exists.

steps.title: Wages for the strike period
steps.body: Crompton Greaves v Workmen (1978): workers are entitled to wages for a strike period only if the strike is **both legal and justified**. A legal but unjustified strike, or an illegal one, does not earn wages. Peaceful participation in an illegal strike may not, by itself, justify dismissal; violence or instigation may.

steps.title: The bus depot
steps.body:
1. Bus transport is a public utility; no notice given → illegal.
2. Conciliation pending → also barred by s.23-type rule.
3. Wage cut for strike days → lawful (Crompton Greaves).
4. Disciplinary action against leaders who instigated → permissible with a fair inquiry; mere participants need proportionate treatment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming wages for any strike – the strike must be both legal and justified.

activity.prompt: Tick what makes a strike illegal under the IR Code
items: No notice given within 60 days before striking
Strike within 14 days of giving notice
Strike during pending conciliation or tribunal proceedings
Strike on matters covered by a settlement in operation

quiz.q: Wages for strike period are payable when the strike is
quiz.why: Crompton Greaves requires both legality and justification.

quiz.q: No fundamental right to strike was held in
options: T.K. Rangarajan v Govt of TN
quiz.why: The Supreme Court in 2003 said government employees have no fundamental right to strike.

quiz.q: Under the IR Code, mass casual leave by 50%+ workers on a day is
quiz.why: The IR Code's definition of strike includes such concerted casual leave.

scenes.text: A textile mill runs out of cotton and lays off 80 workers for 20 days.
A worker earns basic ₹14,000 and DA ₹4,200 per month.

steps.title: Continuous service (s.25B)
steps.body: Uninterrupted service including interruptions due to sickness, authorised leave, accident, legal strike, lock-out or cessation of work not due to the worker's fault. A worker is deemed in continuous service for one year if he has actually worked **240 days** in the preceding 12 months (**190 days** in mines/underground), and for six months if 120 days (95 in mines).

steps.title: Lay-off (s.2(kkk), s.25C)
steps.body:
**Lay-off** = failure, refusal or inability of an employer, due to shortage of coal, power or raw materials, accumulation of stocks, breakdown of machinery, natural calamity or other connected reason, to give employment to a worker on the muster rolls who has not been retrenched.
Compensation: **50% of basic wages + DA** for all days of lay-off except weekly holidays, to a worker with at least one year's continuous service; normally up to **45 days** in 12 months (beyond that by agreement, or employer may retrench after 45 days paying retrenchment compensation).
Establishments above the Chapter VB threshold (ID Act: 100 workers; IR Code: 300) need **prior permission** to lay off.

steps.title: Computing lay-off compensation
steps.body:
Monthly basic + DA = 14,000 + 4,200 = ₹18,200.
Daily rate (using 26 working days) = 18,200 ÷ 26 = **₹700**.
Lay-off: 20 days, of which 3 are weekly holidays → payable days = 17.
Compensation = 50% × 700 × 17 = 350 × 17 = **₹5,950**.
(The divisor convention, 26 or 30, depends on the wage period; state it in exam answers.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including weekly holidays in lay-off compensation days.

activity.prompt: Order the lay-off compensation computation
items: Convert to a daily rate (state divisor)
Count lay-off days excluding weekly holidays
Multiply 50% of daily rate by payable days

quiz.q: Days needed for one year's continuous service (non-mine)
quiz.why: Section 25B requires actual work of 240 days in the preceding twelve months.

quiz.q: Basic+DA ₹13,000/month (26-day divisor), 10 payable lay-off days — compensation
quiz.why: Daily rate is ₹500, half is ₹250, and 250 × 10 equals ₹2,500.

quiz.q: Lay-off compensation rate
quiz.why: Section 25C provides fifty per cent of basic wages and dearness allowance.

scenes.text: A factory with 150 workers retrenches 20 due to automation.
One worker has 8 years 8 months of service and average pay of ₹26,000 a month.

steps.title: Meaning (s.2(oo))
steps.body: Termination of service for any reason other than punishment by disciplinary action, excluding: voluntary retirement, superannuation, non-renewal of a fixed-term contract on expiry (as per the contract), and termination on continued ill-health. Courts have read 'for any reason whatsoever' widely (State Bank of India v N. Sundara Money, 1976).

steps.title: Conditions precedent (s.25F)
steps.body:
For a worker with **one year's continuous service**:
(a) **One month's notice** in writing with reasons, or wages in lieu;
(b) **Compensation = 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or part thereof exceeding six months**;
(c) **Notice to the appropriate Government**.
Non-compliance with (a) and (b) makes retrenchment **void ab initio** (State of Bombay v Hospital Mazdoor Sabha, 1960 line of cases).
**s.25G**: last come, first go in the category, unless reasons recorded.
**s.25H**: retrenched workers get preference in re-employment.
**IR Code**: also requires the employer to contribute **15 days' last drawn wages** per retrenched worker to a **Worker Re-skilling Fund**.

steps.title: Computing retrenchment compensation
steps.body:
Service 8 years 8 months → part exceeding 6 months counts → **9 years**.
Average pay ₹26,000/month → 15 days' pay (26-day convention) = 26,000 × 15 ÷ 26 = **₹15,000** per year.
Compensation = 15,000 × 9 = **₹1,35,000**.
Notice pay in lieu = one month = **₹26,000**.
Total payable at retrenchment = ₹1,61,000 (plus re-skilling fund contribution under the IR Code).
Threshold check: 150 workers → under the ID Act (≥100) prior Government permission was required under s.25N; under the IR Code (threshold 300) it is not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the 'part exceeding six months' rule.
- Paying compensation after termination – it must be paid at the time of retrenchment.

activity.prompt: Order a lawful retrenchment under s.25F (below the Chapter VB threshold)
items: Prepare seniority list in the category (s.25G)
Give one month's written notice with reasons, or pay wages in lieu
Pay retrenchment compensation at the time of retrenchment
Send notice to the appropriate Government

quiz.q: Service 5 years 5 months, average pay ₹20,800 — compensation (26-day convention)
quiz.why: Five months does not exceed six, so 5 years count; 15 days' pay is ₹12,000 and 12,000 × 5 equals ₹60,000.

quiz.q: Non-payment of compensation at retrenchment makes it
quiz.why: Compliance with s.25F(a) and (b) is a condition precedent.

quiz.q: Last come, first go is in
quiz.why: Section 25G prescribes the procedure for retrenchment by seniority.

scenes.text: A company decides to close a loss-making unit employing 350 workers.
Can it close at will?

steps.title: Closure
steps.body: **Closure** = permanent closing down of a place of employment or part of it. Under ID Act **s.25FFA**, 60 days' notice to the Government is required for closure of an undertaking (with 50 or more workers). **s.25FFF**: workers get notice and compensation as if retrenched; where closure is due to unavoidable circumstances beyond the employer's control, compensation is capped at three months' average pay (financial difficulty or accumulation of stock is not such a circumstance).

steps.title: Chapter VB / special provisions
steps.body:
For establishments above the threshold (**100** workers under the ID Act; **300** under the IR Code, which States may adjust), the employer must obtain **prior permission** of the appropriate Government for **lay-off, retrenchment and closure**.
- Closure: application at least **90 days** before intended closure (s.25-O).
- Government decides after hearing; if no decision within **60 days**, permission is **deemed granted**.
- Closure without permission is illegal; workers are entitled to all benefits as if no closure.
Article 19(1)(g) challenge to s.25-O: Excel Wear v Union of India (1978) struck down the earlier version; the re-enacted version was upheld in Orissa Textile & Steel v State of Orissa (2002).

steps.title: The 350-worker unit
steps.body:
1. 350 ≥ 300 → prior permission needed under the IR Code.
2. Apply 90 days before closure with reasons; serve copy on worker representatives.
3. Government hears parties; decides within 60 days or permission deemed granted.
4. On closure, pay each worker 15 days' average pay per completed year (plus notice pay) and re-skilling fund contribution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming the employer can close at will because it is losing money – above the threshold, permission is required.

activity.prompt: Order closure of a large establishment
items: Board decides to close the unit
Apply to the appropriate Government 90 days in advance

quiz.q: Under the IR Code, prior permission for closure applies to establishments with at least
quiz.why: The IR Code raises the threshold for special provisions to 300 workers.

quiz.q: If the Government does not decide a closure application within 60 days
quiz.why: The statute deems permission granted on expiry of sixty days.

quiz.q: Excel Wear v Union of India concerned
quiz.why: The Court struck down the original s.25-O as unreasonable under Art 19(1)(g).

questions.q: Strike notice must be given within how many days before striking (IR Code)?
questions.why: Notice must be given within sixty days before the strike.

questions.q: Strike barred during Board conciliation and for
questions.why: Section 23 bars strikes during and seven days after Board proceedings.

questions.q: Strike barred after conclusion of tribunal proceedings for
questions.why: Strikes are prohibited during and two months after adjudication.

questions.q: Continuous service in a mine for one year needs
questions.why: Section 25B(2) provides 190 days for underground mine workers.

questions.q: Basic+DA ₹15,600/month (26-day), 15 payable lay-off days — compensation
Normal lay-off compensation ceiling in 12 months
questions.why: Section 25C limits compensation to forty-five days unless otherwise agreed.

questions.q: Non-renewal of a fixed-term contract on expiry is
questions.why: Section 2(oo)(bb) excludes it when it is per the contract.

questions.q: Service 12 years 7 months, average pay ₹31,200 — retrenchment compensation (26-day)
questions.why: Seven months exceeds six so 13 years count; 15 days' pay is ₹18,000; 18,000 × 13 equals ₹2,34,000.

questions.q: Re-employment preference is in
questions.why: Section 25H gives retrenched workers preference when vacancies arise.

questions.q: Worker Re-skilling Fund contribution under the IR Code
options: 15 days' last drawn wages per retrenched worker
questions.why: Employers contribute fifteen days' last drawn wages for each retrenched worker.

questions.q: Closure application under s.25-O must be made
questions.why: The employer must apply at least ninety days before intended closure.

questions.q: 'Retrenchment' read widely in
questions.why: The Court held termination for any reason whatsoever, barring exceptions, is retrenchment.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Trade unions, standing orders and discipline
courses.summary: Registration, rights and immunities of trade unions, recognition of negotiating unions, standing orders, misconduct and domestic inquiry, Labour Court's power to modify punishment, protection during pendency of proceedings, and unfair labour practices.
outcomes: State the registration requirements for a trade union
Explain immunities from criminal conspiracy and civil suits
Compute negotiating-union status under the IR Code
Order the steps of a fair domestic inquiry
Apply s.11A and s.33 protections

lessons.title: Registration, rights and immunities of trade unions

scenes.text: Seven workers in a 1,200-worker factory want to register a union.
The Registrar asks for a membership count.

steps.title: Registration
steps.body: Any **seven or more** members may apply. On the date of application, the union must have at least **10% of workers or 100 workers, whichever is less**, engaged in the establishment/industry with which it is connected (Trade Unions Act as amended 2001; carried into the IR Code). Rules must provide for objects, funds, membership, office-bearers, audit, amendment and dissolution. Outsiders as office-bearers are limited (IR Code: not more than one-third or five, whichever is less, in the organised sector).

steps.title: Immunities and funds
steps.body:
- **Criminal conspiracy immunity**: no office-bearer or member is liable for criminal conspiracy for an agreement among members to further lawful objects, unless it is an agreement to commit an offence.
- **Civil immunity**: no civil suit for acts done in contemplation or furtherance of a **trade dispute** on the ground that it induces breach of contract or interferes with trade, unless the act is otherwise unlawful.
- Enforceability of agreements in restraint of trade.
- **General fund** for listed objects; separate **political fund** with voluntary contributions.

steps.title: Counting members
steps.body: Factory: 1,200 workers. 10% = 120; 100 is less → minimum **100 members** needed (plus at least 7 applicants). If the factory had 600 workers: 10% = 60 < 100 → **60 members** suffice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking immunity covers violence – it never protects acts that are otherwise unlawful.

activity.prompt: Tick what is needed to register a trade union
items: Membership of 10% or 100 of workers, whichever is less
Rules covering objects, funds and office-bearers

quiz.q: Factory with 450 workers — minimum members for registration
quiz.why: Ten per cent of 450 is 45, which is less than 100.

quiz.q: Union immunity from civil suits covers acts in furtherance of
quiz.why: Civil immunity applies to acts in contemplation or furtherance of a trade dispute.

quiz.q: Political fund contributions must be
quiz.why: No member can be compelled to contribute to the political fund.

lessons.title: Recognition of negotiating unions and standing orders

scenes.text: Three unions in a plant have 48%, 30% and 15% membership.
Management also needs certified standing orders for its 400 workers.

steps.title: Negotiating union (IR Code)
steps.body:
- A union with **51% or more** of workers on the muster roll is recognised as the **sole negotiating union**.
- If no union has 51%, a **negotiating council** is formed of unions having at least **20%** of workers each (one representative per 20%, per rules).
The ID Act had no central recognition provision; some States had their own laws (e.g., Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions Act, 1971).

steps.title: Standing orders
steps.body: Standing orders define conditions of employment: classification of workers, working hours, holidays, shift working, attendance, leave, termination, suspension, misconduct, grievance redressal. Under the **IR Code** they apply to establishments with **300 or more workers** (the Standing Orders Act applied at 100). Model standing orders apply until the employer's draft is certified by the certifying officer.

steps.title: The plant
steps.body:
No union has 51% → negotiating council of unions with ≥20%: Union A (48%) and Union B (30%) qualify; Union C (15%) does not.
400 workers ≥ 300 → standing orders required under the IR Code.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming the largest union is automatically sole negotiator – 51% is required.

activity.prompt: Order the certification of standing orders
items: Employer prepares draft (based on model standing orders)
Submit draft to the certifying officer
Certifying officer certifies with modifications if needed
Display certified standing orders at the workplace

quiz.q: Sole negotiating union needs at least
quiz.why: The IR Code requires 51% of workers on the muster roll.

quiz.q: Unions with 55%, 25%, 20% — negotiating status
options: Sole negotiating union is the 55% union
quiz.why: A union with 51% or more becomes the sole negotiating union.

quiz.q: Standing orders threshold under the IR Code
quiz.why: The IR Code applies standing-order provisions to establishments with 300 or more workers.

scenes.text: A cashier is accused of misappropriating ₹48,000 from the canteen counter.
The employer wants to dismiss him lawfully.

steps.title: Misconduct
steps.body: Acts listed in standing orders: theft, fraud or dishonesty; wilful insubordination; habitual absence or late attendance; riotous behaviour; taking bribes; habitual negligence; striking illegally. Misconduct must be proved in a fair **domestic inquiry** that complies with natural justice.

steps.title: Steps of a domestic inquiry
steps.body:
1. Preliminary investigation.
2. **Charge-sheet** – specific, with time to reply.
3. Suspension pending inquiry (subsistence allowance as per law/standing orders).
4. Appointment of an impartial **inquiry officer**; notice of hearing.
5. Management witnesses examined; **cross-examination** allowed; documents supplied.
6. Worker's defence evidence; may be assisted by a co-worker/union representative.
7. **Inquiry report** with findings and reasons; copy to worker (ECIL v B. Karunakar, 1993).
8. Punishment proportionate to misconduct, considering past record.

steps.title: The cashier
steps.body: Charge: misappropriation of ₹48,000 on specified dates. Evidence: cash registers, CCTV, witness of supervisor. Cashier cross-examines; produces his own records. Inquiry officer finds charge proved with reasons. Report served; cashier's comments considered; dismissal ordered. Proportionality: dishonesty involving cash generally justifies dismissal (loss of confidence).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not supplying the inquiry report before punishment – violates natural justice per B. Karunakar.

activity.prompt: Order a fair domestic inquiry
items: Hold inquiry with evidence and cross-examination
Prepare reasoned inquiry report and supply to worker

quiz.q: Supplying the inquiry report before punishment was required in
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench held the delinquent must get the report to respond.

quiz.q: A charge-sheet must be
quiz.why: Specific charges allow the worker to prepare a defence.

quiz.q: Misconduct is usually listed in
quiz.why: Certified or model standing orders enumerate acts of misconduct.

lessons.title: Section 11A, section 33 and unfair labour practices

scenes.text: A worker with 20 years' clean record is dismissed for being 15 minutes late twice.
Meanwhile, a wage dispute involving him is pending before the Tribunal.

steps.title: Section 11A
steps.body: In discharge/dismissal cases, the Labour Court/Tribunal may examine whether the punishment is justified and may **set aside** the order and direct **reinstatement** with or without conditions, or give **lesser punishment**. It acts on material on record and cannot take fresh evidence. (Workmen of Firestone Tyre v Management, 1973.) The IR Code retains a similar power.

steps.title: Section 33 – protection during pendency
steps.body:
During pendency of conciliation or adjudication: 
- No change in service conditions to the worker's prejudice in matters connected with the dispute, and no discharge/punishment for misconduct connected with the dispute, without **express written permission** of the authority.
- For matters **not connected**, the employer may discharge/dismiss but must pay **one month's wages** and apply for **approval** simultaneously (s.33(2)(b)). If approval is refused, the dismissal is void (Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank v Ram Gopal Sharma, 2002).
- **Protected workmen** (union office-bearers) have stronger protection (s.33(3)).

steps.title: Unfair labour practices
steps.body: The **Fifth Schedule** (ID Act) lists unfair labour practices by employers (e.g., interfering with union formation, victimisation, discharge for union activity, employing badlis/casuals for years to deny permanent status) and by workers/unions (e.g., coercion, violence, go-slow). They are prohibited and punishable.

steps.title: The late worker
steps.body:
1. Misconduct (two late arrivals) is minor; record clean for 20 years → dismissal shockingly disproportionate → s.11A: reinstatement with a lesser penalty (e.g., warning).
2. Dismissal while a dispute is pending, on an unconnected matter → employer had to pay one month's wages and seek approval under s.33(2)(b); failing that, dismissal is void.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating s.33(2)(b) approval as optional – without it, the order is void.

Keeping workers as casuals for years to deny permanent status

quiz.why: The Fifth Schedule enumerates unfair labour practices.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Wages, bonus and social security
courses.summary: Minimum wages and payment of wages under the Code on Wages, bonus computation, gratuity with worked computations, provident fund and ESI contributions, maternity benefit and employees' compensation under the Code on Social Security.
outcomes: Explain minimum wage fixation, floor wage and the uniform definition of wages
Compute minimum and maximum statutory bonus
Compute gratuity and apply eligibility rules
Compute EPF and ESI contributions
State maternity benefit entitlements

lessons.title: Minimum wages and payment of wages

scenes.text: A laundry pays a helper less than the State minimum wage, saying she 'agreed' to it.
It also deducts 60% of her pay for a damaged machine.

steps.title: Minimum wages
steps.body: The appropriate Government fixes minimum rates (time-rate, piece-rate) considering skill, arduousness, geographical area; reviewed ordinarily at intervals not exceeding **five years**. The Central Government fixes a **national floor wage**; State minimum wages cannot be below it. Paying less than the minimum wage amounts to **forced labour** under Art 23 (People's Union for Democratic Rights v Union of India, 1982 – Asiad case). An agreement to accept less is void.

steps.title: Uniform definition of 'wages'
steps.body: Wages include basic pay, DA and retaining allowance; they exclude items like HRA, conveyance, overtime, bonus, commission and employer PF contributions – but if the excluded items exceed **50%** of total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages (Code on Wages). This affects PF, gratuity and bonus calculations.

steps.title: Payment of wages
steps.body: Timelines: daily – end of shift; weekly – last working day of week; fortnightly – within 2 days of end of fortnight; monthly – within **7 days** of the next month. On removal/dismissal/resignation – within **2 working days**. Authorised deductions only (fines, absence, damage or loss, advances, taxes, etc.), and **total deductions cannot exceed 50%** of wages.

steps.title: The helper
steps.body:
1. Pay below minimum wage → offence; her 'agreement' is void; Art 23 also offended.
2. Deduction of 60% → exceeds the 50% cap → unlawful beyond 50%; damage deduction also requires a show-cause opportunity and must not exceed the loss.
3. Remedy: claim before the authority under the Code for the difference and compensation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating minimum wage as negotiable by contract.

activity.prompt: Tick correct statements on wages
items: Minimum wages cannot be below the national floor wage
An agreement to accept less than minimum wage is void
Total deductions cannot exceed 50% of wages
Monthly wages must be paid within 7 days of the next month

quiz.q: Paying less than minimum wage was held to be forced labour in
quiz.why: The Supreme Court linked below-minimum wages to Article 23.

quiz.q: Total remuneration ₹40,000: basic+DA ₹16,000, allowances ₹24,000. 'Wages' under the 50% rule
quiz.why: Exclusions may be at most ₹20,000 (50%), so the excess ₹4,000 is added to ₹16,000, giving ₹20,000.

quiz.q: Final wages on termination are due within
quiz.why: The Code on Wages requires payment within two working days.

scenes.text: A factory worker earns ₹15,000 a month; the computation ceiling is ₹7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher (assume ₹7,000).
What are the minimum and maximum bonus amounts?

steps.title: Rules (Payment of Bonus Act, carried into the Code on Wages)
steps.body:
- **Eligibility**: employee drawing wages up to the notified ceiling (₹21,000 per month under the 2015 amendment, or as notified) who worked at least **30 working days** in the accounting year.
- **Minimum bonus**: **8.33%** of wages or ₹100, whichever is higher, payable even without profits (subject to the scheme of 'allocable surplus' and set-on/set-off).
- **Maximum bonus**: **20%** of wages.
- **Computation ceiling**: wages for computing bonus are taken at ₹7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher (where wages exceed this).
- Payment within **8 months** of close of accounting year.
- **Disqualification**: dismissal for fraud, riotous/violent behaviour, theft/sabotage, or sexual harassment (under the Code).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying 8.33% to actual wages above the computation ceiling.

activity.prompt: Order the bonus computation
items: Check eligibility (wage ceiling and 30 working days)
Determine computation wage (ceiling or minimum wage, whichever higher)
Multiply by months worked to get annual bonus wages
Apply the declared rate between 8.33% and 20%
Pay within 8 months of close of the year

quiz.q: Minimum bonus on annual bonus wages of ₹96,000
Maximum statutory bonus rate
quiz.why: The law caps bonus at twenty per cent of wages.

quiz.q: Minimum working days for bonus eligibility
quiz.why: An employee must have worked at least thirty working days in the year.

scenes.text: Anand retires after 12 years 7 months; last drawn basic + DA is ₹52,000 per month.
His colleague, a fixed-term employee, leaves after 1 year 3 months.

steps.title: Eligibility
steps.body: Payable on termination after **continuous service of not less than five years** – on superannuation, retirement, resignation, death or disablement due to accident or disease. The five-year condition does **not** apply on **death or disablement**. Under the **Code on Social Security**, **fixed-term employees** get gratuity on a pro-rata basis after **one year** of service.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
Gratuity = **(15 ÷ 26) × last drawn monthly wages (basic + DA) × completed years of service**; a part year exceeding six months counts as a full year. Seasonal establishments: 7 days' wages per season. Piece-rated: average of last 3 months.
**Ceiling**: ₹20 lakh (as notified). Pay within **30 days** of becoming payable; otherwise simple interest. Forfeiture (wholly or partly) for termination due to wilful damage, riotous conduct or offence involving moral turpitude.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing by 30 instead of 26 – the statute uses 26 working days for monthly-rated employees.

activity.prompt: Order the gratuity computation
items: Check eligibility (5 years, or 1 year for fixed-term, or death/disablement)
Count completed years, rounding up parts over six months

quiz.q: Last wages ₹39,000, service 20 years 4 months — gratuity
quiz.why: Four months does not round up, so 20 years count; 39,000 ÷ 26 × 15 is 22,500, and 22,500 × 20 equals ₹4,50,000.

quiz.q: Is five years' service required on death?
quiz.why: The continuous-service condition does not apply on death or disablement.

quiz.q: Fixed-term employees under the Social Security Code get gratuity after
quiz.why: The Code provides pro-rata gratuity to fixed-term employees after one year.

lessons.title: Provident fund, ESI and maternity benefit

scenes.text: Priya's basic + DA is ₹25,000; her colleague Raju's gross wages are ₹18,000.
Priya also plans maternity leave for her first child.

steps.title: EPF
steps.body: Applies to establishments with **20 or more** employees (Code on Social Security). Employee contributes **12%** of basic + DA (+ retaining allowance); employer contributes **12%**, of which **8.33%** goes to the **Employees' Pension Scheme** subject to a wage ceiling of **₹15,000** (i.e., max ₹1,250/month), and the balance to the EPF account. (Certain establishments may have a 10% rate.)

steps.title: ESI
steps.body: Applies to establishments with **10 or more** employees in notified areas; employees with wages up to **₹21,000** per month are covered. Contribution rates (since July 2019): **employee 0.75%**, **employer 3.25%** of wages. Benefits: sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants', medical, funeral expenses, unemployment allowance.

steps.title: Maternity benefit
steps.body: Eligibility: at least **80 days'** work in the 12 months preceding expected delivery. Benefit: **26 weeks** (not more than 8 weeks before delivery) for the first two children; **12 weeks** for the third child onward. Adoptive mother (child below 3 months) and commissioning mother: **12 weeks**. **Crèche** facility for establishments with **50 or more** employees; work from home may be allowed by agreement. Dismissal during maternity absence is unlawful.

steps.title: Computations
steps.body:
Priya (EPF): employee 12% × 25,000 = **₹3,000**. Employer 12% = ₹3,000 → EPS 8.33% × 15,000 = **₹1,249.50 (≈ ₹1,250)**; EPF share = 3,000 − 1,250 = **₹1,750**.
Raju (ESI, wages ₹18,000 ≤ ₹21,000): employee 0.75% = **₹135**; employer 3.25% = **₹585**; total ₹720.
Priya's maternity: first child → **26 weeks** paid at her average daily wage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing EPS at 8.33% of full wages above ₹15,000 – the pension share is capped.

activity.prompt: Tick correct statements
items: EPF employee contribution is 12% of basic + DA
Employer's EPS share is capped at 8.33% of ₹15,000
ESI covers employees earning up to ₹21,000 a month
Maternity benefit for the first two children is 26 weeks

quiz.q: ESI contributions on wages of ₹20,000 (employee, employer)
Maternity benefit for a third child
quiz.why: For women with two or more surviving children the benefit is twelve weeks.

quiz.q: Basic+DA ₹30,000 — employer's EPF (non-pension) share
quiz.why: Employer's 12% is ₹3,600; EPS takes ₹1,250 (capped), leaving ₹2,350 for EPF.

questions.q: Minimum wage review interval ordinarily
questions.why: Rates are reviewed ordinarily at intervals not exceeding five years.

questions.q: Who fixes the national floor wage?
questions.why: The Code on Wages empowers the Central Government to fix the floor wage.

questions.q: Deductions from wages are capped at
questions.why: Total deductions cannot exceed fifty per cent of wages.

questions.q: Annual bonus wages ₹72,000 — maximum bonus
Bonus must be paid within
questions.why: Payment is due within eight months of the close of the accounting year.

questions.q: Last wages ₹65,000, 25 years 9 months — gratuity
questions.why: Nine months rounds up to 26 years; 65,000 ÷ 26 × 15 is 37,500, and 37,500 × 26 equals ₹9,75,000.

questions.q: Gratuity ceiling
questions.why: The statutory ceiling is ₹20 lakh as notified.

questions.q: EPF coverage threshold
questions.why: EPF applies to establishments employing twenty or more persons.

questions.q: Employer ESI rate
questions.why: Since July 2019 the employer rate is 3.25%.

questions.q: Crèche facility is mandatory for establishments with
questions.why: The 2017 amendment requires crèches where fifty or more are employed.

questions.q: Minimum days of work for maternity benefit
questions.why: A woman must have worked at least eighty days in the preceding twelve months.

questions.q: Gratuity divisor for monthly-rated employees
questions.why: The formula uses fifteen days' wages computed on twenty-six working days.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Occupational safety, contract labour, child labour, POSH and employees' compensation
courses.summary: Factories and working conditions under the OSH Code, contract labour regulation and principal employer liability, prohibition of child labour, prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace, and employer liability for employment injuries.
outcomes: Apply the factory thresholds and working-hour limits under the OSH Code
Explain principal employer obligations for contract labour
State the prohibitions on child and adolescent labour
Order the POSH complaint process and time limits
Apply the 'arising out of and in the course of employment' test

lessons.title: Factories, working hours and safety (OSH Code)

scenes.text: A power-using workshop with 25 workers runs 12-hour shifts six days a week, paying single rate for extra hours.
There is no guard on a dangerous press.

steps.title: Factory and occupier
steps.body: Under the OSH Code a **factory** is premises where a manufacturing process is carried on with **20 or more workers with power** or **40 or more without power** (the Factories Act used 10 and 20). The **occupier** (person with ultimate control; for a company, a director – J.K. Industries v Chief Inspector of Factories, 1996) is responsible for safety, health and welfare.

steps.title: Working hours and duties
steps.body:
- Daily limit **8 hours**; weekly **48 hours**; spread-over and rest intervals as prescribed; weekly holiday.
- **Overtime**: at **twice the ordinary rate** of wages, with worker's consent, within prescribed quarterly limits.
- Women may work at night with consent and safeguards as prescribed.
- Safety: fencing of machinery, protection of eyes, precautions against fire and dangerous fumes; health: cleanliness, ventilation, drinking water, latrines; welfare: canteens, crèches, first aid; annual health check-up as prescribed.

steps.title: The workshop
steps.body:
1. 25 workers with power ≥ 20 → factory under the OSH Code.
2. 12 × 6 = 72 hours/week → 24 hours overtime beyond 48; must be paid at **double rate** and within limits.
If ordinary hourly wage is ₹100: overtime pay = 24 × 200 = **₹4,800** per week (not 24 × 100 = ₹2,400).
3. Unguarded press → breach of safety duties; occupier liable to penalty.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the old 10/20 worker thresholds for events after the Codes came into force.

activity.prompt: Tick duties of an occupier
items: Pay overtime at twice the ordinary rate
Limit normal hours to 8 a day and 48 a week

quiz.q: Overtime of 10 hours at ordinary rate ₹120/hour pays
quiz.why: Overtime is at twice the ordinary rate, so 10 × ₹240 equals ₹2,400.

quiz.q: A company's occupier must be a director per
options: J.K. Industries v Chief Inspector of Factories
quiz.why: The Supreme Court held only a director can be named occupier of a company's factory.

quiz.q: OSH Code factory threshold with power
quiz.why: The OSH Code raised the threshold to twenty workers where power is used.

scenes.text: A contractor supplies 60 security guards to a hospital and stops paying wages for two months.
At another site, a 13-year-old is found working at a brick kiln.

steps.title: Contract labour
steps.body: The OSH Code regulates establishments and contractors employing **50 or more** contract workers (earlier 20). Principal employer must be registered; contractor must hold a licence (a single licence can cover multiple States). Contractor pays wages; if he fails, the **principal employer must pay** and may recover from the contractor. Welfare facilities (canteen, rest rooms, drinking water) must be ensured. Core activities: contract labour is generally prohibited in **core activities**, with exceptions. **SAIL v National Union Waterfront Workers (2001)**: abolition of contract labour does **not** automatically make workers employees of the principal employer, unless the contract is a sham.

steps.title: Child and adolescent labour
steps.body: **Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986** (as amended 2016): **children below 14** cannot be employed in any occupation or process, except helping family enterprises (outside school hours, non-hazardous) and as child artists with safeguards. **Adolescents (14–18)** cannot be employed in hazardous occupations/processes listed in the Schedule. Offences are cognizable. Also Art 24 and Art 21A (right to education 6–14). M.C. Mehta v State of TN (1996) directed a welfare fund and compensation of ₹20,000 per child by offending employers.

steps.title: Applying
steps.body:
Guards: 60 ≥ 50 → OSH Code contract labour provisions apply → hospital (principal employer) must pay two months' arrears and recover from contractor.
Brick kiln: 13-year-old → child below 14 → prohibited employment; employer prosecuted; rescue and rehabilitation; brick kilns are hazardous for adolescents too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming automatic absorption of contract workers on abolition – SAIL (2001) rejected it.

activity.prompt: Tick obligations of a principal employer of contract labour
items: Ensure wages are paid; pay if the contractor defaults

quiz.q: Automatic absorption on abolition of contract labour was rejected in
options: SAIL v National Union Waterfront Workers
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench held no automatic absorption follows abolition.

quiz.q: Employment of a child below 14 in a shop is
quiz.why: The 2016 amendment bans employment of children below 14 in all occupations except narrow family and artist exceptions.

quiz.q: If a contractor fails to pay wages, liability falls on
quiz.why: The principal employer must pay and may recover from the contractor.

lessons.title: Prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace (POSH Act, 2013)

scenes.text: An employee receives repeated unwelcome messages from her team lead; the last incident was 2 months ago.
Her company has 60 employees.

steps.title: Background and scope
steps.body: **Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997)** laid down guidelines treating sexual harassment as violating Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21. The **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013** codifies them. 'Sexual harassment' includes unwelcome physical contact, demand for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, showing pornography, other unwelcome conduct of sexual nature; 'workplace' includes places visited during employment, including transport.

steps.title: Machinery and timelines
steps.body:
- **Internal Committee (IC)** in every workplace with **10 or more** employees: Presiding Officer – a senior woman employee; at least two employee members; one **external member** from an NGO or familiar with women's issues; at least half the members women.
- **Local Committee** at district level for smaller workplaces and complaints against the employer.
- Complaint within **3 months** of the last incident (extendable by another 3 months for reasons).
- **Conciliation** may be attempted at the aggrieved woman's request (no monetary settlement as basis).
- Inquiry to be completed within **90 days**; report within **10 days** thereafter; employer acts within **60 days**.
- Penalty on employer for not constituting IC: up to ₹50,000.

steps.title: The complaint
steps.body:
1. 60 employees → IC must exist.
2. Last incident 2 months ago → within 3 months ✔.
3. Written complaint to IC → notice to respondent → inquiry with natural justice → report within 10 days of completion → employer acts (e.g., written apology, withholding promotion, termination) within 60 days.
4. Interim relief: transfer or leave for the complainant during inquiry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking the IC can be all-internal – an external member is mandatory.

activity.prompt: Order the POSH complaint process
items: Complaint filed within 3 months of the last incident
Employer acts on recommendations within 60 days

quiz.q: IC is mandatory for workplaces with at least
quiz.why: Section 4 requires an Internal Committee where ten or more are employed.

quiz.q: Inquiry must be completed within
quiz.why: Section 11(4) requires completion within ninety days.

quiz.q: Guidelines that preceded the POSH Act came from
quiz.why: Vishaka laid down binding guidelines in 1997.

lessons.title: Employees' compensation for injury and disease

scenes.text: A delivery worker is injured while delivering parcels on his assigned route; another worker is hurt while drunk at work.
Who can claim compensation from the employer?

steps.title: Liability
steps.body: Employer is liable to pay compensation for **personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment** (Employees' Compensation Act, 1923, now in the Code on Social Security). Accidents while commuting between residence and workplace are covered under the Code subject to conditions. **Occupational diseases** listed in the schedule are deemed injuries by accident.

steps.title: Tests and defences
steps.body:
- **'In the course of'**: time, place and activity related to employment (notional extension – e.g., arriving through employer's premises; Saurashtra Salt Mfg. Co v Bai Valu Raja, 1958).
- **'Arising out of'**: causal connection between employment and injury.
- **Defences** (for injury not resulting in death or permanent total disablement): worker was **under the influence of drink or drugs**; **wilful disobedience** of safety orders/rules; **wilful removal or disregard** of a safety device.
- Payment as soon as due; delay beyond one month may attract interest and penalty.

steps.title: The two workers
steps.body:
Delivery worker: injury on assigned route during duty → in the course of and arising out of employment → compensation payable.
Drunk worker: if injury causes temporary disablement → employer may use the drink defence. If he dies or suffers permanent total disablement, the defence is **not** available.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying the drunkenness defence to death cases.

activity.prompt: Order the analysis of an employment injury claim
items: Was the person an employee under the law?
Did the injury occur by accident or scheduled occupational disease?
Was it in the course of employment (time, place, activity)?
Did it arise out of employment (causal link)?
Is any statutory defence available, given the injury type?

quiz.why: The statutory defences do not apply to death or permanent total disablement.

quiz.why: The Supreme Court discussed notional extension of time and place in Saurashtra Salt.

quiz.q: Scheduled occupational diseases are
quiz.why: Contracting a scheduled disease in specified employment is deemed an injury by accident.
